projects.name: Plant SOS
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop to the XIAO ESP32-C3 (5V); the XIAO's onboard regulator powers the OLED from its 3.3V rail, and the soil sensor's VCC is gated by a GPIO (D2) so it only sees 3.3V during the ~10 ms read window.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Stick the two metal prongs into your plant's dirt. A tiny screen shows a happy face when the soil is wet, a sleepy face when it's getting dry, and a crying face when the plant is thirsty - and a red LED blinks at you until you water it.

**Why it's fun**: Your plant basically gets a face and tells you how it feels. Spit on the prongs, dunk them in a glass of water, hold them in the air - the little face changes right in front of you like the plant is reacting to what you do.

## Parts list

- 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED)
- 1x Soil Moisture Sensor (the two-prong probe + small comparator board; we only use the analog "AO" pin)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (the little blue/white screen; talks over 2 wires)
- 1x LED 5mm Red (the "thirsty" warning blinker) - the legs plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed
- 1x Resistor 220R (current limit for the red LED - never wire an LED straight to a GPIO) - leads plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (no soldering - everything plugs in)
- Jumper wires M-M (for the OLED and sensor connections - not for the LED itself)

## Wiring notes

Power rails first:

- XIAO **3V3** pin -> breadboard red (+) rail
- XIAO **GND** pin -> breadboard blue (-) rail

OLED (I2C, 4 wires - it shares the same 2 data lines no matter how many I2C things you add later):

- OLED **VCC** -> red rail (3.3V)
- OLED **GND** -> blue rail
- OLED **SDA** -> XIAO **D4** (GPIO 6, the default SDA on XIAO ESP32-C3)
- OLED **SCL** -> XIAO **D5** (GPIO 7, the default SCL on XIAO ESP32-C3)

Most 0.96" SSD1306 modules answer at I2C address **0x3C**, but a meaningful minority ship at **0x3D** (sometimes selectable by a resistor jumper on the back of the board). The sketch tries 0x3C first, then 0x3D, and prints which one worked over Serial - so you don't have to guess.

Soil sensor (analog - we read a voltage that changes with moisture):

- Sensor **VCC** -> XIAO **D2** (GPIO 4) - **not** the 3.3V rail. The sketch turns this pin on for ~10 ms around each reading and off in between. Continuously powering a resistive probe electrolyses the metal prongs and they corrode in weeks; gating the supply slows that down dramatically.
- Sensor **GND** -> blue rail
- Sensor **AO** -> XIAO **D0** (GPIO 2, an ADC-capable pin)
- The sensor's **DO** pin is left disconnected - that one is just an on/off threshold and we want the smooth analog value instead.
- Most common 4-pin LM393 boards happily accept 3.3V on VCC, which is what D2 supplies. A rare variant has an on-board 3-pin regulator and insists on 5V - if your board's silkscreen says "5V only", wire VCC to the XIAO's **5V** pin instead and accept the corrosion trade-off (or use a transistor to gate the 5V line).

Red LED (active-high - "HIGH = on"):

- XIAO **D1** (GPIO 3) -> one leg of the 220R resistor
- Other leg of the 220R -> long leg (anode, +) of the red LED
- Short leg (cathode, -) of the LED -> blue rail (GND)
- The LED legs and the resistor leads plug straight into the breadboard tie-points. No jumper wires for this part.

Sanity check before plugging in USB: LED short leg goes to GND, and there is exactly one resistor in series with the LED.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click **OK**.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type **esp32**, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download - grab a snack.
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the list.
4. Install the two screen libraries. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and:
   - Search **Adafruit GFX** and install **"Adafruit GFX Library"** by Adafruit.
   - Search **Adafruit SSD1306** and install **"Adafruit SSD1306"** by Adafruit. If it asks to install dependencies (like Adafruit BusIO), click **Install All**.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the XIAO into your laptop with a **USB-C cable**. The tiny orange LED on the XIAO should light up. (If nothing lights up, try a different cable - lots of cheap USB-C cables are charge-only with no data wires.)
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared. On Windows it is **COM3**/**COM4**/**COM5**; on a Mac it is **/dev/cu.usbmodem...**; on Linux it is **/dev/ttyACM0**. Unplug-and-replug to see which port disappears and comes back - that one is yours.
3. There are no WiFi passwords or secrets to fill in for this sketch - nothing to edit. (You can tune `WET_BELOW` and `DRY_ABOVE` near the top later, but leave them alone for the first run.)
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-pointing arrow). The status bar shows **"Compiling..."** for 30-60 seconds, then **"Uploading..."**. If it hangs at "Connecting..." for more than 10 seconds, **press and hold the small B (BOOT) button on the XIAO, tap the R (RESET) button next to it, then let go of B**. That forces flashing mode. After the first successful upload you almost never need this trick again.
5. When you see **"Done uploading"**, open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate dropdown on the right to **115200** (must match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch or you get gibberish).
6. **What should happen:** The OLED lights up with a face within a second or two. The Serial Monitor prints `OLED found at 0x3C` (or `0x3D`) and then a moisture number every second, like `soil raw: 3100`. Now the fun part - pinch the prongs with wet fingers or dunk them in a glass of water: the number changes a lot, and the face changes from crying to sleepy to happy. Hold the prongs in the air and the red LED starts blinking once per second to say "I'm thirsty!"

**Common gotchas:**

- **Stuck on "Connecting..." during upload.** Do the **BOOT + RESET** dance from step 4: hold **B**, tap **R**, release **B**, then click Upload again.
- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish.** Baud rate dropdown is wrong - set it to **115200**.
- **OLED stays completely black but Serial Monitor prints sensor numbers.** Either SDA and SCL are swapped (SDA goes to **D4**, SCL goes to **D5**), or the sketch says "OLED not found" - meaning the screen isn't being detected at 0x3C or 0x3D. Re-check the VCC and GND wires to the screen.
- **Face never changes - always the same expression.** Your sensor's polarity is reversed. Watch `soil raw:` in Serial: dunk the prongs in water, then hold them in air. If **air gives a smaller number than water**, change `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW = true;` to `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW = false;` near the top and upload again.
## Talking points

- Soil sensors work by measuring how easily electricity flows between the two prongs. Wet soil conducts; dry soil resists. The little board on the sensor converts that into a voltage on the AO pin. On the most common (LM393) boards a wet probe gives a **low** number and a dry probe gives a **high** number, but a few clones (and most capacitive replacements) flip that. The code has a `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` flag at the top - watch the Serial Monitor while you dunk the probe in water vs. hold it in air, and flip the flag if the relationship is reversed. The thresholds below it stay readable either way.
- The ESP32-C3 ADC turns that voltage into a number between **0 and 4095** (12 bits). We map "raw number" -> "happiness" with two thresholds.
- I2C is wonderful: SDA + SCL + power, and you can chain more sensors on the same two wires later (each with a unique address). Each device has its own address - that's why we needed to find the OLED at 0x3C or 0x3D.
- The face is drawn with three primitives: two filled circles for eyes, and either the bottom half of a circle (smile), a straight line (sleepy), or the top half of a circle plus two tear drops (crying). The "half a circle" trick uses `drawCircleHelper`, which is Adafruit_GFX's quadrant-selectable arc - cheaper than drawing a full circle and clipping.
- The LED only blinks when truly thirsty. A solid LED would be annoying; blinking screams "do something" without being constant.

## Things to change once it works

- **Calibrate the thresholds.** The defaults in the sketch are a starting guess. Hold the probe in air -> note the number printed to Serial; that's your "very dry". Stick it in a glass of water -> note that number; that's "very wet". Pick thresholds about a third and two-thirds of the way between. (And confirm which end is which - that's what `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` is for.)
- Plant the probe to the depth shown on the prongs (about 4 cm). Deeper isn't better - the metal contacts must stay above the water line of the pot's drainage saucer.
- Swap to a **capacitive** soil sensor when the resistive prongs corrode (gated power buys you weeks-to-months instead of weeks, but capacitive probes don't corrode at all). Same wiring, just better hardware - and remember to recheck `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW`, capacitive boards often invert.
- Add a buzzer on another GPIO for an audible "feed me" chirp once a day instead of just the LED.
- Have the XIAO publish moisture to MQTT once the Orange Pi is online, so the plant's mood appears on a phone dashboard.
- Add a small smoothing average (e.g. 10 readings) so a single noisy sample doesn't flip the face.

## Why this is interesting

It turns an invisible thing (soil moisture) into something a 10-year-old can read at a glance. There's a real, immediate consequence: water the plant and the face changes. It's also a clean introduction to the two most useful sensor categories - **analog** (a voltage you read with `analogRead`) and **I2C** (a digital bus you talk to with a library) - in the same small project, plus one quietly important trick (gating sensor power from a GPIO) that the same beginner can reuse on every battery-or-corrosion-sensitive sensor they meet next.

projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (5V in). The ESP32's VIN pin re-exposes that 5V to power the MAX7219 matrix; the ESP32's onboard 3V3 regulator powers the SW-420 sensor and drives the GPIO logic.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Thump the table next to it. A yellow lamp lights up while it counts your shakes, then a tiny 8x8 grid of red lights draws a bar graph showing how big your "earthquake" was, with a label that scrolls past like "TINY TREMOR" or "GODZILLA".

**Why it's fun**: It is basically a Richter scale for whacking the desk. Take turns with your dad or your brother and see who can pound out the biggest quake without knocking the breadboard off the table.

## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain)
- 1x SW-420 vibration switch module (the "earthquake" sensor)
- 1x 8x8 LED matrix with MAX7219 driver board (the display)
- 1x yellow LED (the warning lamp that lights while a quake is being measured)
- 1x 220 ohm resistor (current-limit for the yellow LED)
- 1x breadboard, ~12 DuPont jumpers
- 1x USB cable (laptop to ESP32; this is also where the 5V for the matrix comes from)

## Wiring notes

Two power rails this time, not one. Bring the ESP32's `3V3` pin to one red breadboard strip, and the ESP32's `VIN` pin (which is the USB 5V passing through the board) to a *separate* red strip. Tie `GND` to the blue strip - both rails share ground.

- **8x8 LED matrix (MAX7219):** `VCC` to the **5V / VIN** rail, NOT 3V3. The MAX7219 datasheet wants 4.0 to 5.5 V; running it on 3.3 V is folk wisdom and can brown out the ESP32's onboard regulator when the panel lights up. `GND` to GND. `DIN` to `GPIO 23` (MOSI), `CS` to `GPIO 5`, `CLK` to `GPIO 18` (SCK). The MAX7219 reads anything above ~2 V as HIGH, so the ESP32's 3.3 V logic signals drive it fine directly.
- **SW-420 module:** `VCC` to **3V3**, `GND` to GND, `DO` (digital out) to ESP32 `GPIO 27`. The little blue trim-pot on the module sets the trigger threshold - if it triggers constantly even when still, turn that pot clockwise until the on-board "trigger" LED only blinks when you actually tap the board.
- **Yellow LED:** long leg (anode) through the 220 ohm resistor to `GPIO 26`. Short leg (cathode) to GND. The resistor stops the LED from burning out.
- Keep the SW-420 mounted firmly on the breadboard - if it dangles on jumper wires, the wires themselves will jiggle and trigger false quakes.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a chunky download, give it a couple of minutes.
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> ESP32 Dev Module**. That is the right pick for the NodeMCU-32S.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries**, type `MD_MAX72XX` in the search box, and install **"MD_MAX72XX" by majicDesigns**. This is the library that talks to the 8x8 matrix; without it the sketch will not compile.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a USB cable. The NodeMCU-32S uses a **Micro-USB** cable (the small flat one, same shape as on older phones). Make sure it is a *data* cable, not a charge-only cable - if the laptop does not go "ding" when you plug it in, try a different cable.
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in (on Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`, on Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*`). If nothing new shows up, unplug and re-plug the cable.
3. There are no WiFi passwords or secrets to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline, so you can skip straight to upload.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a bit, then "Connecting...". If you see a row of dots and dashes that never finishes (`....____....____`), hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until you see "Writing at 0x..." start scrolling, then let go. Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-reset and do not need this, but if yours is stubborn, the BOOT-button trick fixes it every time.
5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200** (that is what `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch expects - any other number gives you garbled junk).
6. Tap the breadboard with your finger. The yellow LED should snap on, and the 8x8 matrix should start drawing a little bar graph. After 10 seconds the bar freezes for a beat, then a label like `MOUSE FART` or `BUMP` scrolls across the matrix and the yellow LED switches off. You should also see the pulse count print in the Serial Monitor each round. If you see all of that, it worked!

**Common gotchas:**

- **Display looks scrambled, mirrored, or upside-down.** Cheap 8x8 matrix modules come wired in four different layouts. Find the line `#define HARDWARE_TYPE MD_MAX72XX::FC16_HW` near the top of the sketch and try the other three values in the comment above it (`GENERIC_HW`, `PAROLA_HW`, `ICSTATION_HW`), re-uploading after each change, until the bar graph draws upright.
- **Yellow LED never lights.** Long leg (anode) goes through the 220 ohm resistor to GPIO 26, short leg (cathode) goes to GND. If it is in backwards, no damage - just pull it out, flip it around, and push it back in.
- **The matrix triggers a quake the instant power touches it, without you tapping anything.** The little blue trim-pot on the SW-420 module is too sensitive. Turn it clockwise a quarter-turn at a time until the on-board trigger LED only blinks when you actually tap the breadboard.
- **Upload fails with "Failed to connect to ESP32: Timed out waiting for packet header".** Almost always the BOOT-button trick from step 4 - hold BOOT until "Writing at..." appears, then let go.
## Safety notes

Nothing in this build runs above 5 V, so the mains-safety warnings that apply to the 2-channel relay project explicitly do NOT apply here. The only real hazards are: (a) backwards LED polarity will simply not light, no damage; (b) shorting 5V to GND on the breadboard will trip the laptop's USB port protection but not hurt the ESP32. Unplug USB before re-wiring anything.

## Talking points

- The SW-420 isn't really a "sensor" in the analog sense - it's a tiny spring around a pin that briefly closes a circuit when shaken. So we don't measure shake *strength*, we count shake *pulses* per unit time. Lots of pulses in 10 seconds = bigger quake.
- We use a hardware *interrupt* on the sensor pin. Interrupts let the chip drop whatever it's doing the instant a pulse arrives and bump a counter. That way we never miss a bump even while the matrix is busy drawing. The interrupt is armed only *after* the boot animation, so bumps during startup don't trick the board into thinking a quake started before you arrived.
- The bar graph is drawn column by column. Eight columns, eight "Richter" levels. Each level also gets a label that scrolls across afterwards using a small built-in font.
- 25 ms debounce: a single physical tap can ring the spring several times within a few milliseconds. We ignore extra pulses inside a 25 ms window so one tap counts as one bump.
- We deliberately stick to the low-level `MD_MAX72XX` library and write the scrolling text by hand instead of mixing in the higher-level `MD_Parola`. Mixing the two on the same panel can cause one library's internal buffer to overwrite the other's drawing - confusing to debug as a beginner.

## Things to change once it works

- If the matrix shows garbled, scrambled, mirrored or upside-down output, change `HARDWARE_TYPE` in the code. Try `GENERIC_HW`, then `PAROLA_HW`, then `ICSTATION_HW` until it looks right. This is the single biggest gotcha with cheap matrix modules.
- Lower the SW-420 sensitivity pot (turn clockwise) to make it harder to trigger - then you have to really thump the table to reach "GODZILLA".
- Add a second LED (red) for "BIG ONE" and above, so the warning lamp escalates.
- Replace the verdict labels with funny ones aimed at Andy's son.
- Once the Orange Pi is online, publish each quake's count + level to MQTT so the Pi can keep a high-score table.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project that *reacts* to the physical world instead of timing or button presses. It teaches three new ideas at once: reading a digital sensor through an interrupt, accumulating events over a time window, and driving a real graphical display (the 8x8 matrix) with a library. And the feedback loop is irresistible: you hit the table, the matrix lights up, you hit it harder, it scrolls "GODZILLA". Hard to put down.

<![CDATA[// Earthquake Cam
// ESP32 NodeMCU + SW-420 vibration switch + MAX7219 8x8 LED matrix + warning LED.
// On any shake, count the bumps over a 10-second window and show a Richter-style
// bar graph + a verdict label ("MOUSE FART" ... "GODZILLA").
//
// Library needed (install once in Arduino IDE Library Manager):
//   "MD_MAX72XX"  by majicDesigns
//
// Arduino IDE board:  ESP32 Arduino > ESP32 Dev Module
//
// POWER NOTE: the matrix VCC goes to the ESP32's 5V / VIN pin (USB-powered),
// NOT to 3V3. The MAX7219 datasheet wants 4.0 to 5.5 V. The ESP32 GPIO logic
// is 3.3 V but the MAX7219 reads anything above ~2 V as HIGH, so direct
// connections from GPIO to DIN/CS/CLK work fine.

#include <SPI.h>
#include <MD_MAX72xx.h>

// ---- Pin map (matches the wiring diagram) ----
const int PIN_SW420    = 27;   // SW-420 digital OUT
const int PIN_LED_WARN = 26;   // Yellow warning LED through 220R
const int PIN_MATRIX_CS = 5;   // MAX7219 CS / LOAD
// MOSI = GPIO 23, SCK = GPIO 18 (hardware SPI defaults on ESP32)

// ---- Matrix config ----
// If the display looks garbled, scrambled, mirrored, or upside-down,
// try the OTHER values below in order. This single line is the #1
// thing that varies between cheap 8x8 modules.
//   FC16_HW       <- most common on "FC-16" red modules (try first)
//   GENERIC_HW    <- many no-name eBay/Aliexpress modules
//   PAROLA_HW     <- original Parola-branded boards
//   ICSTATION_HW  <- IcStation-branded boards
#define HARDWARE_TYPE MD_MAX72XX::FC16_HW
#define MAX_DEVICES   1
MD_MAX72XX matrix = MD_MAX72XX(HARDWARE_TYPE, PIN_MATRIX_CS, MAX_DEVICES);

// ---- Event counting ----
const unsigned long WINDOW_MS   = 10000UL;   // 10 second measuring window
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 25UL;      // ignore re-triggers inside this gap

volatile unsigned long lastPulseMs = 0;
volatile unsigned int  pulseCount  = 0;

void IRAM_ATTR onShake() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastPulseMs >= DEBOUNCE_MS) {
    lastPulseMs = now;
    pulseCount++;
  }
}

// Map a count to a 1..8 "Richter" level for the bar graph.
int countToLevel(unsigned int count) {
  if (count <= 1)   return 1;
  if (count <= 3)   return 2;
  if (count <= 6)   return 3;
  if (count <= 10)  return 4;
  if (count <= 18)  return 5;
  if (count <= 30)  return 6;
  if (count <= 50)  return 7;
  return 8;
}

const char* levelToVerdict(int level) {
  switch (level) {
    case 1: return "MOUSE FART";
    case 2: return "TIPTOE";
    case 3: return "BUMP";
    case 4: return "STOMP";
    case 5: return "TRUCK";
    case 6: return "QUAKE";
    case 7: return "BIG ONE";
    default: return "GODZILLA";
  }
}

// ---- Tiny 5x7 font for the scrolling verdict (uppercase + space only). ----
// Each glyph is 5 columns wide; bit 0 = top row, bit 6 = bottom row.
struct Glyph { char c; uint8_t col[5]; };
const Glyph FONT[] = {
  {' ', {0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00}},
  {'A', {0x7E,0x11,0x11,0x11,0x7E}},
  {'B', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x36}},
  {'C', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x22}},
  {'D', {0x7F,0x41,0x41,0x22,0x1C}},
  {'E', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x41}},
  {'F', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x01}},
  {'G', {0x3E,0x41,0x49,0x49,0x7A}},
  {'H', {0x7F,0x08,0x08,0x08,0x7F}},
  {'I', {0x00,0x41,0x7F,0x41,0x00}},
  {'K', {0x7F,0x08,0x14,0x22,0x41}},
  {'L', {0x7F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x40}},
  {'M', {0x7F,0x02,0x0C,0x02,0x7F}},
  {'N', {0x7F,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x7F}},
  {'O', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x3E}},
  {'P', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x06}},
  {'Q', {0x3E,0x41,0x51,0x21,0x5E}},
  {'R', {0x7F,0x09,0x19,0x29,0x46}},
  {'S', {0x46,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x31}},
  {'T', {0x01,0x01,0x7F,0x01,0x01}},
  {'U', {0x3F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x3F}},
  {'Z', {0x61,0x51,0x49,0x45,0x43}},
};

const uint8_t* glyphFor(char c) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(FONT)/sizeof(FONT[0]); i++) {
    if (FONT[i].c == c) return FONT[i].col;
  }
  return FONT[0].col;  // space if missing
}

// Build a column buffer for a whole message: 5 cols per glyph + 1 blank gap,
// plus 8 blank cols of padding at the start and end so it scrolls cleanly.
size_t buildMessage(const char* msg, uint8_t* out, size_t outCap) {
  size_t n = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  for (const char* p = msg; *p && n + 6 < outCap; p++) {
    const uint8_t* g = glyphFor(*p);
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) out[n++] = g[i];
    out[n++] = 0x00;
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  return n;
}

// Scroll a 1..N column buffer across the 8-column matrix, ~60 ms per step.
void scrollColumns(const uint8_t* cols, size_t n) {
  for (size_t start = 0; start + 8 <= n; start++) {
    matrix.clear();
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
      matrix.setColumn(7 - c, cols[start + c]);
    }
    delay(60);
  }
}

// Draw a vertical bar graph: `level` columns lit from the left, full height.
void drawBar(int level) {
  matrix.clear();
  for (int col = 0; col < level && col < 8; col++) {
    matrix.setColumn(col, 0xFF);   // light all 8 rows in this column
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(200);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println(F("Earthquake Cam booting..."));

  pinMode(PIN_LED_WARN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);

  // INPUT_PULLUP is defensive: most SW-420 breakouts have an LM393 comparator
  // with its own pull-up, but bare-module variants without the comparator
  // need the MCU to pull the line high. Adding INPUT_PULLUP is harmless on
  // the comparator boards and saves the bare ones.
  pinMode(PIN_SW420, INPUT_PULLUP);

  matrix.begin();
  matrix.control(MD_MAX72XX::INTENSITY, 4);   // 0..15
  matrix.clear();

  // Friendly boot "READY" scroll BEFORE we arm the interrupt, so that bumps
  // landing during setup don't leave a stale pulseCount > 0 when loop() starts.
  uint8_t buf[64];
  size_t n = buildMessage("READY", buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // Now arm the shake interrupt and zero the counter for a clean start.
  pulseCount  = 0;
  lastPulseMs = 0;
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(PIN_SW420), onShake, FALLING);

  Serial.println(F("Ready. Bump the sensor to start a measurement."));
}

void loop() {
  // Idle: wait for the very first pulse to open a measurement window.
  if (pulseCount == 0) {
    delay(10);
    return;
  }

  // A shake just happened. Light the warning LED and count for WINDOW_MS.
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, HIGH);
  unsigned long windowStart = millis();
  Serial.println(F("Quake window opened."));

  // Show a small "live" tick on the matrix while counting (column 0 blinks).
  bool tick = false;
  unsigned long lastTickMs = 0;
  while (millis() - windowStart < WINDOW_MS) {
    if (millis() - lastTickMs >= 250) {
      lastTickMs = millis();
      tick = !tick;
      matrix.clear();
      matrix.setColumn(0, tick ? 0x18 : 0x00);  // middle two rows blink
    }
    delay(5);
  }

  // Snapshot the count, then reset for the next quake.
  noInterrupts();
  unsigned int finalCount = pulseCount;
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();

  int level = countToLevel(finalCount);
  const char* verdict = levelToVerdict(level);

  Serial.print(F("Pulses in window: "));
  Serial.print(finalCount);
  Serial.print(F("  ->  level "));
  Serial.print(level);
  Serial.print(F("  ("));
  Serial.print(verdict);
  Serial.println(F(")"));

  // Show the bar graph for 2 seconds...
  drawBar(level);
  delay(2000);

  // ...then scroll the verdict label across the matrix once.
  matrix.clear();
  uint8_t buf[96];
  size_t n = buildMessage(verdict, buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // All done. Turn the warning lamp off and go back to idle.
  // Drain any pulses that arrived during the display so we don't immediately
  // re-trigger from the user celebrating their GODZILLA score.
  noInterrupts();
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);
  Serial.println(F("Quake window closed. Waiting for the next bump."));
}

projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via the board's USB port, 3.3V on the GPIO header)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Four colored LEDs flash a pattern at you - red, yellow, green, blue. You press the buttons underneath in the exact same order. Get it right and the pattern grows by one. Get it wrong and the game is over.

**Why it's fun**: It is the classic Simon Says toy, but YOU built it. Challenge your dad to see who can remember the longest sequence, and watch the flashes get faster and faster until your brain melts.

## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - runs the state machine and the randomizer)
- 1x Red, 1x Yellow, 1x Green, 1x Blue 5mm LED (the four "Simon" pads)
- 4x 220 ohm resistors (one in series with each LED so the LED does not burn out)
- 4x tactile push-buttons (one under each LED)
- 1x breadboard, ~18 DuPont jumpers
- USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (also how power gets in)

No external pull-up resistors are needed because every button GPIO chosen here (32, 33, 13, 19) supports the ESP32's internal pull-up.

## Wiring notes

LEDs (one per color, repeat the same pattern four times):

- ESP32 GPIO -> 220 ohm resistor -> LED anode (long leg)
- LED cathode (short leg, with the flat side) -> breadboard GND rail
- GPIOs used: Red = 25, Yellow = 26, Green = 27, Blue = 14

Buttons (also one per color):

- One leg of the button -> an ESP32 GPIO
- The opposite leg -> breadboard GND rail
- No external pull-up resistor needed - the sketch turns on the ESP32's internal pull-up, so the GPIO sits HIGH at rest and reads LOW when pressed
- GPIOs used: Red = 32, Yellow = 33, Green = 13, Blue = 19

Power rails:

- ESP32 `GND` -> breadboard "-" rail. All four LED cathodes and all four button ground legs come here.
- The `3V3` pin is not needed for this project - every GPIO already provides its own pull-up internally.

Pin notes (worth knowing):

- GPIO 34, 35, 36, 39 are INPUT-ONLY on the ESP32 and have NO internal pull-up. They look tempting because there are four of them, but a button wired only between an input-only pin and GND will float when released and give random readings. If you ever want to use one anyway, add an external 10 k ohm pull-up resistor from the pin to 3V3.
- Avoid GPIO 0, 12, 15 for buttons - they are boot-strapping pins and can stop the board from starting if held LOW or HIGH at power-on.
- GPIO 2 is the on-board blue user LED on this board. Do not reuse it for a button - the LED and the button would fight each other.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK.
2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for "esp32" and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, takes a minute or two).
3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **"NodeMCU-32S"**.
4. No extra libraries are needed for this sketch - only `Arduino.h`, which is built in.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a USB cable. Use a **data** USB cable, not a charge-only one (if the board's red power LED comes on but the laptop never makes the "device connected" sound, swap the cable).
2. Tools -> Port. Pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in (on Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX`, on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`).
3. Nothing to edit in the sketch this time - there are no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in for Simon Says.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, second from the left at the top). The bottom of the IDE will say "Compiling..." for a few seconds, then "Connecting....." while it flashes. If "Connecting....." dots keep scrolling for more than 10 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." appear, then let go. Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-flash without this, but a few stubborn ones need the trick.
5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin..."** the upload worked. The game starts immediately - you should see the four LEDs do a short startup blink, then flash the first one-color "sequence".
6. (Optional) Tools -> Serial Monitor, and set the baud rate dropdown (bottom right) to **115200** to match the sketch's `Serial.begin(115200)`. You will see messages like `Round 1` and `Sequence: RED` so you can peek at what Simon is "thinking".

Press the button under the LED that just flashed. If the next round adds one more flash, you are playing! If all four LEDs blink three times together, you got it wrong - it will start a fresh game on its own.

**Common gotchas:**

- **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no light. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees so the long leg (anode) is on the resistor / GPIO side and the short leg (flat side of the plastic) is on the GND rail, push it back in.
- **Button feels "stuck on".** Tactile buttons have **four** legs but only two pairs are actually connected - the other pair shorts when you press. If a button reads pressed all the time, rotate it 90 degrees in the breadboard so the correct pair straddles the gap.
- **"Connecting....." never finishes on upload.** Hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until you see writing progress, then let go. If that still fails, try a different USB cable - charge-only cables are the #1 culprit and they look identical to data cables.
## Talking points

- The "memory" of the game is just an array of numbers. Each new round appends a fresh random value (0-3) and replays the whole array from the start.
- Debouncing: when you press a tactile button the metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, so the GPIO sees several rapid LOW/HIGH/LOW transitions. The sketch reads the pin, waits a tiny moment (`DEBOUNCE_MS`), and reads again to confirm.
- `INPUT_PULLUP` flips your intuition: pressed = LOW, not pressed = HIGH. That is because the internal resistor pulls the pin to 3.3 V by default, and the button shorts it to GND when you press it. This is why pin choice matters - GPIOs without a built-in pull-up have nothing to flip back to HIGH.
- The speed-up: every successful round trims the gap between LED flashes. That is the difficulty curve, baked into one variable.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a tiny passive buzzer on another GPIO and play a different tone per colour (real Simon does this).
- Save the high score to flash with the `Preferences` library so it survives a reset.
- Add a 2-player mode: alternate who has to repeat the sequence.
- Replace the four discrete LEDs with a single WS2812 strip and use colour directly.
- Make it WiFi-aware and POST the high score to the Orange Pi hub (once the Pi is online).

## Why this is interesting

Pure software project - no sensors, no analog, no I2C. Everything interesting happens in the code: the array, the random call, the loop that plays it back, the loop that reads the player. It is the perfect introduction to a finite state machine (SHOW_SEQUENCE -> WAIT_FOR_PLAYER -> CHECK -> WIN/LOSE) without any new electrical concepts. And the game is genuinely fun, which keeps a 10-year-old engaged long enough to ask "but how does it remember?" - which is exactly the question worth answering.

projects.name: Stopwatch + Lap Memory on Serial Monitor
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via USB, the onboard regulator makes 3.3V for the chip; no external parts so nothing else needs feeding).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug the ESP32 into your laptop and open the Serial Monitor. Tap the BOOT button to start a stopwatch, tap again to stop, hold it down to save a lap time, and a tiny blue light blinks once a second while the clock is running.

**Why it's fun**: Race your dad down the hallway, time how long you can hold your breath, or see who can stack ten cups the fastest, and every lap gets saved so you can compare runs. One little button does three different jobs depending on how you press it, which feels a bit like a secret code your fingers know.

## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the entire project - nothing else needed)
- 1x USB-C cable from your laptop

That is the whole shopping list. This version of the project was deliberately re-scoped so it can be built with **only the hardware already in Andy's kit**. An earlier draft used a TM1637 4-digit display, an SSD1306 OLED, two tactile push-buttons, a breadboard, and jumpers - none of which are in the kit yet. When those parts arrive, see "Things to change once it works" for the upgrade path.

## Wiring notes

There is no wiring. Plug the USB-C cable from your laptop into the ESP32. That is it. The two pieces of "hardware UI" we use are both already on the board:

- **BOOT button** (next to the USB-C jack). It is wired to GPIO 0 with a built-in pull-up. Pressed = LOW, released = HIGH. We use it as our one user button.
- **Built-in blue LED** on GPIO 2 (the small LED next to the WiFi shield, not the red power LED). It blinks once a second while the stopwatch is running and is off when stopped, so you can see the state at a glance without looking at the screen.

The "display" is the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Open it with `Tools > Serial Monitor` (or Ctrl+Shift+M) after upload.

**Do not press the EN button while timing** - EN is a hardware reset, it reboots the chip and you lose the run. Only BOOT is safe to press.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. If there is already a URL in there, add a comma before pasting.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box, find "**esp32** by Espressif Systems", and click Install. It is a big download (a few hundred MB), so this is a good time to get a snack.
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. That tells the IDE which chip you are talking to.
4. No extra libraries are needed for this project. The sketch only uses `<Arduino.h>`, which comes built in with the ESP32 board package you just installed.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with the USB-C cable. The little red power LED on the board should light up.
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that appeared when you plugged the board in. On Windows it looks like `COM5` (the number changes), on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`. If nothing new shows up, your USB cable might be a "charge only" cable - try a different one.
3. There are no passwords or placeholders to edit in this sketch. It is ready to upload as-is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a few seconds, then "Connecting..." while it talks to the chip. **If it gets stuck on `Connecting........_____`**, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need that nudge on the very first upload; after that they usually behave on their own.
5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." the upload is done. Now open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** (or press **Ctrl+Shift+M**). In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code.
6. You should see a welcome message and then a `00:00` clock sitting there waiting. Tap the BOOT button once - the blue LED next to the WiFi shield starts blinking once per second and the clock starts counting `00:01`, `00:02`, `00:03`. Tap BOOT again to stop. Hold BOOT for about a second while it is running and you will see a `Lap 1` line print with hundredths of a second. That is the whole thing working.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Serial Monitor stuck on gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`.** The baud rate is wrong. Look at the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor and change it to **115200**. The default is often 9600, which makes everything come out garbled.
- **Upload fails with `Failed to connect to ESP32: Timed out waiting for packet header`.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the board, click Upload again, and keep holding BOOT until you see "Writing..." in the output. Some boards need this every time, some only on the first flash.
- **Blue LED never blinks even though the Serial Monitor says it is running.** A few NodeMCU-32S clones wire the built-in LED to GPIO 5 or GPIO 22 instead of GPIO 2. Open the sketch and change `const uint8_t PIN_LED = 2;` to `5` or `22`, then re-upload. The stopwatch itself still works either way - the LED is just a bonus.
## Talking points

- **Why `millis()` instead of `delay()`.** `delay(1000)` would freeze the chip for a whole second, during which it cannot read the button or update the LED. `millis()` just asks "how many milliseconds since boot?" without stopping anything, so the same `loop()` can poll the button, blink the LED, and print the time all at once.
- **One button, three actions, via a small state machine.** A short tap (< 600 ms) toggles start/stop. A long press (>= 600 ms while held) records a lap if running, or resets everything if stopped. The function `readButton()` measures how long the button was held and reports a `SHORT_PRESS` or `LONG_PRESS` event. The `loop()` then decides what that event means based on whether the stopwatch is currently running. That separation - "low-level: was it short or long?" vs. "high-level: what does that mean right now?" - is the core idea of a state machine, and it shows up in almost every embedded project later.
- **Active-LOW buttons.** When BOOT is *pressed*, GPIO 0 reads `LOW` (0V), not `HIGH`. That is because the pin is pulled up to 3.3V by default, and pressing the button shorts it to ground. This is the single most common thing beginners get backwards, so it is worth re-reading: pressed = LOW.
- **Debouncing.** Real metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when you press them - the pin flickers HIGH/LOW/HIGH/LOW before settling. `readButton()` ignores any change that happens within 25 ms of the last change, which filters that out so one press is one event.
- **Why GPIO 0 is "free" to use as a button at runtime.** GPIO 0 is sampled at *boot* to decide between normal-run mode and flash-upload mode (that is why you sometimes have to hold BOOT during upload). Once the sketch is running, GPIO 0 is just a regular input - so we can re-use the BOOT button as our user button without any extra hardware.
- **Why the built-in LED is GPIO 2 on this board.** A few clones put it on GPIO 5 or GPIO 22 instead. If the LED never blinks, change `PIN_LED` to 5 or 22 - the rest of the sketch will still work.

## Things to change once it works

- **Upgrade to a real display.** When a TM1637 4-digit display arrives, replace the `Serial.print` calls in `showBigTime()` with `TM1637Display::setSegments()` and keep everything else identical. Add an SSD1306 OLED for the lap list. (That is the original "big stopwatch face + scrolling lap history" project, deferred until the parts are in hand.)
- **Add a buzzer.** When the relay board is wired up to switch a piezo, beep once per lap so Andy's son can time himself without watching the screen.
- **Persist the best-ever lap.** Use the `Preferences` library to save `bestLapMs` to ESP32 flash so it survives a power cycle.
- **Push laps over WiFi.** Once the Orange Pi One is booted and running Mosquitto, publish each lap time over MQTT to the Pi for plotting in Grafana. That makes this the first project that talks to the future hub.
- **Increase `MAX_LAPS`** from 20 to 100 - the ESP32 has plenty of RAM.

## Why this is interesting

This project teaches the three skills that come up in nearly every later IoT project - **non-blocking timing with `millis()`**, **debounced button input with a state machine**, and **storing a short history in a fixed-size array** - using only the hardware that is already on the desk. There is nothing to wire wrong and nothing to fry. By the end, the same `loop()` that times your son's 100-metre sprint will be a working template for the next dozen projects, where the "display" becomes a TM1637 or an OLED and the "button" becomes any other GPIO input.

projects.name: Family Doorbell Web Page
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or USB wall charger into the ESP32's USB-C port (5V, the board's onboard regulator drops it to 3.3V for the chip)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Press the button on the breadboard. Every phone in the house that has the web page open goes "Ding!" and the counter jumps up by one.

**Why it's fun**: It is a real doorbell you built yourself, and Dad's phone buzzes the second you push the button from the other room. Sneak up, mash it five times, and watch every screen in the house freak out at once.

## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - hosts the web page and watches the button)
- 1x push button (the doorbell itself)
- 1x breadboard (holds the button without soldering)
- 4x DuPont jumper wires (one to GPIO 4, one to GND, two spare)
- 1x USB cable (powers the ESP32 from a laptop or USB wall charger)

No resistor is needed for the button: we turn on the ESP32's internal pull-up resistor in code (`INPUT_PULLUP`). The LED that lights up on each press is the blue one already built into the NodeMCU board, so it has its own resistor on the PCB.

## Wiring notes

The button has 4 legs but they are wired in pairs internally. Sit the button across the breadboard's centre gap. Use diagonally opposite legs - that way you can't accidentally pick two legs that are already shorted together.

- One leg of the button -> ESP32 `GPIO 4`
- Diagonally opposite leg of the button -> ESP32 `GND`

That's all the wiring. When the button is open, GPIO 4 reads HIGH (pulled up internally to 3.3V). When pressed, GPIO 4 is shorted to GND and reads LOW. The code watches for that transition.

Power comes from the USB cable on the ESP32 - no separate power supply, no battery, nothing to plug into mains.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open the IDE, go to **File -> Preferences**, and in the "Additional board manager URLs" box paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK.
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install "**esp32 by Espressif Systems**" (it is a big download, give it a few minutes).
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**.
4. No extra libraries to install. `WiFi.h` and `WebServer.h` both come built-in with the ESP32 board package you just installed.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with the USB-C cable. You should see a tiny red power LED come on near the USB port.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the COM port that just appeared (on Windows it will be something like `COM5`; on a Mac it will look like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`). If you are not sure which one is the ESP32, unplug it, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the new one that showed up.
3. In the sketch, change `WIFI_SSID` to the name of your home WiFi (it is already set to `"GeeFam"` - leave it if that is right) and change `PASSWORD_HERE` to your actual WiFi password. Keep the quote marks around it.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling..." for a bit, then "Connecting....". If it sits on "Connecting" with lots of dots, hold down the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 board until the upload starts, then let go. (After the first successful upload you usually don't have to do this again.)
5. Once it says "Done uploading", go to **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (drop-down in the top-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**.
6. Press the small **EN** (reset) button on the ESP32. In the Serial Monitor you should see it connect to WiFi and print an IP address like `192.168.1.42`. Type that IP address into any phone or laptop on the same WiFi, hit go, and you should see the "Family Doorbell - All quiet." page. Press the button on the breadboard and the page should flash "Ding!" within a second.

**Common gotchas:**

- **WiFi band**: the ESP32 can only see **2.4 GHz** WiFi, not 5 GHz. If your router shows two networks (one ending in `-5G`), pick the one without `-5G` for `WIFI_SSID`.
- **"Connecting...___" forever on upload**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down while the dots are scrolling, and let go once it starts writing. This puts the chip into download mode by hand.
- **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters**: the baud rate is wrong. The code calls `Serial.begin(115200)`, so the Serial Monitor drop-down must also say **115200**.
## Talking points

- The button is just a switch. No "smartness" in it. The ESP32 is what turns "switch closed" into "tell every phone in the house".
- The web page doesn't get pushed to; it asks the ESP32 every second "has the count gone up?". That's called polling. It's the simplest approach that works on every phone browser without extra libraries.
- We count rings instead of just storing "is ringing". A counter means two phones loading the page at slightly different times still both notice the same press.
- Debouncing: a physical button's metal contacts bounce when they touch, so one press can look like 3-5 presses electrically. The 400 ms timer in the code ignores those echoes.

## Things to change once it works

- Make the page beep or vibrate the phone (a tiny bit of Web Audio API or `navigator.vibrate`).
- Add a mDNS name (`ESP32.local`) so you don't have to memorise the IP.
- Push instead of poll: switch to Server-Sent Events (`/events` endpoint) so the page updates instantly with no 1-second lag.
- Log the last 10 rings with timestamps so you can see who rang while you were out.
- Move from the breadboard button to a real doorbell button by the front door (still 2 wires).

## Why this is interesting

This is the smallest possible "real" IoT loop: a thing in the physical world (a button) makes a thing on a screen change (a web page), with nothing in between except WiFi. Andy gets to feel the whole shape of an event-driven system in one afternoon - sensor -> microcontroller -> network -> UI - and his son gets immediate, obvious feedback (Dad's phone goes "Ding!" when he pushes the button). It's also the natural feeder project for the Orange Pi hub later: replace the polling page with an MQTT publish and the doorbell becomes one of many sensors on the home bus.

projects.name: Garage Light Web Switch (with Relay)
projects.power_supply: USB-A to USB-C cable into the NodeMCU-32S (5V, also feeds the relay coil via the JDVcc-bridged jumper), plus a separate 12V DC barrel-jack supply for the LED strip on the switched side of the relay.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Open a web page on your phone and tap a big button. CLICK - a light across the room turns on. Tap it again, CLICK, and the light turns off.

**Why it's fun**: Your phone is now a magic wand for a real light, and you can hear the little click every time you tap. Show your friends - they will think you wired up the whole house.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brains and web server)
- 2-ch Songle relay board (only channel 1 is used here)
- 12V LED strip, short piece, or any 12V low-voltage lamp
- 12V DC power supply for the LED strip (separate from the ESP32 USB power)
- Breadboard (holds the ESP32 only)
- DuPont jumper wires (M-F from ESP32 header to relay header, M-M for the 12V load side)
- USB-A to USB-C cable (the NodeMCU-32S has a USB-C connector)

Heads-up: only the ESP32 and the relay board are confirmed on hand from the kit list in CLAUDE.md. The 12V strip, 12V supply, breadboard, jumpers, and USB-C cable are not listed there. Confirm these are actually in the box before starting, or we will be stuck halfway through wiring.

## Wiring notes

Two power worlds meet in this project. Keep them straight.

ESP32 side (5V from USB):

- ESP32 `5V` pin -> relay header `VCC`
- ESP32 `GND` -> relay header `GND`
- ESP32 `GPIO 26` -> relay header `IN1`

The breadboard is just a perch for the ESP32 and a convenient place to start the three jumpers that run to the relay header. The relay board already has its own logic pin header, so nothing else is wired on the breadboard rails.

The relay's JDVcc jumper stays in its default position (bridged to Vcc), so the relay coil is powered from the ESP32's 5V USB rail. This is the simplest wiring and fine for a small DC load.

12V side (the load being switched):

- 12V supply `+` -> relay channel 1 `COM` screw terminal
- Relay channel 1 `NO` screw terminal -> LED strip `+`
- LED strip `-` -> 12V supply `-`

The 12V supply ground does NOT need to touch the ESP32 ground. That is the whole point of the relay: the high-side wire is broken and remade by a mechanical contact, with no electrical connection back to the ESP32.

Active-LOW gotcha: the Songle board energizes the coil when IN1 is pulled LOW. The code drives the pin HIGH before calling `pinMode(..., OUTPUT)` so the relay does not click ON during boot.

3.3V trigger caveat (per CLAUDE.md, `Relay_2CH_Songle/` section): most Songle clones will trigger fine off a 3.3V ESP32 GPIO because the optocoupler LED only needs a small forward current. A few stubborn ones really do want a 5V swing - if relay 1 clicks unreliably, only sometimes, or only after the board warms up, that is the first thing to suspect. Workaround is a tiny NPN transistor or a level-shifter feeding IN1; ask before reaching for those, it is rarely needed.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. File -> Preferences -> "Additional boards manager URLs". Paste in `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. (If there is already something in that box, add a comma first, then paste.)
2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for **esp32** and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". This takes a few minutes - good time for a snack.
3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **NodeMCU-32S**.
4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. `WiFi.h` and `WebServer.h` both come with the ESP32 board package you just installed.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the NodeMCU-32S into the laptop with the **USB-A to USB-C** cable. A little red power LED on the board should light up.
2. Tools -> Port. Pick the one that just appeared (Windows: `COM3`, `COM4`, etc.; Mac: `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; Linux: `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If nothing shows up, the cable might be charge-only - try a different USB-C cable.
3. In the sketch, find these two lines near the top and put in your real WiFi info:
   - `WIFI_SSID` - replace `"GeeFam"` if your network is named something else.
   - `WIFI_PASSWORD` - replace `"PASSWORD_HERE"` with your actual WiFi password (keep the quotes).
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting..." with little dots. If the dots keep going for more than 10 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the NodeMCU-32S until you see "Writing..." - that is the one weird trick most ESP32 boards need on the first flash.
5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin... Done uploading," it worked.
6. Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate (bottom-right dropdown) to **115200** - that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code. Tap the EN (reset) button on the NodeMCU-32S so it reboots and you catch the start-up messages.
7. You should see the ESP32 connect to WiFi and print an IP address like `192.168.1.42`. Type that address into a web browser on your phone (the phone has to be on the **same WiFi network**). The big circular button page loads - tap it, and you should hear the relay **CLICK** across the room.

**Common gotchas:**

- **5 GHz WiFi.** The ESP32 only speaks 2.4 GHz. Most home routers broadcast both - make sure the phone (and the ESP32) are on the 2.4 GHz network, not the 5 GHz one. If WiFi never connects, this is almost always why.
- **BOOT button on first upload.** If "Connecting....." just dots forever and then fails, hold the BOOT button on the NodeMCU-32S the whole time it says "Connecting" and let go when "Writing" starts. After the first successful flash it usually does not need the trick again.
- **Serial Monitor baud wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`, the baud rate is wrong. Set it to **115200** in the bottom-right corner.
- **Relay clicks once at power-up.** If you hear a CLICK the moment the ESP32 boots (before you tap the button), that is the active-LOW trap - the pin floats LOW briefly during reset. The code sets it HIGH first, so you should not see this; if you do, the IN1 wire is on the wrong GPIO or loose.
## Talking points

- The relay is a remote-controlled light switch. The ESP32 cannot handle 12V directly, so it tells a tiny electromagnet (the relay coil) to physically push two metal contacts together.
- Hear the click? That is the contacts closing. That click is also why you should not switch a relay thousands of times a second.
- The web page is just HTML the ESP32 builds as a string and sends back when your phone asks for it. The big button is a link to `/on` or `/off`. The ESP32 sees the request, flips the pin, and redirects you back to `/` so the page updates.
- `digitalWrite(pin, LOW)` turns the light ON here. That feels backwards, and it is. Most opto-isolated relay boards use "low-level trigger".
- Because the button is a plain link with a 303 redirect, every tap reloads the whole page. That is fine for learning, but it will feel a little sluggish on a phone - half a second of white flash between taps. The first upgrade below fixes that.

## Things to change once it works

- Replace the link-style buttons with a `fetch()` call so the page does not fully reload on every tap (the current 303-redirect design forces a full reload, which is why it feels slow).
- Add channel 2 with a second button for a second light.
- Add a `/status` endpoint that returns JSON so a phone app or Home Assistant can poll it.
- Once the Orange Pi hub is up, switch from "web page" to MQTT: ESP32 subscribes to `home/garage/light/set`, publishes state to `home/garage/light/state`.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project where a tap on a phone moves a thing in the real world. Everything before this was the ESP32 talking to its own onboard LED. Now there is a 12V load, a separate power supply, and a mechanical click you can hear from across the room. That click is the bridge from "blinky tutorials" to "actually controlling the house".

projects.name: WiFi Signal Strength Meter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a power bank (user-supplied) to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S USB-C port (5V). The board powers the OLED off its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug it in and a tiny screen lights up with a bar that grows and shrinks as you walk around the house. The fatter the bar, the stronger the WiFi where you're standing.

**Why it's fun**: You become the WiFi detective. Hunt down the dead zones, find the magic spot in the back bedroom where the signal finally comes back, and prove to your dad once and for all which room has the worst internet.

## Parts list

From Andy's inventory:

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the "brain" - reads WiFi signal strength and drives the screen)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - SSD1306, 128x64 monochrome (the little screen that shows the bar graph)
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) (for tidy wiring without solder)
- 4x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc (we use 4 of the 40-pack: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL between ESP32 and OLED)

Not in the inventory - grab from around the house:

- USB power bank (any 5V "phone charger" pack with a USB output)
- USB-C cable to go from the power bank to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S's USB-C port

These two are treated as user-supplied because they aren't catalogued in the electronics stock - any spare phone-charging gear will do.

## Wiring notes

The OLED is an "I2C" device, which means it talks to the ESP32 over just two signal wires plus power and ground - four wires total. I2C is great because you can hang several different I2C devices off the same two pins later without needing more GPIO.

- OLED `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3` pin (the OLED is happy with 3.3V; do NOT use the 5V pin or the screen can be damaged)
- OLED `GND` -> ESP32 `GND` pin
- OLED `SDA` -> ESP32 `GPIO 21` (the default I2C data pin on the ESP32)
- OLED `SCL` -> ESP32 `GPIO 22` (the default I2C clock pin on the ESP32)

Plug both modules into the breadboard so nothing is dangling, then run the four jumpers between them. When you finish testing on the laptop, unplug the USB cable and move it to the power bank - everything keeps running because the ESP32 is happy with any 5V USB source.

Before uploading: open `WiFiRSSIMeter.ino` and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real GeeFam WiFi password. Per the project convention, credentials live inside the sketch (not in any CLAUDE.md or commit).


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open the Arduino IDE. Go to **File -> Preferences**. In the **Additional boards manager URLs** box, paste this URL and click OK:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Search for `esp32`, find **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** and click **Install**. It downloads a few hundred megabytes, so give it a minute.
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** (or "ESP32 Dev Module" if NodeMCU-32S isn't listed - both work).
4. Install the two screen libraries via **Tools -> Manage Libraries**. One at a time, search for and click **Install** on:
   - `Adafruit SSD1306` by Adafruit (the OLED driver)
   - `Adafruit GFX Library` by Adafruit (the drawing helper - the IDE may offer to install it as a dependency, say yes)

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable**. A red LED on the ESP32 should glow.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new port that appeared. On Windows it's something like `COM5`; on a Mac `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`; on Linux `/dev/ttyACM0`. If you can't tell which one, unplug the cable, peek at the menu, plug back in, and pick the entry that appeared.
3. Open the sketch and find `const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "PASSWORD_HERE";`. Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real GeeFam WiFi password (keep the quotes).
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the toolbar). The IDE compiles for a minute, then shows "Connecting...." while it flashes the board. If it sits there printing dots and underscores for more than 10 seconds, hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until the upload starts, then let go.
5. When the upload finishes you'll see "Hard resetting via RTS pin". The OLED should light up and say "Connecting to: GeeFam" with dots ticking across.
6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** if you want to peek - this sketch doesn't call `Serial.begin()`, so the window will stay quiet. All the action is on the OLED.
7. **You'll know it worked when:** the OLED first shows "Connected!" with an IP address like `192.168.1.42`, then switches to the live meter - a number like `-58 dBm`, a word like `Good`, and a bar that wobbles as you tilt the board. Walk into the next room and watch the bar shrink. That's the whole game.

Once it's running, unplug the USB-C cable from the laptop and plug it into the power bank instead. The sketch is stored in flash, so it boots back up and reconnects to GeeFam on its own. Now you're free to roam.

**Common gotchas:**

- **5 GHz WiFi won't work.** The ESP32 radio only speaks 2.4 GHz. If GeeFam has separate 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz network names, set `WIFI_SSID` to the 2.4 GHz one, otherwise the OLED sits on "Connecting..." forever.
- **First upload needs the BOOT button.** If the IDE prints `Connecting......_____....` and gives up, hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the upload bar starts moving, then release. After the first successful flash this usually isn't needed again.
- **OLED stays black.** Almost always: VCC went to the 5V pin instead of 3V3 (don't do that - it can kill the screen), SDA and SCL got swapped (try swapping the two signal wires), or the address isn't `0x3C` (a few rare modules are `0x3D` - change `OLED_ADDR` in the sketch and re-upload).
## Talking points

- **RSSI** (Received Signal Strength Indicator) is just a number in dBm that the WiFi chip reports for the access point it's connected to. -30 dBm is "I'm sitting on the router", -90 dBm is "I can barely hear it". -67 dBm or better is fine for streaming video, worse than -75 dBm is where things get flaky.
- The bar graph is just a filled rectangle whose width is mapped from the RSSI range onto the screen width. It's the same idea as a volume bar in any music app.
- "I2C" uses only two signal wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and an address to pick which device on the bus to talk to. The OLED's address is almost always `0x3C`.
- Because the ESP32 reconnects to WiFi automatically, you can keep walking around even if the signal drops out briefly - the meter will recover on its own.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a peak-hold marker: a thin vertical line that remembers the strongest reading you've seen in this room.
- Show the SSID name and the IP address as small text above the bar, so the kids can confirm which network they're measuring.
- Log readings to SD or send them over MQTT to the (future) Orange Pi hub so you can make a heat-map of the house.
- Add a buzzer that beeps faster when signal gets weaker - a "Geiger counter" mode for finding the strongest spot.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project here that does something genuinely useful around the house: it answers the real question "why is the WiFi bad in the back bedroom?". It also introduces two big concepts in one go - reading a real-world radio measurement (RSSI) and driving a display over I2C - without needing any sensors or extra parts beyond a single screen. Once the OLED is working, every future project that needs a tiny readout (temperature, sensor values, MQTT status from the Pi) reuses exactly the same wiring and code pattern.

projects.name: Distance-Triggered Treat Dispenser
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (or laptop port) into the ESP32 NodeMCU; VIN/5V feeds the HC-SR04 and SG90 with a 470 uF cap across the servo rail, and the HC-SR04 ECHO line is divided 1k/2k down to 3.3V before reaching the ESP32 GPIO.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hold your hand over the box. A motor spins a little cardboard wheel and exactly one M&M drops into your palm. A small red display ticks up so you can see how many treats it has handed out today.

**Why it's fun**: You built a candy machine that obeys your hand like magic, with no button to press. Set a daily limit, race your brother to trigger it the fastest, or aim it at the dog and watch his brain explode.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain - reads sensor, drives servo, updates display)
- HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance module (looks straight up for your hand)
- SG90 micro-servo (rotates the cardboard disk that drops one M&M)
- TM1637 4-digit display (shows the running count of treats dispensed)
- 1k and 2k resistors (voltage divider on the HC-SR04 ECHO line - see Wiring notes)
- 470 uF electrolytic capacitor (across the servo's 5V/GND, prevents brownout resets)
- Breadboard + male-to-male DuPont jumpers
- USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (preferred) or a laptop port for power

You will also build a tiny cardboard chassis: a tube (like an empty toilet-roll tube) holds the M&Ms, a flat cardboard disk on the servo horn has one M&M-sized slot cut out of it. As the servo turns from 0 deg to 90 deg the slot lines up with a hole in the chute and exactly one M&M drops out. This is the fun part - it will probably take three tries to get the disk geometry right.

## Wiring notes

- The HC-SR04 needs 5V on Vcc and its ECHO pin outputs 5V logic. The ESP32's GPIOs are 3.3V (not 5V tolerant on the datasheet), so we drop ECHO with a simple 1k / 2k divider: ECHO -> 1k -> GPIO 18, and GPIO 18 -> 2k -> GND. That gives 5 V x 2k / (1k + 2k) = ~3.3 V at the GPIO. TRIG goes the other way (ESP32 out to sensor in) and a 3.3 V high is enough to trigger the HC-SR04, so no divider needed there.
- The SG90 servo also wants 5V. Both 5V devices share the ESP32's VIN/5V pin (which on the NodeMCU board comes straight from the USB connector). The servo can briefly draw 500-700 mA when it stalls, and that dip on the shared rail can reset the ESP32. We park a 470 uF electrolytic capacitor right across the servo's 5V and GND on the breadboard rail to absorb those dips. Mind the polarity: the striped leg is the negative side and goes to GND. Use a 5V/2A USB charger rather than a laptop port if you can.
- The TM1637 display is happy on 3.3V or 5V; we use 3.3V because the data lines are then natively at ESP32 logic level.
- All grounds tie together on the breadboard's blue rail. This is essential - if the sensor's ground floats, distance readings will be garbage.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open the Arduino IDE, then go to **File -> Preferences**. In the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs", paste this address and click OK:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (a few hundred MB) so give it a minute.
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the list.
4. Install two extra libraries. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**), then one at a time:
   - Search for `ESP32Servo` and install the one by **Kevin Harrington / John K. Bennett**.
   - Search for `TM1637` and install **"TM1637Display"** by **Avishay Orpaz**.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB micro-B data cable**. Important: some cheap micro-B cables are charge-only and the IDE will not see the board. If no port shows up in step 2, try a different cable.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared. On Windows it looks like **COM4** or **COM5**, on a Mac it looks like **/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX** or **/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART**.
3. Open the sketch. This project has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - the only knobs you might want to tweak near the top of the file are `TRIGGER_CM` (how close your hand has to be, in cm) and `SERVO_DISPENSE` (how far the disk rotates, in degrees). Leave them alone for the first run.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will compile for about 30 seconds, then start flashing. If you see `Connecting......_____....` and then a red error, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 board until you see `Writing at 0x...` scrolling, then let go. You only have to do this trick the first time, or after some other tools have grabbed the chip.
5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**.
6. Press the small **EN** (or **RST**) button on the ESP32. You should see a startup line, the display should show `0000`, and the servo should jiggle to its rest position. Wave your hand about 10 cm above the HC-SR04 - the servo should snap to 90 deg, drop one M&M, snap back, and the display should tick up to `0001`. Pull your hand away past 20 cm and try again to see `0002`. If the display lights up but the count never goes up, the sensor is probably not seeing your hand - check the wiring of TRIG and ECHO before changing any code.

**Common gotchas:**

- **First-upload BOOT button trick.** On a fresh ESP32, the IDE often cannot put the chip into flash mode by itself. If Upload hangs at `Connecting......`, hold BOOT, tap EN once, keep holding BOOT until flashing starts, then let go. After the first successful flash this usually fixes itself.
- **Capacitor polarity backwards.** The 470 uF electrolytic has a striped side - that is the negative leg and must go to GND. Wired backwards it can pop, get hot, or just refuse to smooth the servo dips so the ESP32 keeps rebooting every time the servo moves. If the display resets to `0000` every time you trigger a treat, check the cap before anything else.
- **Serial Monitor baud rate wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows a wall of garbage characters like `??????`, the baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch.
## Talking points

- "What is an ultrasonic sensor?" It chirps a sound too high-pitched for us to hear, then times how long the echo takes to come back. Sound travels ~343 m/s, so the code multiplies microseconds by 0.0343 cm/us and divides by 2 (because the chirp goes there and back).
- "Why does it only dispense one M&M, not a stream?" Look at the `armed` variable. We disarm as soon as a hand is detected and only re-arm once the hand has moved back past 20 cm. That hysteresis pattern shows up everywhere in electronics - thermostats, button debouncing, you name it.
- "Why a slotted disk instead of just a flap?" A flap can let two M&Ms through if you're unlucky. A slot exactly one M&M deep is mechanically self-limiting - this is called a "rotary feeder" and is how real candy machines work.
- "Why two resistors on the ECHO wire?" The sensor speaks at 5 V but the ESP32 listens at 3.3 V. The two resistors form a divider that quietly drops the loud 5 V down to a polite 3.3 V before it reaches the chip - cheap insurance against frying a GPIO.
- "Why a fat capacitor next to the servo?" Motors are greedy in short bursts. The cap is a tiny local battery that hands current to the servo during those bursts so the ESP32 next door does not see its supply sag and reboot.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a tiny buzzer (active-high) that beeps once per dispense.
- Display the time-since-last-treat instead of the count, so you can compete with your son for "fastest reaction".
- Publish the count over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) so a Grafana dashboard tracks daily M&M consumption.
- Replace the cardboard disk with a 3D-printed one - same code, much more reliable feed.
- Add a long-press boot button check that resets the counter to zero.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project in the kit that combines a sensor (input), an actuator (output), and a display (feedback) into one closed loop. That is the basic shape of every IoT device. It also forces you to think about mechanical design as part of "the code working" - the firmware is the easy half, the cardboard is the hard half. That's a really useful lesson before moving on to the Orange Pi hub work where you'll be debugging across networks instead of across millimetres of cardboard.
