projects.name: Clap-O-Meter (Live Sound Bar Graph)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard 3.3V regulator powers the KY-037 mic, the OLED, and the red LED through a 330R resistor.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Clap your hands. A bar shoots up across the little screen and a red light flashes. Whisper and the bar barely twitches. Yell and it pegs all the way to the edge.

**Why it's fun**: You finally get to SEE how loud you are, like the bouncing bars on a music speaker. Have a shouting contest with your brother and watch the screen prove who actually won.

A live loudness meter built around the KY-037 microphone. The ESP32 reads the mic, scales the result onto a bar across the OLED, and flashes a red LED whenever the sound crosses a "loud" threshold - so a clap, a shout or a slammed door becomes a thing you can see.

## Parts list

- KY-037 Microphone Sensor (the protagonist) - analog audio input
- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the mic, drives the OLED, controls the LED
- 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - the bar graph and the labels
- 5mm red LED + 330R resistor - flashes on loud sound
- 10uF electrolytic capacitor - decoupling across the mic VCC/GND for a cleaner signal
- Breadboard, a pack of M-M jumpers, a pack of F-M jumpers

## Wiring notes

- The KY-037 runs happily off the ESP32's 3.3V rail. Put VCC and GND on the breadboard power rails first.
- Drop the 10uF electrolytic cap straight across the mic's VCC and GND pins on the breadboard. Longer leg goes to VCC, shorter leg to GND. This soaks up the little voltage wobbles the mic causes when WiFi or the OLED is busy, and the analog reading visibly settles down.
- The mic's A0 (analog out) goes to GPIO34. That pin is input-only on the ESP32, which is exactly what you want for a sensor - nothing in your sketch can accidentally drive it.
- The OLED is I2C: SDA -> GPIO21, SCL -> GPIO22. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins.
- The red LED gets the usual treatment: GPIO23 -> 330R resistor -> long leg of LED -> short leg to GND. Without the resistor the LED burns out and possibly the GPIO with it.
- Leave the D0 pin on the KY-037 unconnected. That's the built-in comparator with the blue trimpot, and we don't use it - the sketch does the threshold work in software so you can tweak it without a screwdriver.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open the Arduino IDE, then go to **File -> Preferences**. In the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs", paste this address: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK.
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type "esp32" in the search box, find the entry "esp32 by Espressif Systems", and click Install. It is a big download, so go grab a drink while it finishes.
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **NodeMCU-32S** from the long list.
4. Now install the two screen libraries. Go to **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**). Search "Adafruit SSD1306" and click Install on the one by Adafruit. It will ask if you want to install dependencies too. Say "Install all" so it grabs the Adafruit GFX Library at the same time.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or USB-A to micro-USB if your board has the older socket, depending on the exact NodeMCU-32S version). Use a real data cable, not a charge-only one - if the IDE never sees the board, the cable is the first thing to swap.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`, on Mac it is `cu.usbmodem...`, on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`. If you are not sure which is the right one, unplug the ESP32, look at the list, plug it back in, and the new line that pops up is yours.
3. There are no passwords or WiFi names in this sketch, so nothing to edit. (Optional: if you want to tweak the loud-clap threshold before flashing, scroll down to `LOUD_THRESHOLD` near the top of the code and change the number.)
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will compile for a minute, then start flashing. If the upload stalls on a line like `Connecting......_____`, press and hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see dots turning into a percentage, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need that nudge the first time; after that they usually flash on their own.
5. When it says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that is what `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch expects). Anything else and you just see garbage.
6. Stay quiet for about a second after the board resets - that is when it measures the "quiet room" baseline. Then clap once. The bar on the OLED should leap to the right and the red LED should blink. Whisper and the bar barely twitches. If the Serial Monitor printed `OLED not found at 0x3C, halting.`, the screen is not wired right - check SDA/SCL and the 3.3V/GND pair before anything else.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Upload stuck on "Connecting..."**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while the dots are scrolling, then release once flashing starts. Some boards need this every single upload, some only the first time.
- **Serial Monitor shows weird symbols like `?z?$??`**: the baud rate in the bottom of the Serial Monitor is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code.
- **10uF capacitor in backwards**: the electrolytic cap has a "+" leg (longer) and a "-" leg (shorter, with a stripe on the can). Longer to mic VCC, shorter to GND. Backwards and it either does nothing useful, gets warm, or in the worst case pops - so double-check before powering up.
- **Bar graph stuck pegged to the right and the LED is solid on**: you were probably clapping or talking during the first second after reset, so the baseline calibrated to a loud room. Unplug, replug, and stay quiet for one second while it boots.
## Talking points

- The mic doesn't output "loudness" - it outputs the audio waveform, swinging above and below a quiet midpoint many hundreds of times a second. We sample on a steady 1 ms tick (~1000 Hz) and measure how far each sample is from the calibrated quiet baseline. That absolute swing is what we draw.
- The bar uses a "peak with decay" trick: every new high pushes the bar up instantly, but a steady countdown drags it back down 20 ms at a time. That's why a clap shoots the bar up and then it slides back - matches how our ears feel loudness.
- The calibration at boot is just a 1-second average of the quiet room. Cover the mic or shout at it during boot and the baseline will be wrong - reset and let the room be quiet for a second.

## Things to change once it works

- Lower `LOUD_THRESHOLD` until a finger snap sets the LED off, or raise it so only a real clap counts.
- Add a second LED at a higher threshold for "very loud" so you have a two-stage indicator.
- Count claps in a 1-second window and use a double-clap as a "switch" - feed that into a relay to make a clap-on-clap-off lamp.
- Log the peak loudness once a second over WiFi to a tiny web page and watch the room's noise level over an evening.

## Why this is interesting

It turns something invisible (sound) into something visible and instantly playable. A 10-year-old can clap and see the bar move - no explanation needed. Underneath it's the same picture a real audio meter on a mixing desk is drawing, which makes it a great springboard into "how does a microphone actually work" without any math.

projects.name: Laser Posture Coach (desk slouch detector)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered via its USB-C port from a laptop or 5 V phone charger; the VL53L0X, OLED, LEDs and button are fed from the ESP32's 3.3 V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny laser on your desk watches your chest while you work. Sit up straight and a green light says "GOOD." Hunch toward the screen and a red light flashes "SLOUCH!" until you straighten back up.

**Why it's fun**: You built a robot hall monitor for your own posture - it catches you slouching before your mom does. Same kind of laser ranging that robot vacuums use to dodge furniture, except yours is yelling at you to sit up.

A laser-based desk posture coach. The VL53L0X sits flat on the desk pointing straight up. When you sit upright, it sees your chest at (say) 500 mm. When you slouch forward toward the screen, that distance shrinks. A green LED + "GOOD" message means upright; a red LED + "SLOUCH!" warning means you've crept too close. A button lets you recalibrate the "upright" distance for your chair height.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (brain, drives I2C and LEDs)
- VL53L0X ToF distance sensor (GY-VL53L0XV2 module) - the protagonist
- 0.96" I2C OLED display - shows live distance and posture verdict
- 1x green 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (good-posture light)
- 1x red 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (slouch warning)
- 1x tactile push-button (3x6x4.3 mm) - recalibrate
- Breadboard + DuPont jumper wires

## Wiring notes

- The ESP32 is powered from a laptop USB port via the on-board USB-C jack. Everything else is fed from the ESP32's 3.3 V and GND rails.
- Both the OLED and the VL53L0X are I2C devices. They share SDA (GPIO 21) and SCL (GPIO 22). They have different I2C addresses (OLED 0x3C, VL53L0X 0x29), so they coexist on the same two wires without any extra hardware.
- The VL53L0X module already has on-board pull-up resistors on SDA/SCL and a 3.3 V regulator + level shifters, so it's safe to power from either 3.3 V or 5 V. We use 3.3 V because the ESP32 is a 3.3 V device.
- LEDs: long leg (anode) to the GPIO through a 330R resistor; short leg (cathode) to GND. Green on GPIO 25, red on GPIO 26.
- Button between GPIO 27 and GND. We turn on the ESP32's internal pull-up so we don't need an external one. Pressed = LOW.
- Aim the sensor straight up. Sit at your normal typing position, press the button to set the target distance, then try slouching forward - the red LED should light when your chest gets ~8 cm closer than the target.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, give it a few minutes).
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"**.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these four, one at a time, by typing the name in the search box and clicking Install:
   - **Adafruit SSD1306** (for the OLED) - if it asks to also install Adafruit GFX and BusIO, say yes.
   - **Adafruit GFX Library** (the font / shape helper the OLED needs).
   - **Adafruit BusIO** (the I2C plumbing the two Adafruit libraries share).
   - **Adafruit VL53L0X** (for the laser distance sensor).

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable that can carry data** (some charging-only cables will not work - if the board does not show up, try another cable).
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that appeared when you plugged in (Windows: `COM3`, `COM4`...; Mac: `/dev/cu.usbserial-...` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; Linux: `/dev/ttyUSB0`).
3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline. You can leave the code alone.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). You will see "Connecting....." in the bottom panel. **If it gets stuck on dots,** hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. You usually only need that trick on the very first upload.
5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin," it is done. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of that window) to **115200** - the same number the sketch uses inside `Serial.begin()`. (If you do not see the Serial.begin line in this sketch, that is fine - the OLED is the main screen here.)
6. **What you should see:** the OLED lights up and shows "Posture Coach", a "Target: 500 mm" line, the live distance in big numbers, and "GOOD" in big letters at the bottom. The green LED is on. Wave your hand close to the sensor (within about 40 cm) and watch the number drop - when it gets ~8 cm under the target, "GOOD" flips to "SLOUCH!" and the red LED takes over. Sit at your normal typing position, press the button once, and the target updates to your actual chest distance.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Upload stuck on "Connecting....."?** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while it tries to connect, and let go when you see "Writing..." start. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this every time, others only on the first flash.
- **OLED stays black or shows nothing?** It is almost always one of three things: SDA and SCL swapped (GPIO 21 = SDA, GPIO 22 = SCL), no power to the OLED's VCC pin, or the OLED's I2C address is 0x3D instead of 0x3C - some clones use the other one. If you suspect address, change `0x3C` to `0x3D` in the `display.begin(...)` line.
- **"VL53L0X not found" on the screen, or distance never changes?** Both I2C devices share the same two wires, so a loose jumper on SDA or SCL kills both. Re-seat the four wires (SDA, SCL, 3V3, GND) and try again. Also check the sensor is the right way up - the tiny black square (the laser) needs a clear view, not blocked by a wire.
- **LEDs do not light?** LEDs only work one way around - long leg (anode) goes through the 330R resistor to the GPIO pin, short leg (cathode) goes to GND. If yours is in backwards there is no damage, just flip it.
## Talking points

- "Time of Flight" really does mean what it says: this chip fires a tiny invisible 940 nm laser pulse and measures how long the photons take to bounce back. Light moves about 30 cm in 1 nanosecond - the chip times that.
- Unlike the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (which uses sound and gives ~1 cm resolution), the VL53L0X reports in millimeters and works fine at close range. That precision is what makes "you slouched 8 cm" detectable instead of "you moved, maybe."
- Two different chips, one pair of wires. I2C lets multiple devices share SDA and SCL by giving each a unique address. The OLED answers at 0x3C; the ToF answers at 0x29.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer (a piezo against a GPIO) that beeps after you've been slouching for more than 10 seconds.
- Log slouch events to the serial monitor with timestamps, then graph "minutes slouched per hour."
- Push posture stats to the Orange Pi (when it's booted) over WiFi/MQTT and build a daily report.
- Use the second VL53L0X (we have two) mounted sideways to also detect when you lean too far back.

## Why this is interesting

This sensor is the cheapest way an Andy-budget project can do real laser ranging - the same family of chips lives in robot vacuums and phone autofocus systems. Pairing it with an OLED on the same I2C bus is a clean first lesson in "multiple devices share two wires," which is the foundation for almost every more advanced sensor project that follows.

projects.name: Magnet Swipe Counter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V USB charger into the ESP32's USB port; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the KY-003 and the OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Wave a magnet past the little sensor and the number on the tiny screen jumps up by one. A green LED blinks at the exact same moment, so every swipe gives you a flash and a fresh count.

**Why it's fun**: It feels like a magic trick because nothing touches anything - the magnet just floats by and the screen reacts. Race your dad to 100 swipes, or stick the sensor on a door and turn it into a secret "who opened my room" detector.

## Parts list

- 1x KY-003 Hall Switch Sensor (the protagonist - a tiny chip that snaps LOW when the south pole of a magnet gets close)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor and drives the screen)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (shows the live count)
- 1x Green 5mm LED + 1x 330R resistor (flashes once per swipe for instant tactile feedback)
- 1x breadboard
- A handful of jumper wires
- Any small magnet from around the house (fridge magnet, motor magnet, the round neodymium ones from old hard drives)

## Wiring notes

The KY-003 module has 3 pins - usually labelled S (signal), middle (VCC) and minus (GND). The middle pin is power, even though it looks like the obvious "data" pin. Double-check the silkscreen before plugging in.

- KY-003 `-` to ESP32 `GND`
- KY-003 middle (`+` or `VCC`) to ESP32 `3V3`
- KY-003 `S` to ESP32 `GPIO 14`

The OLED uses the ESP32's default I2C pins:

- OLED `VCC` to ESP32 `3V3`
- OLED `GND` to ESP32 `GND`
- OLED `SDA` to ESP32 `GPIO 21`
- OLED `SCL` to ESP32 `GPIO 22`

The LED sits on the breadboard:

- ESP32 `GPIO 27` to the long leg (anode) of the green LED
- Short leg (cathode) through the 330R resistor to `GND`

The KY-003 has its own pull-up resistor on board, so you don't need an external one. The sketch also enables the ESP32's internal pull-up as a safety net.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so give it a minute.
3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these two, one at a time:
   - Search "Adafruit GFX" -> install **Adafruit GFX Library**.
   - Search "Adafruit SSD1306" -> install **Adafruit SSD1306**. If the IDE asks "install missing dependencies?", say **Install all**.
4. Pick the board: **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> ESP32 Dev Module** (that is the entry the NodeMCU-32S uses).

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB micro-B cable** (not micro-A, not USB-C). It must be a real data cable - some cheap "charge-only" cables will not show up. The red power LED on the ESP32 should light up.
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-xxxx`, on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If nothing new appeared, the cable is charge-only - try a different one.
3. Open the sketch. This one has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - it is ready to go as-is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the toolbar). The IDE will compile for about 30 seconds, then start uploading. If you see `Connecting....____....` and it stalls, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." in the output, then let go. After the first successful upload you usually do not need to do the BOOT trick again.
5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin" the code is running. The OLED should light up and show **"Magnet Swipe Counter"** with a big **0** underneath.
6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**. You should see `Ready. Wave a magnet near the KY-003.` Wave a magnet across the KY-003: the green LED flashes, the number on the OLED ticks up by one, and the bottom of the screen briefly shows `[ MAGNET DETECTED ]`.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Stuck on `Connecting....`**: hold the **BOOT** button while the upload starts, release once it begins writing. Some boards need this every time, most only the first time.
- **OLED stays dark and the green LED blinks fast forever**: the sketch could not find the OLED on I2C. Double-check SDA is on GPIO 21 and SCL is on GPIO 22, and that the OLED is on 3V3 (not 5V on this build).
- **Magnet does nothing**: the KY-003 only sees the **south pole**. Flip the magnet over and try again - that is the fix nine times out of ten.
## Talking points

- Hall sensors are how your laptop knows the lid is closed and how your phone knows when the magnetic case is shut. They are everywhere and never wear out because nothing physically touches anything.
- The KY-003 only reacts to one pole of the magnet (the south pole). If your magnet doesn't seem to trigger it, flip the magnet over - that is almost always the fix.
- "Active LOW" means the signal pin is normally HIGH (3.3V) and drops to LOW (0V) when the sensor sees a magnet. This is backwards from how most people think about switches, so it's a great example of "the world doesn't always agree with you".
- The 40 ms debounce window in the code is there because a magnet swept past quickly can make the digital line jitter for a millisecond or two. Without debouncing, one swipe could count as three.

## Things to change once it works

- Try different magnets - a small ceramic fridge magnet vs. a tiny neodymium - and see how close you have to get for each. That distance is the sensor's effective range.
- Change `PIN_HALL` to a different pin (e.g. `4` or `15`) and update the wiring to match. Get into the habit of changing both at once.
- Add a "high score" reset by holding the magnet near the sensor for 3 seconds: detect a long LOW instead of a short pulse and zero the counter.
- Replace the OLED with the LCD 1602 + I2C backpack and rewrite `drawScreen()` for the LCD - same data, different display.
- Log each swipe out over WiFi (MQTT to the Orange Pi once it boots) so you have a "door opened" history.

## Why this is interesting

Magnetic sensing is the cleanest "yes / no" the universe gives you in beginner electronics. There is no light to interfere with it, no sound to confuse it, no contact to wear out. Pair that with the OLED and you get a project where every action causes an immediate, satisfying visual change - which is the single most motivating thing when you are learning. It also sets up two real-world projects you will eventually want: a door/window open sensor, and a wheel-rotation speedometer.

projects.code:
<![CDATA[// Magnet Swipe Counter
// Wave a magnet past the KY-003 Hall switch. Each swipe increments a counter
// shown on the OLED, and the green LED flashes once per swipe.
//
// Board: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
// Libraries (install via Library Manager):
//   - Adafruit GFX Library
//   - Adafruit SSD1306

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>

// ---------- Pin assignments (match the wiring diagram) ----------
const int PIN_HALL = 14;  // KY-003 signal output (active LOW when magnet present)
const int PIN_LED  = 27;  // Green LED via 330R to GND

// ---------- OLED setup ----------
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET   -1
#define OLED_ADDR    0x3C
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// ---------- State ----------
unsigned long swipeCount = 0;
int lastHallState = HIGH;          // KY-003 idles HIGH (no magnet)
unsigned long lastEdgeMs = 0;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 40;
unsigned long ledOffAtMs = 0;
const unsigned long LED_FLASH_MS = 120;

void drawScreen(bool magnetNow) {
    display.clearDisplay();

    // Header
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
    display.setCursor(0, 0);
    display.print("Magnet Swipe Counter");
    display.drawLine(0, 10, 127, 10, SSD1306_WHITE);

    // Big count
    display.setTextSize(3);
    display.setCursor(0, 18);
    display.print(swipeCount);

    // Status icon
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setCursor(0, 54);
    if (magnetNow) {
        display.print("[ MAGNET DETECTED ]");
    } else {
        display.print("Wave a magnet by...");
    }

    display.display();
}

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(115200);

    pinMode(PIN_HALL, INPUT_PULLUP); // KY-003 has its own pull-up, but belt-and-braces
    pinMode(PIN_LED, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);

    Wire.begin();  // SDA=21, SCL=22 on ESP32 by default

    if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDR)) {
        Serial.println("OLED not found. Check wiring (SDA=21, SCL=22).");
        while (true) {
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            delay(200);
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
            delay(200);
        }
    }

    drawScreen(false);
    Serial.println("Ready. Wave a magnet near the KY-003.");
}

void loop() {
    int hallState = digitalRead(PIN_HALL);
    unsigned long now = millis();

    // Detect a falling edge (HIGH -> LOW = magnet just arrived) with debounce
    if (hallState != lastHallState && (now - lastEdgeMs) > DEBOUNCE_MS) {
        lastEdgeMs = now;
        if (hallState == LOW) {
            swipeCount++;
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            ledOffAtMs = now + LED_FLASH_MS;
            Serial.print("Swipe #");
            Serial.println(swipeCount);
            drawScreen(true);
        } else {
            drawScreen(false);
        }
        lastHallState = hallState;
    }

    // Turn the LED off after its flash window
    if (ledOffAtMs != 0 && now >= ledOffAtMs) {
        digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
        ledOffAtMs = 0;
    }
}

projects.name: TV Remote LED Color Picker
projects.power_supply: USB cable from Andy's PC to the Arduino Uno - the Uno's onboard 5V rail powers the KY-022 and all four LEDs.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Point your TV remote at a little dark bubble on the breadboard and press a button. A red, green, blue, or yellow LED lights up, one color per button, like you just hacked the remote to control your own tiny stoplight.

**Why it's fun**: You are teaching the Arduino to listen to a TV remote that already lives in your house, which feels a bit like wizardry. Once it works, hide the remote behind your back and make the lights change from across the room while your sister tries to figure out how you are doing it.

## Parts list

- 1x KY-022 IR Receiver Module (the star - a tiny 38 kHz IR demodulator on a breakout board)
- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (5V GPIO; the `IRremote` library is rock-solid on AVR)
- 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points)
- 1x F-M jumper pack (for the 3-pin KY-022 header)
- 1x M-M jumper pack (for the LEDs and resistors on the breadboard)
- 1x Red, 1x Green, 1x Blue, 1x Yellow 5mm LED
- 4x 330R resistors (one per LED)

## Wiring notes

The KY-022 has three pins. Different clone boards label them slightly differently, but the order is always the same: **S** (signal), middle pin is **VCC** on most boards, and the one marked with a `-` is **GND**. If yours has the `-` on the outside instead of the signal, just look at the silkscreen - it's always labelled.

- KY-022 **S** -> Arduino **D2** (the `IRremote` library can use almost any pin; D2 is conventional)
- KY-022 **VCC** -> Arduino **5V**
- KY-022 **GND** -> Arduino **GND**

Each LED gets its own resistor between the Arduino pin and the LED's long leg (anode). The short leg (cathode) goes to the breadboard's GND rail.

- D6 -> 330R -> Red LED anode; Red cathode -> GND rail
- D7 -> 330R -> Green LED anode; Green cathode -> GND rail
- D8 -> 330R -> Blue LED anode; Blue cathode -> GND rail
- D9 -> 330R -> Yellow LED anode; Yellow cathode -> GND rail
- Arduino GND -> breadboard GND rail

When the sketch boots it briefly flashes all four LEDs in sequence as a wiring self-test. If one stays dark, that's the row to recheck before worrying about the IR side.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno.
2. Tools -> Board -> **Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**.
3. Tools -> Manage Libraries. In the search box type **IRremote**, find the one by *shirriff, Armin Joachimsmeyer* (v3.x or v4.x), and click **Install**. This is the library that does all the hard work of decoding the remote.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with the chunky **USB-B** cable (the squarish printer-style end goes into the Uno, the USB-A end into the laptop). The green **ON** LED on the Uno should light up straight away.
2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM\*** on Windows, **/dev/cu.usbmodem\*** on Mac, or **/dev/ttyACM0** on Linux. If you only see one entry, that is the Uno.
3. No passwords or WiFi names to change in this sketch - it is offline. Just leave the code as it is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left of the IDE). The bottom of the IDE will say *Compiling sketch...* then *Uploading...*, and the **RX** and **TX** LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When you see **Done uploading.**, the sketch is running.
5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** - if it is on the wrong number you will just see garbage like `???????`.
6. What you should see: first, all four LEDs flash in order (red, green, blue, yellow) as the wiring self-test. Then the Serial Monitor prints something like `Press the button you want for RED`. Point any remote (TV, soundbar, old DVD player) at the dark bubble and press a button. The Serial Monitor prints a hex code like `0x20DF10EF` and moves on to GREEN, then BLUE, then YELLOW. After the fourth press it says it is ready, and from then on each learned button lights its matching LED for one second. Unknown buttons print a `?` - that is normal, it just means you pressed something the Uno does not have a colour for yet.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish.** The baud rate dropdown is on the wrong number. Set it to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch.
- **An LED stays dark during the self-test.** It is almost always the LED in backwards - the short leg (cathode) is the one that goes to the GND rail, the long leg (anode) is the one that meets the 330R resistor. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. No damage done.
- **Remote presses do nothing and the Serial Monitor stays silent.** Either the KY-022's **S** pin is not on **D2** (check that wire first), or you are pressing a remote with a dead battery. The Uno's built-in pin 13 LED should blink every time *any* IR signal arrives - if it never blinks, the receiver is not seeing the remote at all.
## Talking points

- **Why the dome is dark plastic.** That bubble on the KY-022 is a filter that lets infrared through and blocks visible light. Without it, sunlight or a desk lamp would drown out the remote.
- **Why 38 kHz matters.** Remotes don't send a steady "on" - they send the signal as a 38,000-times-a-second flicker. The receiver is tuned to that flicker, so steady light sources don't fool it.
- **Pressing the same button gives the same code.** That's the whole point of a remote protocol. The sketch learns four of those codes and reacts when it sees them again.
- **Pin 13 blinks for free.** The `ENABLE_LED_FEEDBACK` flag makes the Uno's built-in LED blink every time *any* IR frame arrives. Even an unknown button proves the receiver is alive.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a fifth "off" button that turns every LED off, by extending the learn sequence to five buttons.
- Swap the LEDs for the 2-channel Songle relay (low-voltage DC only - the bedside lamp stays on its own switch) and turn this into a remote-controlled fan or LED strip switch.
- Print the raw `0x...` codes for *every* button on your remote on the Serial Monitor and make a little reference table. You'll see the same prefix on every button - that's the remote's "address".
- Wire up the LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack and have it show the name of the last colour pressed instead of just lighting an LED.

## Why this is interesting

Most beginner sensor projects work in *one* direction: the world changes, the sensor responds. IR receivers flip that around - they give you a way to *send commands in* to the Arduino from across the room, using equipment (a TV remote) that's already in the house. Once you can decode a remote, an enormous chunk of consumer electronics suddenly stops being a black box. And because you're capturing real codes off a real remote, every household ends up with a slightly different demo, which keeps it fresh when Andy's son wants to show it off.

projects.name: Invisible Tripwire Alarm with OLED Face
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard regulator feeds the IR module, OLED, and LED from its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Set up an invisible beam across a doorway. When someone walks through it, a little face on the screen jumps from calm to shocked, a red light snaps on, and a counter ticks up by one.

**Why it's fun**: Sneak it onto your bedroom door and catch your sister mid-snoop - the screen literally goes "!" when she crosses the line. It's the same trick museums use to know when you're getting too close to the dinosaur bones.

A doorway "invisible tripwire" that watches a small patch of air in front of the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module. The moment your hand (or your son's hand) crosses the beam, the OLED face flips from calm "ARMED" to shocked "INTRUDER!", a red LED lights up, and a trip counter on the screen ticks up. Pull your hand away and everything snaps back. It's the same satisfying "did I really do that?" feedback as a museum motion sensor, built in an afternoon.

## Parts list

- 1x IR Obstacle Avoidance Module (the protagonist - a digital "is something in front of me?" sensor)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (for the ARMED / INTRUDER faces and trip counter)
- 1x 5mm red LED (lights while the beam is broken)
- 1x 330R resistor (current-limit for the red LED)
- 1x breadboard, plus F-M and M-M jumper wires

## Wiring notes

- The IR module has a 3-pin header: `VCC`, `GND`, `OUT`. Power it from the ESP32's `3V3` pin and `GND`. (The module accepts 3.3V-5V; 3.3V keeps logic levels safe for the ESP32.)
- `OUT` goes to `GPIO 32`. The module has its own pull-up, so use `INPUT` (no internal pull-up needed).
- The OLED is I2C: `SDA` -> `GPIO 21`, `SCL` -> `GPIO 22`, plus `3V3` and `GND`. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins, so `Wire.begin()` without arguments is enough.
- Red LED: `GPIO 25` -> 330R -> LED anode (long leg) -> LED cathode (short leg) -> `GND`. Resistor first protects the LED if the wire slips.
- The IR module has a small blue trimpot on the back. Turn it with a tiny screwdriver to adjust trigger distance from a couple of centimetres up to about 30 cm. There are also two indicator LEDs on the module itself: a power LED and an "obstacle detected" LED. The obstacle LED lighting up is a great sanity check before you even look at the OLED.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click **OK**.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a chunky download, so give it a minute.
3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install two libraries:
   - Search `Adafruit GFX` -> install **"Adafruit GFX Library"**.
   - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> install **"Adafruit SSD1306"**.
   (If it asks about installing extra dependencies, click **Install all**.)
4. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** (or **"ESP32 Dev Module"** if you don't see it).

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB micro-B cable that can carry data** (some cheap cables are charge-only - if the board never shows up, that is usually why).
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in. On Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM7`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`.
3. This sketch has no WiFi password or other placeholder to fill in - the code is ready to go. Just double-check the pin numbers at the top (`PIN_IR_OUT = 32`, `PIN_LED = 25`) match your wiring.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). You will see "Connecting....." in the bottom panel. If it sits there for more than 5 seconds spamming dots, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this trick on the first upload.
5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin"** the flash is done. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**.
6. The OLED should light up showing **ARMED** with a calm smiley face and `Trips: 0` at the bottom. Wave your hand about 10 cm in front of the IR module - the face should flip to **INTRUDER!** with wide eyes, the red LED should turn on, and the trip counter should tick up by one. Pull your hand away and it snaps back to ARMED. The little obstacle LED on the IR module itself lights up at the same time, which is a handy confirmation that the sensor is seeing your hand.

**Common gotchas:**

- *Upload sits on "Connecting....." forever.* That is the BOOT button trick - hold BOOT down on the ESP32 while the IDE is trying to connect, release once it starts writing. Once the sketch is running, future uploads usually work without it.
- *OLED stays black.* Almost always either swapped SDA/SCL (SDA = GPIO 21, SCL = GPIO 22) or wrong I2C address. The sketch uses `0x3C`, which fits most 0.96" boards - if yours is `0x3D` the screen will just stay dark with no error. Also double-check the OLED's VCC goes to **3V3**, not 5V.
- *Counter shoots up by 5 every time you wave.* The 40 ms debounce window should stop this, but if your IR module is extra twitchy, turn the little blue trimpot on the back a tiny bit anti-clockwise to make it less sensitive, or bump `DEBOUNCE_MS` from 40 to 80 in the sketch and re-upload.
## Talking points

- *Active-LOW logic, again.* Just like the 2-ch relay board: the sensor's `OUT` line sits HIGH normally and pulls LOW when something is detected. Show your son `digitalRead(PIN_IR_OUT) == LOW` and ask him "so... does LOW mean nothing's there, or something IS there?" It's the classic beginner trap that's easier to learn once than to memorise forever.
- *Why debounce?* The IR detector edge isn't perfectly clean - as a hand enters or leaves the beam you might get a few rapid HIGH/LOW flickers across a millisecond or two. Without the 40ms debounce window, one wave of the hand could log 5 trips. With it, you log exactly 1.
- *Why a small built-in face on the OLED instead of just text?* Because feedback that feels like a reaction is more fun than feedback that looks like a log entry. Same information, completely different vibe.

## Things to change once it works

- Add the small piezo buzzer (or a tiny servo arm that "slams" a paper door) so the alarm has audio or motion too.
- Swap the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module for the HC-SR04 ultrasonic and compare: ultrasonic gives you a *distance number*, the IR module only gives you a *yes/no*. Same project shape, very different sensor character.
- Add WiFi: have the ESP32 send a "tripped at HH:MM:SS" line to your laptop or to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) over MQTT, so you can see a log of every doorway crossing.
- Mount the module sideways in a doorway with cardboard so it makes a real "laser-style" beam across the threshold.

## Why this is interesting

Almost every "smart" presence sensor in the world - shop door chimes, automatic taps, elevator door re-open - is doing exactly what this circuit does: a beam, a detector, a digital edge, and a reaction. Building the toy version once makes the grown-up versions stop feeling like magic. It's also a near-zero-frustration project: no analog calibration, no flaky timing, no maths - just "something is here / something is not here" with instant visual payoff.

projects.name: Piggy Bank Coin Counter (TCRT5000 + OLED)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a phone charger or laptop into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the TCRT5000 module, the OLED, and the indicator LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Drop a coin in the slot. The little screen bumps the count up by one, flashes a green LED, and shouts a cheer just for you. Unplug it, plug it back in tomorrow - your total is still there waiting.

**Why it's fun**: It's a piggy bank that actually KNOWS how rich you are, and it celebrates every single coin like you just won a prize. Race your dad to see who can fill theirs first, or sneak up on it and try to drop a coin so fast the sensor misses it (spoiler: it won't).

A real-world piggy bank that knows how much you've fed it. The TCRT5000 sits in the throat of the slot pointing across the gap; whenever a coin passes between the IR LED and the phototransistor, the module's digital output drops, the ESP32 counts it, the green LED blinks, and the OLED bumps the total along with a cheerful message. The count survives reboots because it is written to the ESP32's flash memory.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the screen, stores the count)
- TCRT5000 IR Reflective Tracking Module (the "eye" that catches each coin)
- 0.96" OLED Display, I2C (the running tally and cheer board)
- 5mm green LED + 330R resistor (an instant "I saw that" flash)
- Breadboard + DuPont jumpers (no soldering)

## Wiring notes

- TCRT5000 has four pins: VCC, GND, DO (digital out), AO (analog out). We only use DO.
- Power the TCRT5000 from 3.3V on the ESP32, not 5V. The module's onboard LM393 comparator is happy at 3.3V and that keeps the DO line at 3.3V too - safe for the ESP32 GPIO.
- DO is "active LOW": idle = HIGH, coin overhead = LOW. The onboard pot lets you tune the trigger distance - turn it until the on-board indicator LED just lights when a coin is in position.
- OLED is I2C: SDA = GPIO 21, SCL = GPIO 22 (the ESP32's default I2C pins).
- The green LED's long leg (anode) goes to GPIO 17 through the 330R resistor; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND.
- Common ground everywhere - the sensor module, OLED, and LED all share GND with the ESP32.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, give it a few minutes).
3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these three, one at a time:
   - Search "Adafruit GFX" -> install **Adafruit GFX Library**
   - Search "Adafruit SSD1306" -> install **Adafruit SSD1306**
   - If it asks to also install dependencies (BusIO), say yes.
4. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the long list.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or micro-USB, depending on which NodeMCU-32S you have - check the port on the board). Use a cable you know carries data, not a charge-only one.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just showed up (on Windows it looks like **COM4** or **COM5**, on a Mac it looks like **cu.usbserial-XXXX**). If nothing new appears, try a different cable.
3. There are no passwords or placeholders to change in this sketch - it runs offline.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow at the top of the IDE). You will see "Connecting......" in the black box at the bottom. On the very first upload, if it gets stuck on dots, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." then let go.
5. When it finishes ("Hard resetting via RTS pin"), open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the dropdown on the right to **115200 baud**.
6. You should see `Loaded saved count: 0` in the Serial Monitor, and the OLED should light up with "PIGGY BANK", a big **0**, and "Ready - drop a coin!" along the bottom. Wave a coin (or your fingertip) about a centimetre over the TCRT5000 - the green LED flashes, the number jumps to 1, and a cheer appears.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Upload fails with "Failed to connect"**: this is the BOOT button trick. Hold BOOT on the ESP32, click Upload, and let go of BOOT when "Connecting..." turns into "Writing...". You only need this on stubborn first uploads.
- **OLED stays dark and Serial Monitor says "OLED init failed"**: SDA and SCL are swapped, or the OLED's address is `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. Try swapping the two yellow-ish wires first; if still nothing, change `OLED_ADDR` in the code from `0x3C` to `0x3D` and upload again.
- **Counter races up to 50 the moment you power it on, with no coin**: the little blue pot on the TCRT5000 module is turned too sensitive. Turn it slowly with a small screwdriver until the on-board indicator LED goes OFF when nothing is over the sensor, then ON only when a coin sits above it.
- **Serial Monitor shows garbled symbols like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`**: the baud rate dropdown is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code.
## Talking points

- The TCRT5000 is basically an IR flashlight and an IR camera sitting next to each other. The flashlight always shines forward; the camera only "sees" light if something in front bounces some of it back. A coin held a centimetre above the sensor is a great mirror for invisible IR.
- Why "active LOW"? The comparator chip on the module is wired so that "lots of reflected light" pulls the output down to ground. It is the standard convention for these modules and is worth getting used to - it will come back on the IR obstacle modules and the PIR sensors.
- The debounce timer (250 ms) is there because one coin passing through can briefly flicker the sensor twice as it tumbles. We treat anything inside 250 ms as the same coin.
- `Preferences` is the ESP32's tiny built-in key/value store. We save the count every time it changes, so unplugging the bank does not reset the total.

## Things to change once it works

- Build an actual slot: a cardboard tube or a 3D-printed funnel with the TCRT5000 staring across the throat. A short, narrow chute makes the detection rock-solid.
- Add a "session" counter alongside the lifetime total - reset on a button press.
- Switch the cheer text to count up the cash value if you only feed it one coin type ("$0.25", "$0.50"...).
- Pipe the count to MQTT on the (eventually-booted) Orange Pi so the household can race each other to fill their banks.
- Swap DO for AO (analog out) and look at how the reflected-light reading actually changes with coin distance - a great intro to ADCs.

## Why this is interesting

It teaches the difference between a "raw" sensor reading and an "event". The TCRT5000 gives you a continuous on/off signal, but what you really want is one count per coin - which means edge detection, debouncing, and a tiny state machine. Those are the same three ideas that show up in every button, encoder, and motion sensor project, so once they click here they keep paying off.

projects.name: Porch Night-Light (KY-018 dusk-to-dawn fader)
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable; the KY-018 and the LED both run from the Uno's 5V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Turn off the room lights and watch a little yellow LED slowly glow brighter, like a porch light waking up at sunset. Turn the lights back on and it fades away again, all by itself.

**Why it's fun**: No button, no switch, no app - the light just KNOWS when it's dark. Cup your hand over the tiny sensor and you become the sunset.

A pretend porch-light that turns on by itself when the room gets dark. The KY-018 photoresistor watches the ambient light; a yellow LED on the breadboard fades up as the room darkens and fades back down at sunrise - exactly how a real dusk-to-dawn porch bulb behaves, but built on the kitchen table.

## Parts list

- KY-018 Photoresistor Module (the "eye" - an LDR on a little PCB)
- Arduino Uno R3 (5V, 10-bit ADC - perfect for an analog sensor)
- 1x yellow 5mm LED (stands in for a porch bulb; warm yellow looks the part)
- 1x 220R resistor (current limit for the LED)
- Breadboard + a handful of jumpers (3x F-M for the KY-018 module pins, the rest M-M for the LED side)

## Wiring notes

The KY-018 has a 3-pin header that reads, in most clones, `S`, `+`, `-` (signal, power, ground). Use F-M jumpers straight onto those:

- `S` -> Arduino `A0`
- `+` -> Arduino `5V` (the KY-018 wants 5V, not 3.3V - good habit to lock in now, because when you move to the ESP32 you'll need to remember the ESP32's GPIO and Vcc are 3.3V, not 5V)
- `-` -> Arduino `GND`

The LED lives on the breadboard:

- Arduino `D9` (a PWM pin - the `~` symbol is on it) -> 220R resistor -> LED anode (long leg)
- LED cathode (short leg) -> Arduino `GND`

Pin `D9` matters - the sketch fades the LED, and fading needs PWM. If you put it on `D7` instead it can only go full on or full off.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. Open the Arduino IDE.
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. (The Uno is built-in - no Boards Manager URL needed.)
3. No extra libraries to install for this sketch. Everything it uses (`analogRead`, `analogWrite`, `Serial`) is already baked into the IDE.
4. If Windows doesn't see your Uno at all, your board is a CH340 clone (ours is). Grab the CH340 driver from [sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html](https://sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html), install it, and unplug/replug the Uno.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the big square plug, same as an old printer). The green `ON` LED on the Uno should light up straight away.
2. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the one that says `COM*` (Windows) or `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` (Mac) or `/dev/ttyACM0` (Linux). If you see more than one, unplug the Uno, look again, plug it back, and the new one that appeared is yours.
3. Open the sketch. Nothing to edit - there are no passwords or WiFi names in this one. (If the LED ends up ON in daylight and OFF in the dark, come back and flip `DARK_IS_HIGH` from `true` to `false` near the top, then re-upload.)
4. Click the **Upload** button (the round right-arrow at the top-left). The orange `TX` and `RX` LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When it says **"Done uploading"** at the bottom, the sketch is running.
5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **9600** - that matches the `Serial.begin(9600)` in the sketch.
6. What you should see: a "Calibrating - cover then uncover the sensor" message, about 3 seconds of streaming raw numbers, then a steady stream of readings like `raw=812  dark%=64  led=140`. Cup your hand over the KY-018 and the `dark%` shoots up while the yellow LED fades on. Pull your hand away and watch it fade back down. That's success.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish** (random symbols, weird characters). The baud rate is wrong. Set it to **9600** in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor.
- **LED never lights up, even when you cover the sensor.** The LED is in backwards. The long leg (anode) goes to the 220R resistor / pin D9 side; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. No damage - just turn it around.
- **LED is on in daylight and off in the dark** (backwards behaviour). Your KY-018 clone is wired the other way round. Open the sketch, change `const bool DARK_IS_HIGH = true;` to `false`, and click Upload again.
## Talking points

- Why an analog pin (`A0`), not a digital one. The KY-018 doesn't say "dark / not dark"; it says "this much light", as a voltage from 0 to 5V. The Uno's ADC converts that voltage into a number from 0 to 1023, and that's the number we map into "how bright should the LED be".
- Why smoothing. If the porch bulb just looked at the raw reading and turned on whenever it crossed a threshold, every passing shadow would flicker it. The sketch keeps a running average (an exponential moving average, or EMA) so it reacts to "the sun went down" but ignores "a hand briefly waved past". This is the single most advanced trick in the sketch - everything else is map/constrain/analogWrite.
- Why two thresholds (`DARK_START_PERCENT` and `DARK_FULL_PERCENT`) instead of one. Two thresholds give a gentle fade-in region instead of a snap. This is what a real dusk-to-dawn sensor does inside, and it's also what makes the project feel polished instead of toy-like.
- Calibration at startup. KY-018 clones vary - some give a high reading in the dark, some give a low one, and the absolute values depend on the room. Sampling for ~3 seconds at boot while you cover-then-uncover the sensor lets the sketch figure out what "normal" looks like in your room, so you don't have to hardcode magic numbers. If you miss the prompt entirely, the sketch falls back to sensible defaults (200/900) so it still works.
- The polarity knob. Some KY-018 clones read higher as it gets darker; others read lower. The sketch has one constant near the top, `DARK_IS_HIGH`, that picks which. If the porch light is on in daylight and off in the dark, flip it from `true` to `false` and re-upload. One flag, one line - the rest of the code adapts.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap the yellow LED for the blue or green one and watch the same logic work unchanged - the LED colour is "front-end", the logic is "back-end".
- Cover the KY-018 with a cupped hand. The LED should fade up smoothly over half a second or so, not snap. If it snaps, increase `SMOOTHING` toward 0.2 (faster) or decrease it toward 0.01 (slower).
- Add a second LED on `D10` (also PWM) that comes on only when it's *really* dark - call it the "burglar deterrent" porch flood.
- Once Andy has soldered headers on a relay, the LED could be swapped for the 1-channel relay driving a real low-voltage lamp. (Project as written stays solder-free.)
- The KY-018 vs the LM393 photoresistor module: the LM393 board has a comparator on it and gives you a *digital* dark / not-dark output (and a threshold knob). The KY-018 gives you the *analog* reading and lets you decide. That's why this project uses fading - you can't fade off a digital signal.

## Why this is interesting

This is the cleanest possible example of "sensor in, actuator out, brain in the middle". Every home-automation project Andy will ever build is the same shape: read something about the world, decide what to do, change something in the world. Light -> Arduino -> LED is the smallest honest version of that loop, and once it works the same code structure scales straight up to "soil moisture -> ESP32 -> watering pump" or "motion -> ESP32 -> WiFi notification".

projects.name: Laser Tripwire Alarm (LDR + KY-008 pair)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the board's onboard regulator feeds 3.3V to both the laser module and the photoresistor receiver.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A red laser shoots a thin beam across a doorway and lands on a tiny sensor on the other side. Walk through the beam and a red alarm light snaps ON and stays on until you press the button to reset it.

**Why it's fun**: Set it up across your bedroom door and you instantly know when a sibling sneaks in, even hours later, because the light stays lit until you clear it. It is the closest you can get to building a real spy-movie laser tripwire with stuff that fits on a breadboard.

## Eye safety - read first

The KY-008 is a real 650nm laser diode module (laser-pointer class, typically rated under 5mW but still hazardous). Even brief direct exposure or a glint off a shiny surface can damage the retina, and the damage is painless and permanent. Before powering the board:

- Never look into the beam or the emitter aperture, not even "just to check it's on". If you need to confirm it works, look at the red dot on a matte surface (a piece of paper, a wall, the white face of the LDR module).
- Never aim the laser at a person, a pet, a window, a mirror, polished metal, or any glossy surface that could bounce a specular reflection back at someone.
- Aim it once with the receiver taped down, then leave it. Treat it like a loaded staple gun: it's pointed somewhere specific, and you don't pick it up to "see where it goes" while live.
- The sketch turns the laser ON as soon as the board boots. Plug power in only after both modules are pointed at each other and taped in place.

## Parts list

- 1x Photoresistor Module (LM393 comparator) - the receiver. It has a built-in pot to set the dark/light threshold and a clean digital DO output.
- 1x KY-008 Red Laser Module (650nm) - the emitter. The narrow beam crosses the doorway and lands on the receiver.
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the receiver, controls the laser, latches the alarm.
- 1x red 5mm LED + 220R resistor - "the wire's been tripped" indicator that stays on.
- 1x tactile push-button - re-arm button to clear the latched alarm.
- Breadboard + DuPont jumpers.

## Wiring notes

Reminder: the laser turns on the moment the ESP32 boots. Finish all wiring, point the laser at the receiver, and tape both modules down BEFORE you plug the USB cable in.

- Both modules run on 3.3V from the ESP32 (the laser module is happy at 3.3V; it's a touch dimmer than at 5V but still very visible at room range).
- The LM393 receiver module has 4 pins: VCC, GND, DO (digital out), AO (analog, ignored here). Only DO is connected to the ESP32.
- The DO pin is **active LOW when bright**. With the laser hitting the LDR, DO reads LOW. When something blocks the beam, DO goes HIGH. The code reflects this exactly.
- The KY-008 has 3 pins in a row. On this clone they are:
  - **S** (signal) -> GPIO 23 on the ESP32. Drive HIGH to turn the beam on.
  - **middle pin** -> **NC, leave disconnected**. Do not feed 3V3 here; it is not a power input on this module.
  - **-** (GND) -> GND rail.
- The LED goes from GPIO 22 through a 220R resistor to GND. Standard ESP32 LED hookup.
- The re-arm button connects GPIO 4 to GND. The internal pull-up does the rest.

**Aiming and calibration**

1. With the USB cable still unplugged, lay out the laser and the receiver across the doorway and tape them down so they can't drift. Point the emitter at the white LDR window on the receiver.
2. Plug in USB. The laser turns on automatically. Do not look at the emitter; look at the receiver to confirm the red dot landed on the white window.
3. Turn the blue trim-pot on the receiver module slowly. Its onboard signal LED will flip ON when dark, OFF when bright. Find the spot where the laser-on state is **just barely** counted as "bright" (LED just off). That's your most sensitive setting.
4. Wave a finger through the beam (not your eye). The red alarm LED should latch on, and serial should print `>>> TRIPWIRE BROKEN <<<`.
5. Press the button to re-arm.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

Before you plug anything in, double-check the laser is pointed at the white face of the LDR module and both modules are taped down. The sketch turns the laser ON the instant the board powers up, and you do not want a live beam swinging around the room while you fiddle with the IDE.

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open the IDE, go to **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. In the search box type `esp32`. Find "esp32 by Espressif Systems" and click Install. It takes a few minutes - good time for a snack.
3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**.
4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch - it only uses the built-in `pinMode`, `digitalRead`, `digitalWrite`, and `Serial` stuff that comes with the ESP32 core.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a USB cable (make sure it is a **data** cable, not a charge-only one - if the board lights up but no COM port appears, that is usually the cable).
2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on a Mac it is `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`).
3. This sketch has no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in - leave the pin numbers alone unless you wired it differently.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). If you see "Connecting......_____" dots scrolling for more than 5 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. This is normal on the NodeMCU-32S the first time.
5. When upload finishes you should see "Hard resetting via RTS pin". The laser comes on right then.
6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the monitor window) to **115200**. You should see:
   ```
   Laser Tripwire Alarm starting...
   Laser is ON. Aim it at the white dot on the LDR module
   and turn the blue trim-pot until the module's signal LED
   just barely turns OFF. Then block the beam to test.
   ```
   Now use a small screwdriver on the blue trim-pot on the LDR module: turn it slowly until the tiny green "signal" LED on the module just barely switches off while the beam is hitting it. Wave your hand through the beam - the green LED on the module should pop on, and your red alarm LED should latch on with `>>> TRIPWIRE BROKEN <<<` printed in the Serial Monitor. Press the re-arm button to clear it.

**Common gotchas:**

- **"Connecting......_____" forever on upload.** The NodeMCU-32S often needs the **BOOT** button held down during the first upload. Press and hold BOOT, click Upload, and only release BOOT once you see "Writing..." appear.
- **Alarm goes off the second you power up, even with the beam aimed correctly.** The trim-pot on the LDR module is set too sensitive. Turn it slowly while watching the green signal LED on the module - you want that LED OFF while the laser is hitting it, and ON when you block the beam. If it never changes, the laser is missing the white dot - re-aim it.
- **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`.** The baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200**, matching the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch.
## Talking points

- **A tripwire is just a "before vs after" test.** The laser doesn't measure anything fancy. It just gives the receiver one easy thing to see. When that one thing disappears, we know something passed through.
- **Why latch the alarm?** A real intruder is only in the beam for a few milliseconds. If the LED only lit while the beam was broken, you'd never see it. Latching means: once tripped, stay tripped until a human acknowledges it.
- **Two modules talking through air.** There are no wires between the laser and the receiver - the beam itself is the signal. That's the same idea as a TV remote, a barcode scanner, or fibre-optic internet, just slower.
- **The LM393 comparator on the receiver.** The little chip on the module compares the LDR's voltage to whatever the pot is set to and gives a clean HIGH/LOW. Without it, you'd be reading a noisy analog value and writing your own threshold code.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a piezo buzzer in parallel with the alarm LED for an audible siren.
- Drive the laser through a transistor and **pulse** it at 1 kHz, then have the receiver only count the alarm if the pulse goes missing. That defeats someone shining a flashlight at the receiver to fool it.
- Bounce the beam off a small mirror so the laser and receiver sit on the same side of the doorway. Easier to install, looks more like a spy movie. (Mirror placement still needs the eye-safety rules: don't aim it where a reflection could find a face.)
- Have the ESP32 publish the trip event over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once the Pi is booted).
- Add a 5-second arming countdown so you can leave the room before the tripwire goes hot.

## Why this is interesting

It's the first project in the kit where two separate active components have to physically agree on something across empty space. The wiring on the breadboard is short and friendly, but the real "circuit" is invisible. That makes the debugging satisfying: nudge the laser, watch the latch hold, press re-arm, and you've built a tiny security system out of a 50-cent LDR module and a laser pointer.

projects.name: Coin Drop Counter (optical slot + OLED)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S USB-C port; the ESP32's onboard regulator feeds 3.3V to the slot sensor and OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Drop a coin through a little slot. The number on the tiny screen jumps up by one, instantly, every single time. Drop ten coins fast and watch it climb to ten without missing a single one.

**Why it's fun**: It feels like the screen is reading your mind because it counts faster than your eye can follow. Challenge your dad to drop five coins faster than you can, then point at the screen when it caught every single one.

## Parts list

- 1x Optical Slot / Speed Sensor (the protagonist - an IR LED facing a phototransistor across a small gap)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C, SSD1306)
- 1x Breadboard
- A handful of male-male and female-male jumpers
- Coins, popsicle-stick wedges, or strips of paper to drop through the slot

No resistors needed - the slot sensor module already has its own pull-up and current-limit resistors on board, and the OLED is I2C with internal pull-ups on the breakout. No LEDs in this build, so no current-limiting resistor either.

## Wiring notes

The slot sensor has 4 pins: `VCC`, `GND`, `D0` (digital out), and sometimes `A0` (analog). We only care about `D0`. When nothing is in the slot, the beam reaches the phototransistor and `D0` sits HIGH. The instant something blocks the beam, `D0` snaps LOW. That falling edge is what we count.

- Sensor `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`
- Sensor `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`
- Sensor `D0` -> ESP32 `GPIO 4`
- OLED `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`
- OLED `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`
- OLED `SDA` -> ESP32 `GPIO 21`
- OLED `SCL` -> ESP32 `GPIO 22`

Orient the slot **vertically** so coins fall down through the gap under gravity - tape the sensor module to the edge of a book or shoebox with the U-shape opening pointing up. A horizontal slot won't work; coins need somewhere to fall.

If drops sometimes don't register even though they clearly passed through the slot, try moving the sensor `VCC` wire from `3V3` to `VIN` (the 5V USB rail on the NodeMCU). The LM393 comparator on these slot modules is spec'd 3.3-5V, but some clones produce a cleaner, sharper falling edge with a full 5V supply. The `D0` output is still safe to feed into a 3.3V ESP32 GPIO - it's just a slow logic-level signal pulled to whatever rail the module runs on, and ESP32 inputs tolerate that fine in practice for this use.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, search for `esp32`, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (about 200 MB) so go grab a snack.
3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**) and install these two, one at a time:
   - Search `Adafruit GFX` -> install **Adafruit GFX Library**.
   - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> install **Adafruit SSD1306**.
   If the IDE asks "install missing dependencies?", click **Install All**.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable that can carry data** (a charge-only cable will look like nothing happens - if the board does not show up, swap the cable first).
2. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on a Mac like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.wchusbserial-*`). If nothing new appears, your laptop may need the CP210x or CH340 USB-to-serial driver - ask your dad to help install it.
3. There are **no passwords or placeholders to fill in** for this sketch (it does not use WiFi). You can flash it as-is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a while, then "Connecting....". If it gets stuck on `Connecting......_____......_____`, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S clones need this on every upload, others never need it.
5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin..."** you are done flashing.
6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor pane, set the baud rate to **115200** (this matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). You should see startup messages, and the OLED should light up showing `0` drops. Wave a finger through the slot and the count should jump to `1` on both the screen and the Serial Monitor. That's how you know it worked.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Stuck on "Connecting......":** hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 the moment it starts trying to connect, let go once "Writing..." appears. Charge-only USB-C cables also cause this - if BOOT does not help, try a different cable.
- **OLED is black but the sketch uploaded fine:** the SSD1306 address is set to `0x3C` in the code. A few clone OLEDs are wired for `0x3D` instead - if the screen stays blank, change `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check `SDA -> GPIO 21` and `SCL -> GPIO 22` are not swapped.
- **Count jumps by 2 or 3 on a single coin:** the coin is bouncing the beam on the way through. Bump the `DEBOUNCE_MS` value near the top of the sketch from `40` up to `60` or `80` and re-upload. If drops are being missed instead, move the sensor's `VCC` wire from `3V3` to `VIN` (the 5V rail) as the Wiring notes describe.
## Talking points

- "What is an interrupt?" Most code in a loop is busy checking things. An interrupt is the chip dropping everything the moment a pin changes, running a tiny piece of code, then jumping back. For something as fast as a coin falling through a 5 mm gap, polling in `loop()` could miss it. An interrupt cannot.
- "Why a `volatile` keyword?" The compiler usually assumes nothing else changes a variable behind its back. `volatile` tells it "no, this can change at any moment because an interrupt might touch it" so it always re-reads from memory.
- "What's debounce?" A coin doesn't break the beam cleanly - it can flicker the signal a few times in a few milliseconds. We ignore any second trigger that comes within 40 ms of the previous one.
- "What does `readSnapshot()` do?" An interrupt can fire halfway through `loop()` reading the shared variables, which would give us a torn, half-updated value. `readSnapshot()` briefly turns interrupts off, copies everything in one go, then turns interrupts back on. That's a "critical section".

## Things to change once it works

- Tape a piece of card with evenly-spaced slits to the side of a spinning fan and you've turned the same sensor into a tachometer (RPM meter). Count slits per second, divide by slit count, multiply by 60.
- Add the buzzer from the kit (or a piezo if you grab one) so each coin makes a beep.
- Make a 10-second window: how many coins can you drop in 10 seconds? Reset on button press.
- Log each drop's timestamp to the Serial Monitor and paste into a spreadsheet to graph drop intervals.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first build in the kit where timing accuracy matters. Polling in `loop()` works fine for buttons and slow sensors, but the moment you start measuring fast physical events - a coin drop, a fan blade, a moving belt - you need interrupts. Once Andy sees the count tick up reliably even when he drops three coins in quick succession, the "why use an interrupt" lesson sticks. Same hardware later becomes the speedometer for a Lego car, the slot encoder on a robot wheel, or a beam-break alarm across a doorway.
