projects.name: Stealth Timer - hold still or the LED dies
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered over its USB-C cable from a laptop or a 5 V USB phone charger; the PIR sensor, OLED and LEDs all run from the ESP32's onboard 5 V and 3.3 V rails.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Stand in front of the little sensor and freeze. A green LED glows and the screen counts how many seconds you hold still. Twitch even a tiny bit and the red LED flashes - your streak resets to zero.

**Why it's fun**: It's a real-life "don't blink" game you built yourself, and the sensor can spot a finger wiggle from across the room. Challenge your dad, your sister, or the dog - whoever holds the longest streak wins.

## Parts list

- 1x HC-SR505 Mini PIR Motion Sensor (the star: a tiny PIR with a clear plastic dome that fires HIGH when it sees a warm body move)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C)
- 1x 5mm green LED (glows while you are holding still)
- 1x 5mm red LED (flashes when you twitch)
- 2x 330R resistors (one in series with each LED)
- 1x breadboard, plus a handful of M-M and F-M jumpers

## Wiring notes

The HC-SR505 has only three pins: `VCC`, `OUT`, `GND`. It accepts 5 V on VCC and its OUT line idles at 0 V and pulses HIGH (about 3.0 V on this module) when triggered, which the ESP32's 3.3 V GPIO can read safely without a level shifter.

Power the PIR and the OLED from the ESP32's `5V` pin (which is the USB rail when you have the board plugged into your laptop). Tie every ground - PIR, OLED, both LEDs - back to the ESP32's `GND`.

The OLED is I2C and goes on the ESP32's default I2C pins: `SDA = GPIO 21`, `SCL = GPIO 22`. The PIR's OUT goes to `GPIO 13`. The green LED's anode goes through a 330R resistor to `GPIO 18`, the red LED's anode goes through its own 330R resistor to `GPIO 19`, and both cathodes go to ground.

Important first-time gotcha: the HC-SR505 needs about 30 seconds after power-up to settle - it will output garbage during that window. The sketch handles this for you by showing a "Warming up PIR" screen and slow-pulsing the red LED. Stay out of view while that's running.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Search for `esp32` and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so go grab a snack.
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the long list.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these three, one at a time. Just type the name into the search box and click Install on the top hit:
   - `Adafruit GFX Library`
   - `Adafruit SSD1306`
   - `Adafruit BusIO` (the IDE may offer to install this for you when you add SSD1306 - say yes)

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with its **USB-C cable**. You should see a tiny red power LED light up on the board.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-...`). If nothing shows up, try a different USB cable - some cheap USB-C cables are charge-only and have no data wires inside.
3. This sketch has no Wi-Fi password or other placeholders to fill in - the pin numbers at the top of the file already match the wiring.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left of the IDE). The bottom of the window will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting..." and you will see dots scroll past. If it gets stuck on "Connecting....." for more than about 10 seconds, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until the upload starts, then let go.
5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the dropdown on the right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code).
6. What you should see: the OLED lights up and says **"Warming up PIR... Stay out of view!"**. Walk away from the desk for about 30 seconds. When the warm-up finishes, the **green LED comes on** and the screen starts counting **"Now : 0.1 s, 0.2 s, ..."**. Wave your hand at the PIR dome - the green LED goes out, the **red LED flashes for about a second**, and the counter resets to zero. That means it works.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Stuck on "Connecting....."** on upload - hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while the IDE shows "Connecting....." until it starts writing. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this on every upload, others only on the first one.
- **OLED stays dark and the Serial Monitor prints "OLED not found"** - the I2C address on these little screens is usually `0x3C` (which is what the sketch uses), but a few are wired for `0x3D`. Swap that one number in the line `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` and upload again. Also double-check SDA is on GPIO 21 and SCL is on GPIO 22 - swapping those two is the #1 reason a fresh OLED looks dead.
- **Red LED flashes constantly, even when nobody is in the room** - you did not wait out the 30-second warm-up, or you are sitting in the PIR's view. Unplug, walk out of the room, plug back in, and stay away until the green LED comes on by itself.
## Talking points

- The HC-SR505 doesn't see *light*. It sees *infrared heat moving across its field of view*. That's why holding still in front of it - even with your eyes open - makes it go quiet.
- Inside that little plastic dome is a Fresnel lens. It splits the view into zones; the sensor only triggers when warmth crosses from one zone into another.
- The OUT pin is digital, not analog. There's no "how much motion" reading - just yes or no.
- The ESP32 is reading the pin millions of times per second, but we only act once per loop with a tiny delay - that's enough.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer that beeps softly the longer your streak gets, so you have to hold still through rising tension.
- Show a tiny "high score" bar graph on the OLED that grows with your best time.
- Save the best streak to ESP32 flash (Preferences library) so it survives a reboot.
- Add a second HC-SR505 aimed sideways and only count "frontal" motion - turns the game into a stealth competition for two people.

## Why this is interesting

PIR sensors are the everyday motion detector you've seen a thousand times - in burglar alarms, in motion-activated lights at the supermarket, in automatic taps. The HC-SR505 is the tiniest, cheapest version of that hardware, and it has exactly one job: tell you whether a warm thing just moved. Turning that single bit of information into a little game is a satisfying way to feel how a real sensor behaves: the warm-up window, the lens zones, the way it doesn't care about a glass of hot water but cares a lot about your hand.

projects.name: Storm Glass - 3-hour pressure trend forecaster
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered from a laptop / phone-charger USB cable; the ESP32's 3.3 V pin supplies both the BMP280 and the OLED through the breadboard rails.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little screen sits on your desk showing today's air pressure, a giant up or down arrow, and one word like "Fair" or "Storm!" The arrow flips direction hours before the weather actually changes outside.

**Why it's fun**: You can predict the weather before the weather app does, then run around the house yelling "I told you it would rain!" Pick it up and walk upstairs and you can literally watch the pressure drop, because you just climbed away from a tiny bit of the sky.

## Parts list

- **GY-BMP280 Barometric Pressure Sensor** - the protagonist. A tiny Bosch chip that measures absolute air pressure to about +-1 Pa. Pressure is what weather forecasters actually watch: rising pressure usually means fair weather coming, falling pressure means a storm coming.
- **ESP32 NodeMCU-32S** - reads the sensor and drives the screen.
- **0.96" OLED Display (I2C)** - shows the current pressure, a big up/down arrow, and a one-word forecast.
- **Breadboard** plus **M-M** and **F-M jumper wires** - both modules share the same two I2C wires (SDA + SCL) plus 3.3 V and GND, so the breadboard just acts as a 4-rail splitter.

## Wiring notes

Both modules are I2C. That means four wires total from the ESP32, no matter how many I2C devices you add:

- ESP32 `3V3` -> breadboard `+` rail -> BMP280 `VCC` and OLED `VCC`
- ESP32 `GND` -> breadboard `-` rail -> BMP280 `GND` and OLED `GND`
- ESP32 `GPIO21` (SDA) -> BMP280 `SDA` and OLED `SDA`
- ESP32 `GPIO22` (SCL) -> BMP280 `SCL` and OLED `SCL`

Both boards already have I2C pull-up resistors on them, so no extra resistors are needed.

The BMP280 sits at I2C address `0x76` on most GY-BMP280 clones. A few clones are at `0x77`. The code tries both so you do not have to care.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (this can take a few minutes - lots to download).
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"**.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (the little book icon on the left) and install these three, one at a time:
   - Search `Adafruit BMP280` and install **"Adafruit BMP280 Library"**. When it asks about installing extra dependencies (Adafruit BusIO + Adafruit Unified Sensor), click **"Install all"**.
   - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` and install **"Adafruit SSD1306"**. Again click **"Install all"** so it grabs Adafruit GFX too.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB cable that can carry data** (some charging cables only carry power - if the board does not show up, try a different cable).
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new port that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-...`; on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyUSB0`).
3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow pointing right, top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting......". If "Connecting" dots keep going for more than 5 seconds, press and hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards do this automatically, but the trick is good to know.)
5. When it says **"Done uploading"**, open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the monitor) to **115200**.
6. You should see lines like `BMP280 found at 0x76` and `OLED ready`, then a pressure reading in hPa printed once a second. The OLED screen should light up showing a number around 1013, a temperature, and a flat arrow `=` (the arrow will not move until at least 3 hours of readings have piled up - that is normal, give it time).

**Common gotchas:**

- **"Connecting......" never finishes on the first upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while you click Upload, and let go once you see "Writing..." appear. Some clone boards need this every single time.
- **Screen stays black but Serial Monitor shows readings.** The OLED is probably at address `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. Or you swapped SDA and SCL - double-check that GPIO21 goes to **both** SDA pins and GPIO22 goes to **both** SCL pins.
- **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `???????`.** The baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code.
## Talking points

- **What is air pressure?** The weight of all the air above you, pressing down. At sea level on an average day it is about 1013 hPa. When a storm front moves in, that number drops; when it leaves, it rises.
- **Why a 3-hour delta?** Weather services use the 3-hour pressure tendency as the basic forecast signal. One single reading tells you nothing - it is the *change over time* that predicts the weather.
- **Why a ring buffer?** We keep 180 readings (one per minute for 3 hours). Instead of growing a list forever, we overwrite the oldest slot every minute. This is the same trick used in audio buffers and game replay systems.
- **I2C is a shared bus.** The OLED and the BMP280 use the *same* two wires. They get along because they have different addresses (`0x3C` vs `0x76`).

## Things to change once it works

- Add a 24-hour delta too (just bump `HISTORY_MINUTES` to 1440 and add a second arrow).
- Plot the history as a tiny line graph across the bottom of the OLED.
- Publish the pressure to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is online, so the Hallway Weather Window project can show it alongside temperature.
- Calibrate to altitude: feed in the local altitude and the sketch can spit out sea-level-equivalent pressure that matches what weather.gov reports.
- Add a piezo buzzer that beeps when the forecast crosses into "Storm!" so you get a warning even when you are not looking at the screen.

## Why this is interesting

This is a real instrument, not a toy. The BMP280 is sensitive enough that you can *see* the pressure change when you walk up a flight of stairs (about -0.4 hPa per 4 metres). And the 3-hour delta really does predict weather - leave it on the kitchen counter for a week and you will start trusting the arrow more than the phone app.

It is also the cleanest example in the kit of the I2C-bus idea: two completely different chips, from two different vendors, sharing two wires. Once Andy is comfortable with this, adding a third or fourth I2C sensor is just plugging it into the same rails.

projects.name: Pocket Battery Health Monitor (OLED + LEDs)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 powered by laptop USB. OLED runs from the ESP32's 3.3V rail; LEDs are driven by GPIO. The voltage module is passive (just resistors) and draws no power. The battery under test connects only to the module's input screws.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Touch the little board's two screws to any battery's plus and minus ends. The tiny screen instantly shows the volts, a bar graph, and one big word: HEALTHY, LOW, or DEAD. A green LED or a red LED lights up too, so you know the answer from across the room.

**Why it's fun**: You become the battery doctor of the house. Go hunting through every drawer, remote, and toy, zap each battery with the probes, and sort them into a "still good" pile and a "throw away" pile - your parents will actually thank you.

## Parts list

- Voltage Sensor Module (0-25V divider) - the star: a tiny board with two resistors (30k + 7.5k) that shrinks a DC voltage down to something the ESP32's 3.3V ADC can survive. The module is rated up to 25V at the input, but as you'll see in Talking points, the ESP32's ADC only stays linear up to about 12V of input. Above that the screen number goes wonky.
- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the divider's output on GPIO 34 and drives the screen
- 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - shows the live number, a bar graph, and the word HEALTHY / LOW / DEAD
- 1x green LED with a 220R limiter and 1x red LED with a 330R limiter - instant "go / no-go" feedback even before you look at the screen. Green gets the smaller resistor on purpose - green LEDs need a higher forward voltage than red, so at 3.3V drive a 330R would leave it visibly dim.
- Breadboard + jumpers - no soldering

A 9V battery (or any low-voltage DC source up to ~12V you want to measure) is the **device under test**. You touch its terminals to the voltage module's input. The whole project itself is powered through the ESP32's USB cable. The voltage module is a passive resistor pair, so it draws no power of its own and does not need a VCC connection.

## Wiring notes

The voltage module has two sides:

- **Screw-terminal side (input):** the thing you measure. The screws are labelled `VCC` (positive) and `GND` (negative). Andy connects the battery being tested here.
- **Pin-header side (output):** three pins labelled `S` (signal, the divided-down voltage), `+` (unused, leave alone), and `-` (ground). The `-` pin **must share ground with the ESP32** or the reading is meaningless.

So the wiring story is: battery `+` and `-` go into the screw terminals. `S` goes to ESP32 GPIO 34. The module's `-` pin goes to ESP32 GND. Same-ground is the rule that makes the whole thing work.

OLED is normal I2C: VCC to 3.3V (most 0.96" I2C OLEDs have an onboard regulator and accept 3.3-5V; the ESP32's 3.3V rail is fine), GND to GND, SDA to GPIO 21, SCL to GPIO 22.

The green LED gets a 220R resistor in series with its anode (long leg). The red LED gets a 330R. Cathodes both to GND.

**Do not** feed more than 25V into the module, and **do not** ever connect AC, mains, or the wall. This project is for batteries and bench DC supplies only.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box. Install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (a few hundred MB) so let it finish - go get a snack.
3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the list.
4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (the little book icon on the left). You need two libraries for the screen:
   - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> Install. It will ask if you want to install dependencies too - say **Install All**.
   - Search `Adafruit GFX Library` -> Install (this one usually came along with the first install, but double-check).

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB cable that carries data** (some cheap charging cables are power-only and will not show up - if the board's red power LED lights but no port appears, swap the cable).
2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on a Mac it looks like `cu.usbserial-xxxx`; on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`.
3. Open the sketch. There are no WiFi passwords or secret keys to fill in for this one - but find the line `const float CAL = 1.00f;` near the top. Leave it at 1.00 for now; you will nudge it up or down later once you check a known-good battery against a multimeter.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting...". If it sits on "Connecting..." for more than 10 seconds and starts printing dots, **press and hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 board until the upload starts. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this on the very first flash.
5. When it says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` call in the code).
6. Within a second or two the OLED should light up showing a voltage near `0.00 V` and the word **DEAD** (because nothing is connected to the screw terminals yet). The red LED should be on, the green LED off. The Serial Monitor will print a fresh voltage reading every loop.
7. Now touch the voltage module's two screw terminals to a battery: **VCC screw to battery +, GND screw to battery -**. A fresh 9V alkaline should show around 9.3-9.6V, the bar graph should jump near full, the word should flip to **HEALTHY**, and the green LED should come on. That is the win.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Upload stuck on "Connecting..."**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the dots turn into a progress bar, then release. First-flash quirk on NodeMCU-32S.
- **Screen stays black but the LEDs work**: the OLED's I2C address is probably `0x3D` instead of `0x3C` on your specific module. Change `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check SDA goes to GPIO 21 and SCL goes to GPIO 22 - swapping them is the #1 wiring mistake.
- **Voltage reads zero or garbage when a battery is connected**: the module's `-` pin on the header side is not connected to ESP32 GND. The battery and the ESP32 must share a ground or the ADC has nothing to measure against. Also make sure the signal wire is on the module's `S` pin going to GPIO 34, not the unused `+` pin.
- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮@⸮⸮`**: the baud rate dropdown is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)`.
## Talking points

- The voltage module is just a **voltage divider**: two resistors in series. The "S" pin sits at the junction and carries a fraction of the input voltage. With 30k on top and 7.5k on the bottom, the ratio is 5:1 - feed 25V in, get 5V at S. Feed 9V in, get 1.8V at S. The ESP32 then multiplies by 5 in software to recover the original number.
- **Why the real measurement ceiling is ~12V, not 25V.** With the attenuation setting we use (`ADC_11db`), the ESP32 ADC is only linear from about 0.15V up to about 2.45V at the pin. Multiply 2.45V by the divider's 5:1 ratio and you get ~12V at the input. Above that, the ADC saturates and the displayed number flattens out - the module isn't damaged, but the reading is no longer trustworthy. The code shows a `>12V (clip)` warning when that happens. For 9V alkalines, 12V SLA at rest, and 18650 cells, you're comfortably inside the linear band.
- Why GPIO 34? It's an **input-only ADC pin** on ESP32 and it's also on ADC1, which (unlike ADC2) keeps working while WiFi is on. Good habit for future projects.
- The ESP32 ADC is famously a little non-linear, so the code includes a `CAL` fudge factor (default 1.00). Once everything works, Andy can compare the OLED reading to a real multimeter on the same battery, and nudge `CAL` until they agree **inside the band he actually cares about** (e.g. 6V-10V for testing 9V alkalines).

## Things to change once it works

- Change `HEALTHY_VOLTS` to suit a different battery. For a 12V lead-acid you'd use ~12.2V (right at the edge of the linear range, so multimeter-calibrate carefully). For a single Li-ion 18650 cell you'd use ~3.5V (well inside the safe range).
- Add a third "warning" yellow LED for the in-between band.
- Add WiFi and post the voltage to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is booted, turning this into a real battery-monitoring node.
- Plot voltage over time on the OLED instead of just a level bar - sample once a second into a 128-wide ring buffer and you get a free oscilloscope.
- To extend the measurement range past ~12V on this exact module, you'd need to either add another resistor in series upstream (extending the divider) or switch the attenuation setting on a different pin - both are good follow-up experiments.

## Why this is interesting

Voltage measurement is the most fundamental thing a sensor can do, and yet it's hidden inside almost every other module - the joystick, the photoresistor, the soil sensor, all secretly produce a voltage and let the microcontroller's ADC read it. Building this project makes that hidden machinery visible. After this, Andy will look at every analog sensor in the kit and recognise the same trick: "it's just a voltage I'm reading and converting to a number."

It's also genuinely useful. Every project from here on uses batteries or DC supplies, and now Andy has a meter he built himself that tells him whether the battery in his hand still has juice. And the "ADC only goes linear to ~2.45V at the pin" lesson is one of those gotchas every ESP32 project eventually trips over - better to meet it here with a clear printout than to chase a phantom bug later.

projects.name: Raindrop Reporter - live wetness on OLED
projects.power_supply: Powered from a USB-C cable plugged into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S. The board's 3V3 pin supplies the raindrop sensor module, the OLED, and the LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Flick water onto a little comb-shaped board and the tiny screen instantly changes from DRY to MISTY to WET to SOAKED, with a blue LED that glows brighter the wetter it gets. There's a wiggling bar on the screen too, so you can watch it climb in real time as the water sits there.

**Why it's fun**: It's a weather detector you build yourself - leave it on the windowsill and you'll know the second rain hits, before anyone else in the house. Try licking your finger and touching the board, or breathing on it really close - you'll see how sensitive it is and feel like a mad scientist running tests.

## Parts list

- 1x Raindrop Sensor (the comb board + its little LM393 amplifier board)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED display (I2C, address 0x3C)
- 1x Blue 5mm LED
- 1x 330R resistor (current limit for the LED)
- 1x Breadboard
- Jumper wires (a mix of M-M and F-M)

## Wiring notes

The raindrop sensor comes in two pieces joined by a 2-wire lead: a flat comb-trace board (the bit that gets wet) and a small amplifier board with the 4-pin header. The amplifier board is where everything plugs in.

- Sensor `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`. The module is happy at 3.3V; do NOT use 5V here even though the silkscreen allows it - the analog output would swing past what the ESP32 ADC tolerates.
- Sensor `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`.
- Sensor `AO` (analog out) -> ESP32 `GPIO34`. GPIO34 is input-only and lives on ADC1, which keeps working while WiFi is on - a small but important detail on the ESP32.
- Ignore the `DO` (digital out) pin. The on-board pot only sets the threshold for `DO`; we read the analog signal directly so we don't have to twist the trimmer.
- OLED: `VCC -> 3V3`, `GND -> GND`, `SDA -> GPIO21`, `SCL -> GPIO22`. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins.
- Blue LED: long leg (anode) goes through the 330R resistor to `GPIO5`, short leg (cathode) to `GND`.

The raindrop sensor is "wet = low value, dry = high value". That's because the comb traces work as a variable resistor: water bridges them, the resistance drops, and the on-board divider pulls AO toward ground.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   Click OK.
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, give it a few minutes.
3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**.
4. Install the two screen libraries: **Tools -> Manage Libraries**. Search for and install:
   - **Adafruit SSD1306** (this is the OLED driver)
   - **Adafruit GFX Library** (this is the drawing toolbox the OLED driver uses; the IDE may ask to install it automatically as a dependency - say yes)

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or micro-USB, depending on which NodeMCU-32S you have - check the port on the board). Use a real data cable, not a charge-only one, or the laptop will not see the board at all.
2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM4`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`). If you do not see one, unplug, wait two seconds, plug back in.
3. This sketch has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - leave the four threshold numbers near the top (`SOAKED_BELOW`, `WET_BELOW`, `MISTY_BELOW`) at their defaults for the first run. You will tune them in a minute.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting....". If "Connecting...." keeps printing dots and never starts uploading, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see the upload start, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards do this automatically; some need the button.)
5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (this matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code).
6. **What you should see:** the OLED lights up with "Raindrop Reporter / warming up..." for about a second, then switches to a live readout showing the raw number (around 4000 in dry air), the word **DRY**, and a wetness bar at zero. Lick a finger and touch the comb-trace board - within a second the number drops, the word flips to **MISTY** or **WET**, the bar climbs, and the blue LED turns on. Flick a drop of water on it for **SOAKED**.

Now tune the thresholds: watch the raw number in the Serial Monitor while the board is dry, while damp from a fingertip, while a real drop sits on it, and while it is properly wet. Edit `SOAKED_BELOW`, `WET_BELOW`, and `MISTY_BELOW` at the top of the sketch so each state matches what you saw, and click Upload again.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Upload stuck on "Connecting....":** hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the upload bar starts moving, then release. Some USB cables are also charge-only with no data lines - swap the cable if a known-good board still will not connect.
- **OLED stays black and the Serial Monitor prints "OLED not found":** SDA and SCL are swapped, or one of the OLED's power pins is not seated in the breadboard rail. Wiggle them, and double-check `VCC -> 3V3` (not 5V).
- **Serial Monitor shows garbage like `~?@@?~`:** the baud rate in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is not set to **115200**. Change it and the text becomes readable instantly.
## Talking points

- Why GPIO34? Show Sandy the ESP32 pinout. ADC2 pins go quiet whenever WiFi turns on - we picked an ADC1 pin so we don't get bitten by that later.
- The `classify()` thresholds were guessed. The real ones come from watching the Serial Monitor while flicking water on the board: write down the value when dry, when finger-damp, when a drop is sitting on it, and when it's fully submerged. Edit the four constants at the top to match.
- Averaging 8 samples is a tiny but useful trick - one stray reading would make the display jitter between MISTY and WET every quarter second otherwise.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer that beeps when state crosses into SOAKED - then it's a basement-flood alarm.
- Log the state changes with `millis()` over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi MQTT broker, so you've got a record of when it rained.
- Use the `DO` pin instead of `AO` and skip the OLED - simpler "rain or no rain" version for the XIAO ESP32-C3.
- Make the wetness bar pulse faster the wetter it gets - visible feedback without needing to read numbers.

## Why this is interesting

The raindrop sensor is the cheapest physical-world-touching sensor you have - it's literally two interleaved copper combs and a comparator. This project shows the full beginner-friendly chain: a noisy real-world analog signal, smoothed by averaging, classified into human-readable buckets, then displayed two different ways (text + bar graph + LED). It's also the simplest hook into "act on the world": once you can confidently detect rain, the same code pattern works for soil moisture, water level, and any other resistive/analog sensor in the kit.

projects.name: Tub Filler Traffic Light
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable. The Uno's onboard 5V rail then feeds the water sensor, the LCD, and the LED resistors.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Dip a little probe into a glass of water. A screen shows a bar graph filling up, plus a percent. Three LEDs glow like a stoplight - red when it's nearly empty, yellow when it's getting close, green when the "tub" is full.

**Why it's fun**: It reacts instantly. Lift the probe out and the bar drops; push it back in and the green light pops on. It feels like a real gadget you'd see stuck to the side of a bathtub or a fish tank, and you built it.

## Parts list

- Arduino Uno R3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the LCD and LEDs)
- Water Level Sensor (resistive comb - the protagonist; more water touching the combs = lower resistance = higher analog reading)
- LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (shows a live bar graph and a percent number)
- 3 LEDs (red, yellow, green) - "stoplight" progress indicator
- 3x 330R resistors (current-limiters, one per LED)
- 1x 1M resistor (pull-down on the sensor's signal pin so the reading falls cleanly to 0 when dry)
- Breadboard + a small handful of M-M and F-M jumper wires (one pack of each is plenty)
- A glass of water (the "tub") to dip the sensor into

## Wiring notes

- The water sensor has three pins labelled `+`, `-`, `S`. `+` goes to Arduino 5V, `-` goes to Arduino GND, and `S` is the analog output that goes to Arduino A0.
- The 1M pull-down resistor goes from A0 to GND. This is the "why doesn't it read zero when dry?" fix - without it, the floating input drifts and shows random numbers when there's no water.
- LCD I2C backpack: only 4 wires. VCC -> 5V, GND -> GND, SDA -> A4, SCL -> A5. (On the Uno, A4 and A5 double as the I2C bus.)
- LEDs: each LED's long leg (anode) goes through a 330R resistor to its Arduino pin. Short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Red on D5, Yellow on D6, Green on D7.
- IMPORTANT - do not submerge the top half of the water sensor board. Only the gold combs should ever touch water. The exposed components above will corrode in days if they get wet.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno.
2. Open the Arduino IDE. The Uno's board support is built in, so no extra board package is needed.
3. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**.
4. Install the LCD library: Tools -> Manage Libraries... -> type **LiquidCrystal I2C** in the search box -> install **"LiquidCrystal I2C" by Frank de Brabander**. (Any compatible fork with the same name works too.)

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B cable** (the big square-ish plug, same kind old printers used). The green power LED on the Uno should light up.
2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like **COM3** or **COM4**; on a Mac it is **/dev/cu.usbmodem...**; on Linux it is **/dev/ttyACM0** or **/dev/ttyUSB0**). If you see more than one, unplug the Uno and watch which one disappears - that is the right one.
3. No passwords or WiFi to fill in for this sketch - skip that step.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The TX and RX LEDs near the USB jack will flicker for a couple of seconds. When the bottom of the window says **"Done uploading."** you are good.
5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of that window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code).
6. The LCD should briefly show "Tub Filler / Dip the sensor.." and then switch to the bar graph. With the sensor dry, the Serial Monitor should print a number very close to **0** and the percent on the LCD should read **0%**. Dip the comb into the glass of water and the bar should jump, the percent should climb, and the LEDs should light up in order: red first, then yellow around halfway, then green when it is basically full.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Blank LCD with the backlight on?** Your I2C backpack lives at address `0x3F` instead of `0x27`. Change the `LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2);` line near the top to `0x3F` and re-upload.
- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `??x?`?** The baud rate dropdown in the Serial Monitor is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the code.
- **Percent never goes above ~30% even with the sensor fully submerged?** Your `WET_MAX` is too high for your glass of water. Watch the raw number in the Serial Monitor while the sensor is all the way in, then change `const int WET_MAX = 600;` to whatever you actually see, and re-upload.
## Talking points

- Why a "resistive comb" sensor? It's just two interleaved bare-copper tracks. Water between them conducts a tiny bit of current. More water covering the combs = more conductive paths in parallel = more current = bigger number from `analogRead`. It's the same trick the Soil Moisture Sensor uses, just shaped to read a vertical column instead of a flat patch.
- Why the 1M pull-down? An Arduino analog input that isn't connected to anything acts like a tiny antenna - it picks up mains hum and reads random numbers. Tying it weakly to ground through 1M forces it to read 0 when the sensor is dry, but lets the sensor easily overpower it when water is present.
- The LCD updates fast on purpose - you can dip the sensor in and out and watch the bar graph respond immediately. That tight feedback loop is what makes it fun.

## Things to change once it works

- Calibrate `WET_MAX` to your actual glass of water. Dip the sensor all the way and read the value over Serial - that's your real max. Beginner-typical values land between 500 and 700.
- Add a buzzer that beeps once when the green "FULL" zone is reached - that turns it from a visual toy into an actual "tub is full, come turn the tap off" alarm.
- Swap to the ESP32 and publish the level over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi hub. Same sensor wiring, different brain.
- Try the Raindrop Sensor on the same code with no changes - it's electrically identical, just a flatter comb shape.

## Why this is interesting

This is the cheapest, simplest possible "is there water there?" sensor, and it teaches a real-world lesson the first time you use it: analog inputs don't read clean zero when nothing's connected. Fixing that with a pull-down resistor is a habit that carries over to almost every analog sensor you'll ever use. And visually, dipping a probe into a glass and watching a bar graph fill up is hugely satisfying - especially for a 10-year-old.

projects.name: NE555 Heartbeat Blinker (no code, all chip)
projects.power_supply: 5V from a USB phone charger via the USB-C pigtail (or borrowed from an Arduino Uno's 5V pin) feeds the breadboard rails; the NE555 sips a few mA.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug it in. A red LED blinks once per second, steady and calm, like a tiny heartbeat sitting on your breadboard.

**Why it's fun**: This is your first project that does something real with ZERO code. No laptop, no typing, no uploading - just a little black chip and a few parts, and it blinks forever the second power touches it.

## Parts list

- 1x NE555 Timer IC (8-pin DIP - the famous chip, in production since 1972)
- 1x LED 5mm Red (the heartbeat indicator)
- 2x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - R1 and R2, set the blink rate together with the cap
- 1x Resistor 470R (1/8W 1%) - protects the LED from too much current
- 1x Capacitor 47uF electrolytic - the "memory" element that takes time to fill and empty
- 1x Breadboard
- A few M-M jumper wires
- A 5V source: a USB phone charger broken out with the USB-C pigtail, OR borrow 5V + GND from a powered-on Arduino Uno sitting next to it

## Wiring notes

The NE555 has 8 pins. Hold the chip with the little notch (or dot) at the top - pin 1 is the top-left, then pins count down the left side (1,2,3,4), across the bottom, and back up the right side (5,6,7,8).

Place the chip across the breadboard's center gully so the left pins are on one side and the right pins are on the other - that's what the gully is FOR, so the two sides of the chip don't short to each other.

Connections (every one of these is a short jumper or a component leg pushed into the right hole):

- Pin 1 (GND) -> GND rail
- Pin 2 (Trigger) -> wired straight to Pin 6
- Pin 6 (Threshold) -> top of the 47uF cap (positive leg, the longer one)
- The 47uF cap's other leg (negative, marked with the white stripe) -> GND rail
- Pin 7 (Discharge) -> through R2 (10K) -> Pin 6 / Pin 2 / cap+
- Pin 7 (Discharge) -> through R1 (10K) -> +5V rail
- Pin 8 (Vcc) -> +5V rail
- Pin 4 (Reset) -> +5V rail (must be high or the chip stays asleep)
- Pin 5 (Control) -> leave it floating (a 10nF to GND is optional and we don't need it for a calm 1 Hz blink)
- Pin 3 (Output) -> through 470R -> LED long leg (anode) -> LED short leg (cathode) -> GND rail

That is the whole circuit. Eight pins, four passive parts, one LED.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip and passives, and it runs the second power touches the rails. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no typing. Just plug in power and watch.

**Power it up:**

1. Double-check the wiring one more time with your dad. Especially: the notch on the NE555 points the right way, the 47uF cap stripe (the negative leg) goes to GND, and the LED's long leg is on the 470R side (not on GND).
2. Pick your power source:
   - **USB phone charger + USB-C pigtail**: plug the pigtail's red wire into the breadboard's red (+) rail and the black wire into the blue/black (-) rail. Then plug the USB-C end into the charger.
   - **OR borrow from an Arduino Uno**: run a jumper from the Uno's **5V** pin to your red rail, and another from the Uno's **GND** pin to your blue rail. Then power the Uno over USB as normal.
3. Plug in the charger (or the Uno's USB cable).
4. The red LED should start blinking right away - one slow, calm blink per second, like a heartbeat. That is it. It will keep blinking forever as long as power stays on.

**Want to see what is happening inside the chip?** Grab a multimeter, set it to DC volts (20V range), and follow the TEST POINT 1 through TEST POINT 5 steps in the Code section above. Test Point 4 is the cool one - you can literally watch the capacitor charge up and dump out, over and over, which is what makes the LED blink.

**Common gotchas:**

- **47uF cap in backwards.** Electrolytic caps have a + leg (longer) and a - leg (shorter, with a white stripe down the side). The stripe goes to GND. If you flip it, the cap can get warm or pop - unplug power and turn it around.
- **NE555 in backwards.** The little notch (or dot) at one end marks pin 1. If the chip is rotated 180 degrees, the LED will just sit there dark. Pull the chip out gently, spin it, push it back in.
- **LED in backwards.** No damage done, it just will not light. The long leg (anode) goes to the 470R resistor coming from pin 3; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Pull it out and flip it.
- **Pin 4 (Reset) forgotten.** If you skip the jumper from pin 4 to +5V, the chip stays asleep and nothing blinks. Pin 4 must be tied HIGH.
## Talking points

The NE555 in astable mode is one of the most-built circuits in electronics history. Here is what is actually happening inside:

1. **At power-on**, the cap is empty (0V). The chip's internal comparator sees that, sets its output (pin 3) HIGH, and turns off the "discharge" transistor on pin 7.
2. **The cap charges** through R1 + R2 in series. The voltage on it rises slowly along an RC curve.
3. **When the cap reaches 2/3 of Vcc** (~3.3V on a 5V supply), the upper comparator trips. Output goes LOW. Pin 7 becomes a short to ground.
4. **The cap discharges** through R2 only (R1 is now disconnected from the cap by the discharge transistor). Voltage falls.
5. **When the cap drops to 1/3 of Vcc** (~1.6V), the lower comparator trips. Output goes HIGH again. Pin 7 floats. Back to step 2.

The LED on pin 3 mirrors the output, so it lights when the cap is filling and dims when the cap is draining. The "heartbeat" you see is literally the capacitor breathing.

The blink rate is set by how big the resistors and cap are. Bigger = slower. With R1=R2=10K and C=47uF you get ~1 Hz - one beat per second. Halve the cap, and it blinks twice as fast.

## Things to change once it works

- **Make it faster**: swap the 47uF cap for a 10uF. You should get about 5 Hz - LED looks like a strobe.
- **Make it slower**: swap to 220uF or 470uF. The LED will pulse like a sleeping computer.
- **Make the duty cycle 50/50**: in this classic circuit the LED is on longer than it is off (~66% on). Adding a 1N4148 diode in parallel with R2 (or making R1 much smaller than R2) gets you closer to even on/off.
- **Drive something bigger**: replace the LED+470R with the input of an optocoupler or the base of a BC547 to switch a relay coil. The 555 can sink/source ~200 mA on its own, more than enough for a small piezo buzzer too.
- **Watch it on a logic probe or scope**: pin 6 shows the textbook RC ramp; pin 3 shows the square wave. Seeing both at once is the "aha" of the whole project.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first circuit Andy will build that does something visible **without any code at all**. No Arduino, no ESP32, no compiling, no uploading - just a chip, two resistors, a cap, and an LED. Plug it in, the LED blinks. Pull a wire and it stops. There is no firmware to blame when it doesn't work; the failure is always in the wiring, and you fix it by looking.

It also teaches the R-C time constant - the single most reused intuition in all of analog electronics. Once you feel that "bigger resistor or bigger cap = slower", you understand how every debounce, every filter, every retriggerable timer, and half of every analog audio circuit you'll ever look at, actually works. The NE555 just happens to be the most charming way to meet that idea.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# NE555 Heartbeat Blinker - multimeter test procedure (no MCU, no code).
#
# Power: feed the breadboard rails with 5V from any USB phone charger
# broken out via the USB-C pigtail, or from an Arduino Uno's 5V pin if
# you have it nearby. Anywhere from 4.5V to 9V will work; the LED just
# gets a little brighter at higher voltage.
#
# Set your multimeter to DC volts (20V range) and probe these points
# while the LED is blinking. Black probe stays on the GND rail the
# whole time.
#
# TEST POINT 1 - Pin 8 (Vcc) and Pin 4 (Reset)
#   Expected: steady ~5V (matches your supply).
#   If 0V: power not reaching the chip. Check the rail jumpers.
#
# TEST POINT 2 - Pin 1 (GND)
#   Expected: 0V.
#   If not 0V: GND jumper to the chip is broken.
#
# TEST POINT 3 - Pin 3 (Output, drives the LED)
#   Expected: meter needle bounces between ~0V and ~3.5V at ~1 Hz.
#   (The chip output doesn't quite swing to the full rail - that's
#   normal for an NE555.)
#
# TEST POINT 4 - Pin 6 (Threshold) / Pin 2 (Trigger), tied together
#   on top of the 47uF cap.
#   Expected: a slow ramp between ~1.6V and ~3.3V (1/3 and 2/3 of Vcc).
#   This IS the capacitor charging through R1+R2 and discharging through
#   R2. Watching this voltage ramp up and down is the whole point of
#   the project - it's the "time constant" you've heard about, made
#   visible.
#
# TEST POINT 5 - Pin 7 (Discharge)
#   Expected: pulses to ~0V briefly each cycle, otherwise floats with
#   pin 6. This is the internal transistor that drains the cap.
#
# Period math (so you can predict the blink rate):
#   T_high = 0.693 * (R1 + R2) * C   = 0.693 * 20kOhm * 47uF ~= 0.65 s
#   T_low  = 0.693 *  R2      * C   = 0.693 * 10kOhm * 47uF ~= 0.33 s
#   Total period ~= 0.98 s   ->   frequency ~= 1.02 Hz (heartbeat)
#
# Duty cycle is ~66% high. If you want it closer to 50% (even on/off),
# make R1 much smaller than R2, or use the slightly fancier "diode
# trick" variant - that's a "things to change" item below.
echo "Probe the test points listed above while the LED blinks."

projects.name: NE555 Touch-and-Hold Lamp (monostable one-shot)
projects.power_supply: 5 V DC from any USB source (phone charger, laptop USB-A, or your TP4056 + 18650 pack) - the NE555 happily runs from 4.5-15 V but 5 V is the friendliest.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Tap the button once and the yellow LED snaps on for about 11 seconds, then shuts off by itself. You can let go right away - the light keeps glowing on its own little timer.

**Why it's fun**: It is like a tiny bathroom light that turns itself off, except YOU built it from a chip and a handful of parts. Race a stopwatch against it, or dare your dad to guess exactly when the LED will blink off.

## Parts list

- 1x NE555 Timer IC (the brain - in monostable / one-shot mode this time)
- 1x Tactile Push-button Switch 3x6x5mm (white pin) - the trigger
- 1x LED 5mm Yellow (lights up for the timed duration)
- 1x Resistor 470R - in series with the LED, limits current so the LED does not burn out
- 1x Resistor 100K - the "R" in the timing equation T = 1.1 * R * C
- 1x Capacitor 100uF electrolytic - the "C" in the same equation
- 1x Resistor 10K - pull-up so the trigger pin idles HIGH until the button presses it LOW
- 1x Capacitor 1uF 50V - decoupling cap across the 555's power pins, keeps the chip from glitching
- 1x Breadboard
- Jumper wires (M-M)

Power: 5 V from a USB cable plugged into any USB power source (phone charger, laptop USB-A, or the TP4056 + 18650 setup you already have). The 555 happily runs anywhere from 4.5 V to 15 V, but 5 V is the friendliest for a beginner project.

## Wiring notes

NE555 pinout (looking at the chip from the top with the notch / dot at the LEFT):

```
            +----------+
   GND  1 --|.       8 |-- Vcc (+5V)
   TRIG 2 --|        7 |-- DISCHARGE
   OUT  3 --|        6 |-- THRESHOLD
   RESET 4 -|        5 |-- CONTROL
            +----------+
```

Connections:

1. **Pin 1 (GND)** to the breadboard's blue/GND rail.
2. **Pin 8 (Vcc)** to the red/+5V rail. Also put the 1uF decoupling cap directly across pins 1 and 8 (negative lead to GND).
3. **Pins 6 and 7 tied together** at one junction. That same junction connects to the **bottom** of the 100K resistor and to the **positive (+) lead of the 100uF cap**. The **top** of the 100K resistor goes to **+5V**. The negative lead of the cap goes to GND. (So pins 6, 7, the cap-plus, and one end of the 100K are all the same node.)
4. Watch capacitor polarity - the white stripe / short leg is the negative side and goes to GND.
5. **Pin 2 (TRIG)** connects to the 10K pull-up resistor, other end of which goes to +5V. So pin 2 sits at +5V by default.
6. **One side of the push-button** connects to pin 2; **the other side** connects to GND. Pressing the button briefly pulls pin 2 to GND - that is the "trigger".
7. **Pin 4 (RESET)** to +5V (so the chip never gets reset accidentally - leaving this floating causes weird behavior).
8. **Pin 5 (CONTROL)** can be left unconnected for now (some textbooks add a 10nF cap here but it is not required).
9. **Pin 3 (OUT)** to the **long leg (anode)** of the yellow LED. **Short leg (cathode)** of LED to the 470R resistor. Other end of 470R to GND.

Math sanity check: T = 1.1 * R * C = 1.1 * 100,000 ohms * 0.000100 F = **11.0 seconds**. Press the button, the LED lights for about 11 seconds, then snaps off all at once.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip and passives, and it runs the second power touches the rails. The NE555 is the "brain" here; there is no laptop, no Arduino IDE, no code to upload. Just power it up and press the button.

**Power-up procedure:**

1. Double-check every wire against the Wiring notes one more time *before* plugging anything in. Pay special attention to:
   - The notch / dot on the NE555 is at the LEFT (pin 1 is bottom-left).
   - The 100uF cap's **short leg / white stripe side** goes to GND.
   - The LED's **long leg (anode)** goes to NE555 pin 3, **short leg (cathode)** goes to the 470R resistor.
2. Plug a USB cable into any 5 V source (phone charger, laptop USB-A port, or your TP4056 + 18650 pack).
3. Feed the **+5 V wire to the red rail** and the **GND wire to the blue rail** of the breadboard. Nothing should light up yet - the LED stays dark until you trigger it.
4. Press the tactile button once and let go right away. The yellow LED snaps ON.
5. Start a stopwatch (or just count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two..."). The LED should stay lit for about **11 seconds** and then shut itself off.
6. Press the button again - it relights for another 11 seconds. Each press restarts the timer.

**Optional measurement (skip unless you want to):** If you want to know the *exact* pulse width, the comment block at the top of the code file shows how to wire an Arduino Uno to NE555 pin 3 and read the duration in the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. That is bonus material - the lamp itself does not need it.

**Common gotchas:**

- **LED stays dark forever, even after pressing the button.** Almost always the LED is in backwards. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. (No damage done - LEDs only light up one way around.)
- **LED is dimly lit all the time and pressing the button does nothing.** Pin 4 (RESET) is floating. Make sure pin 4 has a wire going to +5 V, not left dangling.
- **LED flashes for a fraction of a second instead of 11 seconds.** Check the 100uF cap polarity - the white-stripe / short-leg side MUST go to GND. If it is backwards the cap cannot charge properly, and the timing collapses. Also double-check that pins 6 and 7 are tied together at the *same* node as the cap's positive lead and the bottom of the 100K resistor.
## Talking points

**Monostable means "one stable state".** The 555 is sitting quietly with its output LOW and the timing cap held empty (because the internal discharge transistor on pin 7 is shorting it to ground). It will sit like that forever. That is the "stable state".

**What does the button actually do?** The button pulls pin 2 (the TRIG input) below 1/3 of Vcc - briefly. That is the magic threshold. The instant the chip sees that, it flips the output HIGH, releases the discharge transistor, and now the cap can finally start charging up through the 100K resistor.

**How does it know when to stop?** Pin 6 (THRESHOLD) is watching the same cap. When the voltage on the cap climbs past 2/3 of Vcc, pin 6 trips, and the chip snaps the output back LOW and re-shorts the cap to GND. Reset. Ready for the next press.

**Why 1.1?** That number is not magic - it comes from the math of charging a capacitor through a resistor from 0V to 2/3 of Vcc. The formula t = -RC * ln(1 - 2/3) works out to about 1.0986 * RC. Engineers rounded it to 1.1 because that is plenty precise given that real-world electrolytic caps drift +/- 20% anyway.

**Why "touch-AND-hold"?** Because letting go of the button does nothing! The 555 has latched and is going to time out on its own schedule. Holding the button down longer does not extend the time. Pressing the button again while the LED is still on also does nothing - the 555 ignores re-triggers until it finishes the current cycle. This is called **non-retriggerable** behavior, and it is one of the standard 555 monostable's defining traits. (Some folks add an extra transistor to force a retrigger; out of scope here.)

## Things to change once it works

- **Change R or C to change the time.** Swap the 100K for a 220K -> you get ~24 seconds. Swap the 100uF for a 470uF -> you get ~52 seconds. Try a 10K resistor with the 100uF cap and you get ~1.1 seconds (a "blink the LED for a moment" timer).
- **Add a potentiometer.** Replace the 100K with a 1M potentiometer wired as a variable resistor and you have an adjustable bathroom-fan-timer dial. Heads-up: at very high resistances (above ~1M) cheap electrolytic capacitors leak enough current that the cap can never fully charge to 2/3 Vcc - the timer drifts or just hangs on forever. If you want minute-plus timers, switch to a film or ceramic cap for "C" instead of going huge on "R".
- **Drive a relay instead of an LED.** Connect pin 3 to one of the channels of your Songle relay module and now you have an 11-second-on light switch.
- **Try a different color LED.** The 470R works for yellow, red, green - tune it down to 220R if it looks dim.
- **Add a buzzer in parallel with the LED.** Cheap audible kitchen timer.

## Why this is interesting

The astable blinker showed you the 555's other mode (the "always-oscillating" one). The monostable mode is honestly the more useful of the two in real life. Almost every "press a button, something happens for N seconds, then stops" circuit in the world - bathroom fan timers, snooze alarms, automatic doorbells, motor soft-starts, debounce circuits - is some flavor of a 555 monostable.

And the headline equation T = 1.1 * R * C is one of those rare moments where math you do on paper actually matches a stopwatch you hold in your hand. Pick R and C, multiply them, get a time, build the circuit, count "one Mississippi, two Mississippi..." - it works. That feeling is the whole reason analog electronics is fun.

projects.name: Bump Buzzer (NE555 + SW-420)
projects.power_supply: 5V from an Arduino Uno's USB rail jumpered to the breadboard +5V and GND rails (the Uno acts as a USB-to-5V converter; no firmware needs to run on it for the alarm to work).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Bump the table and a red light snaps on while a buzzer screams for about ten seconds, then it goes quiet and waits for the next bump. No code, no buttons - just touch the desk and it freaks out.

**Why it's fun**: Hide it under your little brother's chair, or tape it to the cookie jar, and you get an instant booby trap that catches anyone who sneaks up. The best part is you can tune how jumpy it is with a tiny screwdriver - too touchy and a footstep sets it off, too chill and you can shake the table without a peep.

## Parts list

- 1x NE555 Timer IC - the brain, configured as a monostable one-shot
- 1x SW-420 Vibration Switch Module - the trigger
- 1x 220K resistor - NE555 timing R
- 1x 47uF electrolytic - NE555 timing C
- 1x 10K resistor - pull-up on NE555 TRIG (pin 2)
- 1x 330R resistor - LED current limiter
- 1x 100uF electrolytic - rail decoupling next to the NE555
- 1x Red 5mm LED - visual "ALARM ACTIVE" indicator
- 1x Active piezo buzzer (from the spare-parts drawer - the kind with a sticker that says "5V" on the back; it self-oscillates when you give it DC). If you do not have one, swap it for any item you can drive with a digital HIGH and the LED-and-330R alone is still a quiet test alarm.
- Breadboard, jumper wires
- Arduino Uno - used ONLY as a USB-powered 5V source (no firmware running the alarm)

Note: this design deliberately does NOT use the LM386 audio amplifier. Earlier drafts paired the LM386 with a passive 8 ohm speaker, which is electrically wrong here: the NE555 output is a static DC level while the timer is running, so a coupling cap into the LM386 would only produce a click at the start and a click at the end - not a continuous tone. An active piezo buzzer solves this in one part because it has its own internal oscillator and only needs DC.

## Wiring notes

The NE555 is wired as a classic monostable ("one-shot"):

- Pin 1 (GND) -> ground rail
- Pin 8 (VCC) -> +5V rail
- Pin 4 (RESET) -> +5V (tie HIGH so it is always armed)
- Pin 2 (TRIG) -> pulled up to +5V through the 10K resistor, AND connected DIRECTLY to the SW-420 DO output (no series resistor in this line - a series resistor here would form a divider with the pull-up and TRIG would never reach the 1/3 Vcc threshold needed to fire)
- Pin 6 (THRES) joined to pin 7 (DISCH), and both connected to the top of the 47uF timing capacitor. The bottom of the 47uF goes to GND.
- Pin 7 (DISCH) also connects through the 220K resistor up to +5V. This is the R that, with the 47uF C, sets the pulse length: T = 1.1 * R * C = 1.1 * 220000 * 0.000047 = ~11.4 seconds in theory. In practice 47uF electrolytics carry +/-20% tolerance, so expect anything from ~9 to ~14 seconds. Treat the headline "10 seconds" as a ballpark.
- Pin 3 (OUT) drives two things in parallel:
  1. The red LED through the 330R resistor to GND (visual indicator)
  2. The active piezo buzzer (+ pin to NE555 pin 3, - pin to GND)
- A 100uF bulk decoupling cap sits between +5V and GND right next to pin 8. The NE555 takes a brief gulp of current at the switching edges; the cap smooths that out so the rail does not dip and accidentally re-trigger the timer.

The SW-420 module:

- VCC -> +5V, GND -> GND, DO -> NE555 pin 2 (TRIG) directly
- AO (analog out) left unconnected - we only use the digital comparator output, which is open-collector and pulls cleanly to ground when triggered
- The little blue pot on the SW-420 sets the comparator threshold. Spin it slowly with a screwdriver until tapping the desk fires it but typing nearby does not.

Power-in: plug the Arduino Uno into a laptop USB port. The Uno's 5V pin and GND pin are jumpered to the breadboard rails. The Uno's microcontroller is irrelevant - it is a $5 USB-to-5V converter for this build.


## Flash it and run it

This one is a bit special: the alarm itself does NOT need any code. The NE555 chip, the buzzer, and the SW-420 sensor do all the work by themselves the moment they get power. The Arduino Uno is only there to be a fancy USB-to-5V adapter.

**Step 1 - Power it up the lazy way:**

1. Plug a USB-A to USB-B cable (the chunky square-ish printer-style plug) from your laptop into the Arduino Uno. The green "ON" LED on the Uno should light up.
2. Make sure you have a jumper from the Uno's **5V** pin to the breadboard's **red (+)** rail, and another from the Uno's **GND** pin to the breadboard's **blue (-)** rail. That's it - the breadboard is now powered.
3. Tap the desk near the SW-420. The red LED should snap on and the buzzer should scream for about 10 seconds, then go quiet on its own. Tap again - same thing.
4. See the tiny blue square pot on the SW-420 module? That's the sensitivity knob. Turn it with a small screwdriver: clockwise usually = more touchy, counter-clockwise = chill. Find the sweet spot where typing nearby does nothing but a real desk-tap fires the alarm.

**Step 2 (OPTIONAL) - Use the Uno to tune the sensor before you build the NE555 part:**

If the alarm is being weird and you want to "see" what the SW-420 is doing, there's a helper sketch you can load on the Uno first. You only do this BEFORE wiring up the NE555.

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

*One-time setup (only the first time you ever flash an Uno):*
1. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**.

*Every time you flash:*
1. Temporarily run a jumper from the SW-420 **DO** pin to the Uno's **D2** pin (and make sure SW-420 VCC and GND are still on the rails).
2. Plug the Uno into your laptop with the USB-B cable.
3. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM\*** with "Arduino Uno" next to it (on Mac it'll look like `cu.usbmodem...`).
4. Open the helper sketch in the Arduino IDE.
5. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow icon at the top-left). Wait for "Done uploading" at the bottom.
6. Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate in the bottom-right dropdown to **115200**.
7. You should see lines like `[idle] DO=1 total shakes=0` ticking by every 2 seconds. Tap the desk and a `SHAKE #1` line should pop up. If it spams shakes when you breathe near it, turn the blue pot counter-clockwise a touch. If it never fires no matter how hard you smack the desk, turn it the other way.
8. When you're happy, unplug the D2 jumper - you don't need it for the actual alarm. The Uno goes back to being just a 5V battery.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Electrolytic capacitors are polarity-sensitive.** The 47uF and 100uF caps have a long leg (+) and a short leg with a white stripe on the can (-). If you put them in backwards they can pop, get hot, or just refuse to work. Long leg toward +5V / NE555 pin 7, short leg toward GND.
- **NE555 chip orientation.** The little notch (or dot) on top of the chip marks the pin 1 end. Get this backwards and pin 1 swaps with pin 8 - the chip will get warm and nothing will work. Double-check before powering up.
- **LED in backwards = no light, no damage.** If the red LED never turns on but you can hear the buzzer, just flip the LED around. Long leg goes toward NE555 pin 3 (through the 330R), short leg toward GND.
- **Buzzer that only clicks instead of screams.** That means you grabbed a *passive* buzzer (no built-in oscillator) instead of an *active* one. The active one usually has a sticker on top saying "5V" and makes a tone the moment you touch it across a battery. Swap it.
## Talking points

- A monostable is a circuit that, when poked, produces ONE output pulse of a fixed length, then waits. That is the whole job. Poke = trigger LOW for an instant; output = HIGH for ~10 seconds; then back to sleep.
- Why this matters: real shakes (and real alarm conditions in general) are spiky. A door slam is 50 ms. A footstep on a creaky floor is 200 ms. You do not want a buzzer that beeps for 50 ms - you want it to scream until someone walks over and notices. The 555 turns a blip into a sustained event.
- The formula T = 1.1 * R * C is one of the most useful in hobby electronics. 220K * 47uF gives ~11 seconds nominal, but with +/-20% electrolytic tolerance and resistor tolerance stacked, expect 9 to 14 seconds in practice. Want a longer alarm? Swap the 47uF for a 100uF (~24 s) or bump R to 560K (~29 s).
- Pin 2 of the 555 is TRIGGER, and it is edge-sensitive on the falling edge: it fires the moment the voltage drops below 1/3 of VCC. That is why we pull it UP with a 10K and let the SW-420 yank it DOWN. Do NOT put a series resistor between the SW-420 DO and pin 2 - it forms a divider with the pull-up and the trigger threshold is never crossed.
- Active vs passive sound makers: an ACTIVE piezo buzzer contains its own oscillator and just needs DC across it - perfect partner for a 555 monostable, because the 555 output is a steady HIGH while the timer is running. A PASSIVE speaker needs an actual changing waveform; pairing a passive speaker with a monostable produces just a click-on and a click-off, no sustained tone. This is a common beginner trap.

## Things to change once it works

- Change the pulse length: swap the 220K for 100K (~5 s), or for 1M (~52 s, nearly a minute of howling).
- Add a momentary push-button across the 47uF timing cap (from cap-top to GND) - pressing it dumps the cap and silences the alarm early. This is your "acknowledge" button.
- Add a 1N4148 diode across the 47uF cap with the cathode (the stripe end) at pin 7 (DISCH) and the anode at the cap top - this lets DISCH pull the cap to ground quickly through the diode on cycle end, so the cap is ready to fire again immediately. (Without it, a fast re-trigger may get a short pulse because the cap was still partly charged.)
- Replace the SW-420 with the Angle / Tilt ball switch from the kit - now it is a "do not pick this up" alarm for a parcel or a treasure chest.
- Step up to an intermediate version: add a SECOND NE555 wired as an astable oscillator at ~2 kHz, gate it with the monostable output, and feed THAT through an LM386 into an 8 ohm speaker. Now you get a proper square-wave tone for the full alarm window and you can play with the pitch by changing the astable's RC.

## Why this is interesting

You have just built the same building block that is inside car alarms, doorbell extenders, fridge-door-left-open beepers, and old smoke detectors: a sensor whose output is a flicker, stretched by a timer into an output a human cannot miss. Two parts of vocabulary - "monostable" (one pulse per poke) and "active vs passive sound maker" - and one chip from 1972 that still ships in the millions every year. The timing is set by two passive components you can swap with a pair of tweezers, and the whole alarm runs on no code at all.

There is already an "Earthquake Cam" project in the system that uses the SW-420 to trigger a camera capture; the Bump Buzzer is the audio-output sibling of that idea. Same sensor, different reaction: one records, one screams.
