projects.name: LM358 Photodiode Preamp Lux Meter
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop into the Arduino Uno; the Uno's 5V rail powers the LM358, the KY-018 module, and the OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Point the little light sensor at a lamp, a window, or the inside of a closet. The tiny screen shows a number that goes UP when there's more light and DOWN when it gets dark.

**Why it's fun**: Walk around the house hunting for the brightest and darkest spots like a light detective - under the couch, behind the curtains, inside the fridge when the door pops open. Cup your hands over the sensor and watch the number crash to almost zero, like you just turned off the sun.

## Parts list

- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone, XL) - reads the amplifier output and drives the OLED
- 1x LM358 Op-Amp (dual) - one half is the transimpedance amplifier, the other half generates a virtual ground
- 1x KY-018 Photoresistor Module - the LDR is repurposed as a light-driven current source
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - shows the millivolts, microamps and estimated lux
- 1x Resistor 47K (1/8W 1%) - feedback resistor Rf, sized so the LDR's mA-scale current does not saturate the op-amp (gain ~47 mV per uA)
- 2x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - equal pair forming the 2.5V virtual-ground divider
- 1x Capacitor 1uF 50V (electrolytic) - feedback cap across Rf, rolls off noise and stops the stage oscillating (a 100nF ceramic film cap is a cleaner choice for this spot - the polar electrolytic will work but adds a little slow drift from leakage; swap if you have one in the spares drawer)
- 1x Capacitor 10uF - decouples the virtual-ground node so it stays stiff
- 1x Capacitor 100uF - bulk decoupling on the LM358 V+ pin
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - solderless
- Jumper wires (M-M and F-M assortments)

## Wiring notes

**Power.** Arduino Uno provides 5V and GND from the USB rail. The LM358 runs single-supply from those rails.

**LM358 power pins (do not skip this).** The LM358 only has 8 pins and two of them are easy for a beginner to forget. Wire them first:
- **Pin 4 -> GND rail**
- **Pin 8 -> +5V rail**, with the 100uF cap from pin 8 straight to GND right at the chip body

If the chip has no power, nothing else in this build will do anything and you will chase a dead circuit for an hour. Confirm with a multimeter across pins 4 and 8 before going further.

**Virtual ground (op-amp B = pins 5, 6, 7).** Two 10K resistors form a divider from 5V to GND, meeting at the non-inverting input (pin 5). Tie pin 6 to pin 7 to make a unity-gain buffer. Op-amp B now outputs a rock-solid 2.5V on pin 7, which we call VREF. Drop a 10uF cap from VREF to GND.

**Transimpedance stage (op-amp A = pins 1, 2, 3).** Connect VREF to the non-inverting input (pin 3). The inverting input (pin 2) is the "summing junction". Put Rf = 47K from pin 2 to the output pin 1, with the 1uF cap (or a 100nF ceramic) in parallel with Rf.

**Light input.** The KY-018 has VCC, GND, and AO (analog signal). We are NOT using its AO comparator path. Instead, power the module from 5V/GND as normal, and run a jumper from the module's AO pin (or directly off whichever LDR lead is easiest to reach on your particular module) over to the summing junction at op-amp A pin 2. On a KY-018 the LDR sits between VCC and the AO output pin (with a 10K pulldown to ground), so AO is electrically one end of the LDR and that is exactly the node we want to grab. Because pin 2 is held at VREF (2.5V) by op-amp feedback, the voltage across the LDR is roughly (5V - 2.5V) = 2.5V, and the resulting current flows into the summing junction. The op-amp swings its output below VREF by exactly (I_LDR x Rf) volts.

**Why 47K (and not 1M like every photodiode datasheet shows).** A real photodiode passes nanoamps to a few microamps. An LDR is much chattier - in normal room light its resistance falls to a few kilohms, so with ~2.5V across it you get tens of microamps, sometimes hundreds. With a 1M feedback resistor you would need (say) 100 uA x 1M = 100V at the op-amp output, which is obviously impossible, so the LM358 just slams into the bottom rail and you read a pinned, useless value. 47K keeps the stage living happily inside the chip's swing range. The price is sensitivity: gain is only ~47 mV per uA instead of 1 V per uA. That is fine for a learning meter.

**Reading it.** Arduino A0 reads op-amp A's output (pin 1). Arduino A1 reads VREF (op-amp B output, pin 7) directly. The sketch subtracts the two so you measure dV around the virtual ground rather than absolute volts - this cancels supply drift (a trick called ratiometric measurement).

**OLED.** SDA -> A4, SCL -> A5, VCC -> 5V, GND -> GND.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. Plug the Uno in once with the USB cable so Windows / macOS sees it. CH340 clones sometimes need a driver - if no COM port shows up, search "CH340 driver" for your OS and install it.
2. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**.
3. Tools -> Manage Libraries. Search for and install each of these (pick the latest version of each):
   - **Adafruit SSD1306** (this will offer to also install Adafruit GFX and Adafruit BusIO - say yes to all of them)
   - **Adafruit GFX Library** (in case it did not get pulled in automatically)
4. The `Wire` library for I2C is already built in - nothing to install for that one.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-A to USB-B cable (the big square plug, same as an old printer).
2. Tools -> Port. Pick the one that says COM* (Windows) or /dev/cu.usbmodem* (Mac) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux). If two ports show up, unplug the Uno, see which one disappears, plug it back in - that one is yours.
3. No passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs purely on the wired sensor.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The TX / RX LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When it says "Done uploading" at the bottom you are good.
5. Tools -> Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** (must match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code or you will see garbage characters).
6. What you should see:
   - The OLED lights up and prints `LM358 Lux Meter` for about a second, then starts showing live numbers.
   - The Serial Monitor prints a "Boot self-check" block telling you to expect VREF between 2.45 and 2.55 V.
   - Cup your hand over the KY-018 sensor. The lux number on the OLED should drop close to zero. Point it at a lamp - the number jumps up. That means the whole chain (LDR -> LM358 -> Uno -> OLED) is working.

**Common gotchas:**

- **OLED stays black.** The SSD1306 module sometimes ships at I2C address `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. If the Serial Monitor prints `OLED init failed`, edit `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check SDA goes to A4 and SCL goes to A5 on the Uno - swapping those two is the #1 reason an OLED looks dead.
- **Serial Monitor shows weird symbols like `ÿüÿ`.** The baud rate dropdown is not on 115200. Set it to 115200 and the text becomes readable.
- **Cap polarity backwards.** The 100uF, 10uF and 1uF caps are electrolytic - the short leg (and the white stripe on the side) is the negative leg and must go to GND / the lower-voltage side. Putting one in backwards can make it heat up or pop, so check each one before plugging in USB.
## Test procedure (do this before you trust any number)

1. Power the Arduino over USB. Open Serial Monitor at 115200.
2. With a multimeter, probe VREF (LM358 pin 7) against GND. Expected: **2.45 - 2.55 V**. If it is closer to 0 or 5, the divider or the op-amp B feedback wire is wrong.
3. Probe Vout (LM358 pin 1) against GND. With the LDR covered (dark) it should sit very close to VREF, i.e. about 2.5V. Serial should show **dV ~ 0 mV** and **Iph ~ 0 uA**.
4. Uncover the LDR and point it at the room light. dV should go **negative** (a few hundred mV down to maybe -1V), and Iph should rise into the microamp range. The OLED should show a non-zero lux estimate.
5. Shine a phone torch directly onto the LDR. dV should go more negative but **must not pin at -2.5V**. If it pins, your Rf is too big - drop to 22K or 10K. The sketch also flashes `PIN!` on the OLED when it detects this.
6. (Optional) Use a phone lux-meter app to read the room. Adjust `K_LUX_PER_UA` in the sketch until the OLED roughly agrees.

## Talking points

- **Transimpedance amplifier (TIA).** A photodiode (or photoconductive LDR) is a *current* device. A TIA forces the sensor to live at a fixed voltage and converts the current into a voltage you can read with an ADC. The gain is just one number: Rf. Bigger Rf, more volts per microamp, but also more noise and slower response - and, as we learned the hard way above, very easy to saturate when the sensor is leakier than you expected.
- **Virtual ground.** The op-amp's golden rule (when there is negative feedback) is "the two inputs end up at the same voltage". We pin the non-inverting input at 2.5V, so the inverting input *also* sits at 2.5V even though nothing connects it there directly. That phantom 2.5V is the virtual ground.
- **Honest caveat on "bidirectional" current.** The LM358 is famous for poor high-side headroom on a single supply - its output can only swing to about V+ minus 1.5V, i.e. ~3.5V on a 5V rail. With VREF at 2.5V that means we have only ~1V of room above VREF (and ~2.5V below). So while the virtual-ground trick *does* let single-supply chips handle bidirectional current in principle, this specific chip clips the positive direction badly. Use a rail-to-rail op-amp (e.g. MCP6002) if you actually need both directions. In our build the LDR only sinks current, so we only need the downward swing, and the LM358 is fine.
- **Feedback capacitor.** Rf alone with the sensor's capacitance forms a phase-shift trap that makes op-amps ring or oscillate. A small Cf across Rf gives the loop a deliberate roll-off and keeps it stable.
- **Why subtract VREF in software.** The Arduino's ADC reference drifts with USB voltage. Both VREF and the signal drift together, so dV = Vsig - Vref is immune to that drift. This is ratiometric thinking.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap Rf to 100K for a meter that responds more to dim rooms (will pin in direct sunlight). Or drop to 10K-22K for an outdoor / sunlight meter.
- Replace the LDR with an actual photodiode (BPW34, or even a salvaged clear LED used in reverse). The TIA circuit does not change at all, only the sensor swaps - and *then* you finally get to use a 1M or 10M Rf the way the textbooks show, because a photodiode passes microamp-scale current rather than the milliamp-ish current an LDR can pass.
- Add a calibration mode: point at a known-lux source from a phone app and adjust K_LUX_PER_UA in the sketch.
- Add a peak-hold / decay display on the OLED.

## Why this is interesting

The transimpedance amplifier is the single most useful op-amp pattern you will ever learn. Every laser-power meter, optical communications receiver, pulse oximeter, and lab photodiode amplifier on Earth is some variant of this exact circuit. Pair it with the virtual-ground trick and you have unlocked single-supply analog design - the foundation for every battery-powered op-amp project on the kit. The "wait, why is my output pinned?" gotcha is also a small but valuable lesson: textbook circuit values assume textbook sensors, and a real part on your bench can be wildly different.

projects.name: LM324 Quad Window Comparator 9V Battery Gauge
projects.power_supply: 9V battery itself - the same battery being measured powers the gauge through a momentary TEST button and a L7805 regulator that creates a stable 5V reference rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hold the button and a row of four LEDs lights up - blue, green, yellow, red - to show how much juice your 9V battery has left. As the battery gets weaker, the lights drop off one by one like a fuel gauge in a car.

**Why it's fun**: No code, no screen, no computer brain - just a chip and some parts that magically "decide" things on their own. Test every old battery in the junk drawer and find out which ones still have life left and which ones are dead.

A pure-analog, zero-firmware twin of the Pocket Battery Health Monitor - same job (tell me if this 9V battery is still good), no microcontroller, no OLED, no code. Just one quad op-amp doing four comparisons at once and four LEDs that drop off as the battery drains.

## Parts list

- 1x LM324 quad op-amp (the brain - four comparators in one package)
- 1x L7805 +5V linear regulator (creates a stable reference rail that does NOT sag as the battery drains)
- 4x 5mm LEDs: blue, green, yellow, red (one per channel)
- 6x 10K 1% resistors (4 for the reference ladder, 2 for the battery divider)
- 4x 1K resistors (LED current limiters - 5V/1K = ~3 mA, plenty bright on modern LEDs)
- 1x 100uF cap (input bulk smoothing for the 7805)
- 1x 10uF cap (output bulk on the 7805 - borderline-OK on its own at this tiny load; in a "real" design you'd add a 0.1uF ceramic alongside)
- 1x 1uF cap (sits right by the LM324's V+ pin - keeps it stable)
- 1x small tactile push-button (TEST button - holding it powers the circuit so the gauge does not silently drain the very battery it's measuring)
- 1x breadboard, jumper wires
- 1x 9V battery (the thing being measured AND the power source - that's the fun part)

## Wiring notes

The 9V battery is BOTH the load-under-test and the power supply. That sounds like cheating but it's exactly how a fuel gauge in a car works - same circuit, same source.

**Power path:** 9V battery (+) -> TEST button -> raw 9V rail (filtered by 100uF) -> L7805 IN. L7805 OUT = stable +5V rail (filtered by 10uF). The LM324's V+ pin (pin 4) is tied to the +5V rail, NOT the raw 9V. V- (pin 11) goes to battery GND. The LEDs are also anchored to the +5V rail through their 1K resistors, so the op-amp output only ever has to swing between 0 V and ~5 V - no awkward mixed-rail story.

**Reference ladder (the four thresholds):** four 10K resistors stacked between +5V and GND make a uniform 4-step divider with three taps at 4.00 V, 3.00 V, and 2.00 V, plus the bottom-of-the-stack at 1.00 V. We use those four reference voltages (4.00 / 3.00 / 2.00 / 1.00) directly - no further "tuning," because uniform 10K resistors only give uniform 1.00 V steps from a 5.00 V rail. Live with that, it works.

**Battery sense:** a 10K/10K divider from the raw battery rail to GND gives V_batt/2 at its midpoint. So a fresh 9 V battery presents 4.5 V there, a tired 6 V battery presents 3.0 V. That single midpoint goes to ALL FOUR negative inputs of the LM324, tied together.

**The trip points** (sense input = V_batt/2):

| LED    | Reference tap | Sense threshold | V_batt threshold |
| ------ | ------------- | --------------- | ---------------- |
| Blue   | 4.00 V        | 4.00 V          | 8.0 V            |
| Green  | 3.00 V        | 3.00 V          | 6.0 V            |
| Yellow | 2.00 V        | 2.00 V          | 4.0 V            |
| Red    | 1.00 V        | 1.00 V          | 2.0 V            |

In practice on a 9V alkaline: fresh battery (9.5 V) = all four LEDs lit. As it drains: Blue drops off at 8 V, Green at 6 V (battery is now firmly "tired"), Yellow at 4 V (basically dead - and the L7805 also drops out of regulation around here, so the readings get unreliable). Red is effectively always lit while the circuit has power - reframe it as "circuit power present / sanity LED" rather than a real low-battery alarm.

**The comparator trick:** with V_batt/2 on the - input and a fixed reference on the + input, the op-amp output goes HIGH (close to V+) when reference > sense, and LOW (close to GND) when sense > reference. We want LEDs to be ON when the battery is HIGH, so each LED has its CATHODE on the op-amp output and its ANODE through a 1K resistor to the +5V rail. The LED lights when the output goes LOW (the op-amp SINKS current to ground), which happens when V_batt/2 is greater than that channel's threshold. As the battery drains, V_batt/2 falls below each threshold one by one and the LEDs turn off blue -> green -> yellow.

**Why a stable reference matters:** if both the reference AND the battery sense came from the same battery, the ratio between them would stay constant as the battery drained - the LEDs would never change. The L7805 anchors the reference at 5.000 V no matter what the battery is doing (down to about 7 V of input, then the 7805 itself drops out of regulation).


## Flash it and run it

**The gauge itself has no brain to flash.** Pop a 9V battery in the clip, hold the white TEST button, and the LEDs decide what to show all by themselves. No laptop, no code, no Wi-Fi - the chip just thinks. Let go of the button and everything switches off so the gauge doesn't quietly drink the battery it's measuring.

**What you should see:**

- Fresh 9V battery (around 9.0 V): all four LEDs lit - blue, green, yellow, red.
- A used battery around 7 V: blue drops out, green + yellow + red still on.
- A tired battery around 5 V: blue and green both gone, only yellow + red.
- A nearly dead battery around 3 V: just red, faintly.
- A truly dead battery (under ~2 V): nothing lights up at all - the 7805 needs about 7 V on its input to make a clean 5 V, so down there the whole gauge just gives up. That itself is a "this battery is toast" signal.

**Optional: hook up the Arduino sketch to peek inside (only if you want to)**

This is for the grown-up who's curious whether the trip points really happen where they should. You only need the Arduino IDE for this part - the gauge does not need it.

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. Tools -> Board -> "Arduino Uno".
2. No extra libraries needed - this sketch only uses `analogRead` and `Serial`, both built in.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-B cable (the big square-ish plug).
2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says COM* (Windows) or cu.usbmodem* (Mac) or ttyACM0 (Linux). If you're not sure which is the Uno, unplug it, look at the list, plug it back in, and grab the new entry.
3. No passwords or Wi-Fi settings to fill in - this sketch is plain offline logging.
4. Wire the helper: **one** jumper from the gauge's VSENSE node (the midpoint of the 10K / 10K battery divider) into Uno **A0**, and **one** jumper from gauge GND to Uno GND. That's it - two wires. Do NOT build another 10K/10K divider on the Uno side, and do NOT tap the raw 9V rail into A0 (you'd fry the Uno's input).
5. Click Upload (the right-arrow icon at the top).
6. Tools -> Serial Monitor, set the baud dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200**.
7. Hold the TEST button on the gauge. You should see lines like `V_batt = 8.73 V   [ BLU GRN YEL --- ]` ticking past twice a second. Compare the letters in the brackets to which LEDs are actually lit on the breadboard - they should agree.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Capacitor polarity backwards.** The 100uF, 10uF, and 1uF are all electrolytic - they have a + leg (longer) and a - leg (shorter, marked with a white stripe on the can). Backwards = pop, smoke, sad day. The + leg goes toward the higher-voltage side (battery+ on the 100uF, 5V rail on the 10uF and 1uF).
- **LED in backwards = no light, no damage.** Long leg (anode) goes to the LM324 output side through the 1K resistor; short leg (cathode, flat spot on the rim) goes to +5V. If a channel stays dark when it should be on, flip that LED.
- **Forgetting to share grounds with the Uno.** If you only run the VSENSE wire to A0 without also tying gauge GND to Uno GND, A0 will read garbage - bouncing numbers that don't match the LEDs. Two wires, not one.
- **Serial Monitor at the wrong baud.** The sketch prints at 115200. If the Monitor is set to 9600 (the default) you'll just see gibberish like `⸮⸮p⸮⸮` - change the dropdown, don't re-flash.
## Talking points

- **Open-loop op-amp = comparator.** Op-amps are normally used WITH feedback (input to output through a resistor) to make stable amplifiers. With no feedback they have wild gain (~100,000x) and slam the output to one rail or the other based on which input is higher. That "slamming" is exactly what a comparator does. There's a real dedicated comparator IC (LM339) sitting in the same parts drawer - the LM324 is a slightly-slower, dual-purpose stand-in here, picked because it's already in the bin.
- **Why four channels?** One LM324 chip contains four independent op-amps. They share power pins (4 and 11) but their inputs and outputs are otherwise separate. So one chip = four comparators = a bar-graph display, all for the price of one IC.
- **Why a separate reference rail?** Already covered above, but worth saying out loud: if the reference scaled with the battery, nothing would ever trip. The L7805 is the load-bearing part that makes the whole circuit MEAN something.
- **Why tie all four - inputs together?** All four comparators are watching the same battery. Only the + reference differs per channel. That's the "quad window" idea: four windows looking at one signal at four different heights.
- **Why is the LED on the cathode side?** When the LM324 output goes LOW it can SINK current to ground much more cleanly than it can SOURCE to V+. LM324 outputs can swing to within a few hundred millivolts of GND but only to about 1.5 V below V+. Sinking through the LED + 1K to +5V is the clean choice - and it's exactly the gotcha that trips up everyone the first time they see a comparator drive a load.
- **Why uniform 1V steps and not "nicely tuned" trip points?** Honest answer: four 10K resistors between 5V and GND can only give 1.00 V steps. To get e.g. 4.25 / 3.75 / 3.25 / 2.75 V you'd need different resistor values in the ladder. The uniform ladder is the "use what's in the drawer" answer; once it works, you can swap values for finer resolution near 7-8 V where a 9V battery actually lives.

## Things to change once it works

- **Move the thresholds where they matter.** A 9V alkaline is interesting between 6.5 V and 9.5 V. Bunching the four trip points there is the obvious upgrade: replace the uniform ladder with non-uniform values (e.g. 1.5K / 2.2K / 2.2K / 4.7K from the inventory) so taps land near 4.25 / 3.75 / 3.25 / 2.75 V on the reference side = 8.5 / 7.5 / 6.5 / 5.5 V on the battery side. Same circuit, just better-tuned divider math.
- **Add hysteresis.** Tie a 1M resistor from each output back to its + input. Now the threshold "snaps" up slightly after the LED turns off, so a flickering battery doesn't make the LED flicker. Same trick a thermostat uses to keep from cycling near the setpoint.
- **Use the dedicated comparator (LM339 / LM393).** They have open-collector outputs which need a pull-up but switch faster and cleaner than an LM324 used open-loop. Drop-in for a v2.
- **Monitor a different battery.** Want to check a 12 V SLA? Change the battery divider from 10K/10K to 10K/4.7K, leave everything else alone - now the trip points are at 14.6 / 11.0 / 7.3 / 3.7 V on the battery side.
- **Solder it onto a prototype PCB** with a 9V battery clip - now it's a permanent gadget you can clip onto any 9V battery in the drawer to see which ones are still good.

## Why this is interesting

This is a finished, useful tool by the end of an afternoon: clip it onto any 9V battery and you can tell at a glance whether it's fresh, half-used, or trash. ZERO microcontrollers, ZERO code, one IC quietly doing the job of four. Understanding why the LM324 has four op-amps in it (and what to do with all of them) is the foot in the door for every analog circuit you'll ever build: filters, oscillators, sensor front-ends, audio mixers. They all stack op-amp stages exactly like this. Bonus: building this teaches the most counter-intuitive trick in beginner electronics - "the LED lights when the output goes LOW" - which trips everyone up the first time and never again after.

LED current-limiting (one per LED - 5V/1K = ~3 mA, plenty visible)
Momentary TEST button - hold to power the gauge so it does not drain the battery it is measuring
Stable 5V reference rail (battery would otherwise drift the threshold)

projects.name: No-MCU Dark Detector (LM358 Schmitt Trigger)
projects.power_supply: 9 V wall supply into an L7805 linear regulator that makes the +5 V rail. 100 uF input cap (35 V), 100 uF output cap (25 V) - polarity matters, striped lead to GND on both. No microcontroller is involved.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Cover the little sensor with your hand. A red LED snaps on and you hear the relay click. Uncover it and a moment later it clicks off. No code, no Arduino - the board just knows it got dark.

**Why it's fun**: Wire the relay to a desk lamp and you've built a thing that turns the light on by itself when the sun goes down. Wave your hand over the sensor at twilight and listen - a cheap circuit would chatter click-click-click, but yours clicks once and stays put, because you taught it to make up its mind.

## Parts list

- 1x LM358 Op-Amp (dual) - channel A is the Schmitt comparator, channel B is a unity-gain buffer that drives the indicator LED
- 1x KY-018 Photoresistor Module - the eye
- 1x 1-channel Relay Module - the muscle (low-voltage DC only) - driven directly from the LM358 output through a 1K series resistor
- 1x L7805 Linear Regulator (+5V) - TO-220, produces the +5 V rail from a 9 V wall supply
- 1x Resistor 100K (1/8W 1%) - top of the threshold divider
- 1x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - bottom of the threshold divider
- 1x Resistor 220K (1/8W 1%) - positive-feedback resistor (the project rests on this one - it sets the dead-band)
- 1x Resistor 1K (1/8W 1%) - series resistor on the relay-module IN line
- 1x Resistor 330R (1/8W 1%) - LED current limit
- 1x LED 5mm Red - visible DARK indicator
- 1x Capacitor 100uF 35V (electrolytic) - L7805 INPUT cap (9 V side)
- 1x Capacitor 100uF 25V (electrolytic) - +5 V rail decoupling, absorbs the inrush surge when the relay coil energises
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm
- Jumper wires (M-M and F-M, one pack each)

There is NO Arduino, no ESP32 and no microcontroller anywhere on the board. That's the whole pedagogical point - we earn the +5 V rail honestly with an L7805 and a 9 V supply.

## Wiring notes

Power comes in from a 9 V wall supply into the L7805 (pin 1 = IN, pin 2 = GND, pin 3 = OUT, tab is GND). A 100 uF 35V electrolytic sits across the input pins and a 100 uF 25V electrolytic sits across the output pins. Polarity matters - the striped / short-lead side of each cap goes to GND. Reversed electrolytics will vent. Check before power-on.

LM358 pinout (top view, dot top-left): 1=OUT_A, 2=IN-_A, 3=IN+_A, 4=GND, 5=IN+_B, 6=IN-_B, 7=OUT_B, 8=Vcc.

- **Sense path:** KY-018 'AO' -> LM358 pin 2 (inverting input). Bright -> high voltage; dark -> low voltage.
- **Threshold divider:** +5 V -> 100K -> node X -> 10K -> GND. Node X sits at 5 * 10/(100+10) = 0.4545 V nominal.
- **The hysteresis:** node X also feeds LM358 pin 3. From pin 1 (channel-A output) a 220K resistor runs back to pin 3. THIS is the Schmitt trick - the output tugs the threshold up or down depending on which state it is in.
- **Relay drive:** LM358 pin 1 -> 1K series -> relay module IN pin. The 1-ch relay module's input is a high-impedance optocoupler-style stage with its own onboard transistor and its IN-pin threshold sits around 2 V. The LM358 output swings ~0.6 V low to ~3.5 V high, which is comfortably outside that threshold in BOTH directions, so it drives the module directly with no BJT buffer. The module is active-LOW: when the LM358 is LOW (room bright) the module energises the relay; when the LM358 is HIGH (room dark) the module releases. Wire the load across COM and NC so that 'dark = load on' matches the indicator LED.
- **Indicator LED:** the second LM358 channel is wired as a unity-gain buffer (pin 5 tied to pin 1, pin 6 tied to pin 7). When channel A goes HIGH (dark), channel B also goes HIGH and pushes current out pin 7 through 330R to the red LED to GND. This keeps the LED off the relay-module IN pin entirely, so the LED and the relay module never fight each other for current.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, runs the second power touches it. No laptop, no USB cable, no Arduino IDE. Just a 9 V wall supply and a multimeter.

**Power-up procedure (do these in order, with your dad watching the caps):**

1. **Power OFF.** Look at both electrolytic caps one more time. The stripe (and the shorter lead) goes to GND. If you got one backwards it will hiss or pop the first time you plug in, so it is worth the extra ten seconds.
2. **Check the L7805 sits flat** with its tab pointing the way the wiring notes say. Pin 1 takes the 9 V from the wall supply, pin 2 is GND, pin 3 is the +5 V that feeds everything else.
3. **Set your multimeter to DC volts**, 20 V range. Put the black probe on the GND rail and leave it there.
4. **Plug in the 9 V wall supply.** Nothing visible should happen yet - no smoke, no smell, no popping. If anything pops, yank the plug.
5. **Touch the red probe to the +5 V rail.** You want to read between 4.9 V and 5.1 V. If you read 9 V the regulator is in backwards. If you read 0 V the input cap is probably reversed and shorting the supply.
6. **Uncover the KY-018 so room light hits it.** The red LED should be OFF and the relay should be silent (or its little onboard LED should be off, depending on which way your module is wired).
7. **Cup your hand over the KY-018 to make it dark.** Within a second the red LED snaps on and you hear the relay click. Lift your hand - after a moment it clicks back off. One clean click each way, no chatter. That is the hysteresis doing its job.
8. **Walk through the TP1 to TP5 voltages** listed in the bash script in the Code section. They are your map - if something is wrong, the wrong voltage tells you which corner of the board to look at.

**What "working" looks like:** cover the sensor, LED on, relay click. Uncover, wait a beat, LED off, relay click. Wave your hand back and forth slowly over the sensor at the threshold point - it should pick a side and stick to it, not chatter.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Electrolytic cap in backwards.** The 100 uF caps are the only parts on this board that can actually hurt you (a vented cap spits hot electrolyte). Stripe-to-GND, every time. If a cap gets warm in the first ten seconds, unplug immediately.
- **LM358 rotated 180 degrees.** The little dot or notch goes top-left. If the chip is flipped, pin 8 (which wants +5 V) is sitting on GND and pin 4 (which wants GND) is sitting on +5 V - the chip will get hot fast and not work. Touch it carefully after a few seconds; if it is hot, power off and re-seat it.
- **Relay clicks endlessly at twilight (chatter).** That means the 220K positive-feedback resistor is missing, in the wrong holes, or going to the wrong pin. Without it, the LM358 is just a plain comparator and will buzz right at the threshold. Check that one end is on LM358 pin 1 and the other end is on pin 3.
## Talking points

This is the circuit you build to understand WHY twilight makes plain comparators misbehave. A bare LM393 or a plain LM358 with no feedback will sit right at the trip point as the sun sets and the output will chatter - flicker on, off, on, off - because the input is wobbling through the threshold a hundred times a second. A Schmitt trigger fixes that by having two thresholds: one to turn on, a different one to turn off. The gap between them is called the hysteresis window.

How does it create two thresholds out of one circuit? Positive feedback. The 220K resistor takes a fraction of the output and adds it back to the threshold on pin 3. When the output is LOW (room is lit, relay off), pin 3 sits just a hair above the nominal 0.455 V. When the output is HIGH (room is dark, relay on), pin 3 gets tugged up toward 0.58 V. The trip point literally moves out of the way of the input as the input approaches it. That's the whole idea.

You can compute the window honestly. Thevenin the 100K/10K divider to V_div = 0.4545 V with source impedance R_div = 100K||10K = 9.09K. The threshold at pin 3 with R_f = 220K from the output is V_th = (V_div * R_f + V_out * R_div) / (R_f + R_div). With V_out_low ~ 0.6 V (the LM358 cannot reach true 0 V - that's a real, annoying spec of the part) you get V_th_low ~ 0.460 V. With V_out_high ~ 3.5 V (Vcc - 1.5 V is the LM358's upper swing limit) you get V_th_high ~ 0.575 V. Dead-band ~ 115 mV. Plenty to outvote any noise from a wobbling LDR at dusk.

We deliberately use the second LM358 channel as the LED driver instead of tapping the relay-module IN pin. That separation matters: the relay module's input is high-impedance and easily upset if you parallel a milliamp-class LED across it. Using channel B as a unity-gain buffer costs us nothing (the dual op-amp is already in the socket) and keeps the loads cleanly separated.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap the 220K feedback resistor for 100K (much wider dead-band, sluggish) or 470K (narrower, snappier but trending back toward chatter). Plot the window with your DMM.
- Remove the feedback resistor entirely and watch the output chatter at twilight. That's the bug a Schmitt trigger exists to fix - seeing the broken version makes the fix click.
- Replace the relay with a buzzer for an audible 'it's getting dark' alarm.
- Add a window comparator by wiring an LM393 in parallel with its own divider and feedback network, so you light a separate LED for 'too bright'.
- Replace the relay output with a MOSFET driving an LED strip and you've turned this into a real automatic night-light, no microcontroller in sight.

## Why this is interesting

The existing Porch Night-Light uses an ESP32 to read the LDR and fade an LED via PWM - that project is about software smoothness. THIS project is the same idea solved entirely in analog hardware: three resistors, a dual op-amp, and an L7805 to make the rail. There is no code path to debug, no ADC sample window to tune. The whole behaviour is set by three resistor values and the op-amp's swing limits. Once you have lived with a Schmitt trigger you start spotting them everywhere - inside every comparator IC datasheet, in 74HC14 inverters, in PIR sensor front-ends, in PWM controller chips like the UC3842 you have in the kit. Hysteresis is the cure for 'the input is right on the edge' and that situation comes up constantly.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# LM358 No-MCU Dark Detector - multimeter bring-up procedure
# This is a pure-analog circuit. There is no firmware to flash.
# Power the board from a 9 V wall supply into the L7805 (NOT from a USB port).
# Walk through these test points in order with a DMM set to DC volts.

set -e

cat <<'TESTS'
==================================================================
 PRE-FLIGHT (power OFF, board un-powered)
==================================================================
 1. Confirm L7805 orientation. With the printed face toward you and
    the tab pointing up: pin 1 = IN (9 V), pin 2 = GND, pin 3 = OUT
    (+5 V). The tab is internally connected to GND.
 2. ELECTROLYTIC CAP POLARITY (read twice, beginners blow these up):
       - The 100uF 35V input cap: striped side / short lead -> GND.
         Long lead -> L7805 pin 1 (9 V input).
       - The 100uF 25V output cap: striped side / short lead -> GND.
         Long lead -> +5 V rail.
       Reversed electrolytics will pop, hiss, or vent. Check them
       with the cap leaning away from your face before powering up.
 3. Confirm LM358 orientation: notch / pin-1 dot top-left. Pin 4 =
    GND, pin 8 = +5 V (Vcc). Channel A (pins 1/2/3) is the Schmitt
    comparator. Channel B (pins 5/6/7) drives the indicator LED.
 4. Confirm KY-018: '-' to GND rail, 'middle' to +5 V rail,
    'S' (AO) to LM358 pin 2 (inverting input).
 5. Confirm relay module: VCC -> +5 V, GND -> GND, IN <- 1K series
    resistor <- LM358 pin 1. NO BC547 anywhere.
 6. Confirm indicator LED: LM358 pin 7 -> 330R -> LED anode (long
    lead) -> LED cathode (short lead, flat side) -> GND. LM358
    channel B is wired as a buffer: pin 5 (IN+) tied to pin 1
    (channel-A output), pin 6 (IN-) tied to pin 7 (its own output).

==================================================================
 POWER ON. Apply 9 V to the L7805 input. First sweep: room bright
 (uncover the KY-018). Second sweep: cover the KY-018 fully.
==================================================================

 TP1  +5 V rail (L7805 pin 3)  . . . . . . . . . expect 4.9 - 5.1 V
 TP2  GND rail  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.00 V
 TP3  LM358 pin 8 (Vcc)  . . . . . . . . . . . expect same as TP1
 TP4  LM358 pin 4 (GND)  . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.00 V

 TP5  KY-018 AO into pin 2 (the SENSE voltage)
        BRIGHT room . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 2.5 - 4.5 V
        COVERED (dark)  . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.1 - 0.6 V
      If both readings look identical, the KY-018 trim-pot is
      pegged - turn it until you see a clear bright/dark swing.

 TP6  LM358 pin 3 (the threshold, with hysteresis)
        Bright state (op-amp output LOW) . . . expect ~0.46 V
        Dark   state (op-amp output HIGH) . . . expect ~0.58 V
      The ~115 mV jump between the two readings IS the hysteresis
      dead-band. That gap is what stops the relay from buzzing at
      twilight. (Math: V_th = (V_div*R_f + V_out*R_div)/(R_f+R_div)
      with V_div=0.455 V, R_div=100K||10K=9.09K, R_f=220K. V_out
      sits at ~0.6 V low / ~3.5 V high on an LM358.)

 TP7  LM358 pin 1 (channel-A output)
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.1 - 0.7 V
                                                (LM358 cannot reach
                                                true 0 V - the low
                                                rail is ~0.6 V)
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 3.3 - 3.8 V
                                                (LM358 swing limit
                                                is Vcc - 1.5 V)

 TP8  LM358 pin 7 (channel-B output, the LED driver)
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . tracks pin 1, LED off
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . tracks pin 1, LED on

 TP9  Relay module IN pin
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ~0.1 - 0.7 V (module
                                                sees a LOW, relay
                                                energises - module
                                                is active-LOW)
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ~3.3 - 3.8 V (module
                                                sees a HIGH, relay
                                                releases)
      Wire your load across the relay's COM and NC terminals so
      'dark = load on' matches the red indicator LED.

==================================================================
 HYSTERESIS DEMO - the whole point of the project
==================================================================
 1. Slowly cover the KY-018 with a finger, watching the red LED.
    Note the light level at which it CLICKS ON.
 2. Slowly uncover. The LED will NOT click off at the same light
    level - it stays on until the room is noticeably brighter.
 3. The dead-band between those two light levels is the hysteresis
    window. Swap the 220K feedback resistor for 100K to widen it,
    or 470K to narrow it, and watch the dead-band change size.
    Remove the feedback resistor entirely and you'll see the relay
    chatter at twilight - which is the bug a Schmitt trigger fixes.

==================================================================
 TROUBLESHOOTING
==================================================================
 * Relay chatters near twilight       -> feedback resistor open or
                                         missing (should be 220K)
 * Relay never turns on at all        -> KY-018 trim-pot wrong, or
                                         pin 2/3 swapped
 * Relay always on                    -> KY-018 AO stuck low; rotate
                                         module trim-pot clockwise
 * LM358 output stuck near 2.5 V      -> pin 4 (GND) not connected,
                                         OR input is hovering exactly
                                         on the threshold (cover the
                                         sensor and re-check)
 * L7805 gets hot fast / output low   -> input cap reversed, or
                                         input/output pins swapped
TESTS

Bulk decoupling across the +5 V rail - smooths the inrush surge when the relay coil energises. NOTE polarity: long lead / unmarked side = +5 V, short lead / striped side = GND. Reversed it will pop.
Input bulk cap for the L7805 (between 9 V input and GND). NOTE polarity: striped side = GND.
Visible 'DARK' indicator driven by the SECOND LM358 channel (pin 7) so it never fights the relay-module input stage

Module is active-LOW but its onboard transistor sinks the coil current - so when our op-amp output goes HIGH (dark) the module's IN is HIGH and relay is OFF; we wire the relay's COM/NC pair to the load so 'dark = load on'.

Positive-feedback resistor from op-amp output back to pin 3 - SETS the hysteresis (~115 mV dead-band with this divider)

projects.name: LM386 Pocket Speaker Amp (matchbox half-watt)
projects.power_supply: 5V from a USB-C phone charger or power bank via the USB-C pigtail. LM386 happily runs 4-12V so a 9V battery works too if you want it portable - just keep the pin 7 BYPASS cap in place at the higher voltage.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone into the breadboard, hit play, and a tiny speaker the size of a coin blasts your music loud enough to fill the room. The whole amplifier fits in a matchbox.

**Why it's fun**: You built a real boombox out of one black chip and a handful of parts, no batteries or apps required. Crank it up at the dinner table and watch everyone wonder where the song is coming from.

## Parts list

- 1x LM386 Audio Power Amp (8-pin DIP)
- 1x 1uF electrolytic - input DC blocker
- 2x 10uF electrolytic - one is the gain-set cap between pins 1 and 8, one is the pin 7 BYPASS cap to GND
- 1x 47uF electrolytic - supply bypass
- 1x 100uF electrolytic - bulk reservoir on the 5V rail
- 1x 220uF electrolytic - output DC blocker to speaker
- 1x 10K resistor - series input attenuator (acts as a fixed volume control)
- 1x breadboard
- 1x USB-C female pigtail for 5V power in (any phone charger / power bank)
- Hookup wires
- *You supply:* a small 8-ohm speaker (anything from a dead toy or old set of earbuds will do), a 3.5mm headphone jack or a chopped aux cable, and the phone to play music from

> The textbook LM386 circuit adds a 10R + 47nF ceramic snubber (a "Zobel network") from pin 5 to GND to damp ultrasonic ringing. We skip it because we don't stock 47nF ceramics, and on a short breadboard the LM386 is usually stable without it. If you hear a faint high-pitched whine after everything else works, that's why - the proper fix is to add the Zobel, not to substitute a 47uF electrolytic (a factor-of-1000 different value, which would short the output through the 10R resistor across the entire audio band and cook the chip).

## Wiring notes

LM386 pinout (notch at top):

```
    +-----+
1 --|     |-- 8     1 = GAIN
2 --|     |-- 7     2 = -IN (to GND)
3 --|     |-- 6     3 = +IN  (audio from phone)
4 --|     |-- 5     4 = GND
    +-----+         5 = OUT
                    6 = Vcc
                    7 = BYPASS (10uF to GND - required at high gain)
                    8 = GAIN
```

On the breadboard:

1. Drop the LM386 across the centre groove.
2. **Power.** USB-C pigtail: red wire to the breadboard's `+` rail, black to the `-` rail. Wire LM386 pin 6 to `+`, pin 4 to `-`. Drop the 100uF (long leg to `+`) and the 47uF (long leg to pin 6) across the rails right next to the chip.
3. **Gain = 200x.** This is the famous trick: a 10uF cap from pin 1 to pin 8 bypasses an internal 1.35K resistor and pushes the gain from the default 20x all the way up to 200x. Long leg of the 10uF goes to pin 1.
4. **BYPASS cap (non-optional at high gain).** Second 10uF: long leg to pin 7, short leg to the `-` rail. Pin 7 is the LM386's internal reference-voltage pin. Without this cap to ground the chip hums audibly and is far more likely to break into oscillation. Every datasheet "typical application" circuit at gain=200 shows this cap - omitting it is the most common reason a beginner LM386 build sounds noisy.
5. **Input.** Phone jack tip -> 1uF cap (orient the `+` leg toward the phone to match convention - the phone output sits near 0V DC, but `+` toward the higher DC potential is the standard rule) -> 10K resistor -> LM386 pin 3. Phone jack sleeve -> `-` rail. Pin 2 -> `-` rail.
6. **Output.** LM386 pin 5 -> 220uF (long leg to pin 5) -> one speaker terminal. Other speaker terminal -> `-` rail.

Plug the USB-C, plug the phone, hit play, and turn the phone's volume to about half.


## Flash it and run it

This one is mostly **plug in and play music** - the amp is pure analog, so the second 5V power hits it, it is alive. No code needed for the main job.

**Power-up procedure (the main event):**

1. Double-check the LM386 is sitting across the centre groove with the **notch facing up** (pin 1 top-left).
2. Double-check every electrolytic cap's long leg (`+`) is on the side the wiring notes said. Capacitors put in backwards are the #1 reason a fresh build does not work.
3. Plug a small 8-ohm speaker between the far end of the 220uF output cap and the `-` rail. Speaker polarity does not matter for sound.
4. Plug your 3.5mm jack into the 1uF input cap (tip wire) and the `-` rail (sleeve wire). Do NOT plug your phone in yet.
5. Plug the USB-C pigtail into a phone charger or power bank.
6. The amp should be silent. Touch a finger to the **bare metal of pin 3** of the LM386. The speaker should HUM loudly - a low buzzy 50/60 Hz mains hum. That is your body acting as an antenna for the mains in the walls, and it proves the gain is working. If you hear that hum, the amp is alive.
7. Unplug the USB-C, plug your phone into the 3.5mm jack, plug USB-C back in, hit play on the phone. Start the phone volume around halfway.

**Optional - flash an Arduino Uno as a test-tone generator:**

Only do this if step 6 above did NOT produce a hum and you want to feed the amp a known-good signal to narrow down the problem. You will need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

*Every time you flash:*

1. Disconnect the phone jack tip wire from the 1uF input cap. In its place, run a jumper from **Arduino Uno pin 9** to the same spot (the `+` leg of the 1uF cap).
2. Run another jumper from **Arduino Uno GND** to the breadboard `-` rail. Both grounds must be tied together or the Uno's signal has no reference.
3. Leave the amp powered from its own USB-C 5V. Do not power the LM386 from the Uno's 5V pin.
4. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-A-to-USB-B printer cable.
5. In the Arduino IDE: **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**.
6. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the COM* port that appears when you plug the Uno in (try unplugging and replugging to see which one disappears).
7. Paste in the sketch from the Code section. No libraries to install, no WiFi password to set - this sketch is plain `tone()`.
8. Click **Upload** (the right-arrow icon at the top). Wait for "Done uploading."
9. **Tools -> Serial Monitor**, set the baud rate at the bottom-right to **115200** (matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code).
10. You should see: `LM386 bench test - 1 kHz beep every second` plus a short troubleshooting checklist printed once.
11. From the speaker you should hear a clean **1 kHz beep** roughly twice a second (0.4 s on, 0.6 s off). If you hear that, the amp is 100% fine and the original problem was somewhere in the phone-jack wiring.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Capacitor polarity backwards.** Especially the 220uF output cap (`+` to pin 5) and the pin 7 BYPASS 10uF (`+` to pin 7). A backwards electrolytic can sound dead, scratchy, or even pop and leak. If in doubt, pull each one and re-seat it long-leg-where-the-wiring-notes-say.
- **No common ground when using the Uno test.** If you forget the jumper from Uno GND to the breadboard `-` rail, you get silence or random noise instead of a beep. The Uno's pin 9 signal is measured against Uno GND, so the amp must share that ground.
- **Serial Monitor baud wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`, the baud dropdown in the bottom-right is not on **115200**. Fix the dropdown - do not change the code.
## Talking points

- The LM386 has been in production since 1983. It is the audio version of the NE555 - cheap, indestructible, taught in every electronics class, and still in current designs.
- The chip has a built-in feedback network that fixes its gain at 20 by default. Pins 1 and 8 are the two ends of that internal resistor divider. Drop a capacitor across them and at audio frequencies the cap looks like a short, removing the resistor from the loop and shoving gain to 200.
- Pin 7 (BYPASS) connects to an internal reference voltage that biases the input stage. Without a cap from pin 7 to ground, any noise on the supply rail rides straight onto that reference and gets amplified 200x. That is why this cap is the difference between "music" and "music with a loud 60 Hz hum behind it."
- Everything else on the chip is "auxiliary" - input bias, output coupling, supply bypass. The amplification itself is one transistor stage with feedback. That is the entire story of an op-amp / power-amp.
- The 220uF output cap exists because the LM386's output sits at roughly half the supply voltage (2.5V on a 5V rail). If you wired the speaker straight to pin 5 you would push 2.5V DC through the coil constantly - it would get hot and eventually burn out. The cap blocks DC while letting audio (AC) through.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap the 10K series resistor for a 10K potentiometer to get a real volume knob.
- Try removing the gain cap (pin 1 to pin 8) entirely - gain drops to 20, the amp gets noticeably quieter, but it also gets cleaner. Beginner lesson: more gain = more noise.
- Power it from a 9V battery instead of 5V USB. The chip happily runs on 4 to 12V and gets noticeably louder at 9V because the output swing is bigger. Note: at 9V the higher gain headroom makes oscillation much more likely, so the pin 7 BYPASS cap above is absolutely non-optional in that mode - and that is also when you really want to add the 10R + 47nF Zobel snubber the parts list skipped.
- Build a stereo version by wiring up a second LM386 - one chip per channel - sharing the same input jack via two separate 1uF caps.
- Once it works on the breadboard, lay it out on a Double-Sided Prototype PCB and stuff the whole thing into a mint tin with a speaker.

## Why this is interesting

The first time you build an amplifier and music comes out of it, electronics stops being "blink an LED" and starts being a real tool. The LM386 will reappear in dozens of future projects: as the speaker driver for an MCU playing wavetables, as the output stage of a crystal radio, as the buzzer on an alarm. Learning where its pins go once means you never have to look it up again.

projects.name: LM386 Telegraph-Style Code Practice Oscillator
projects.power_supply: Powered from an Arduino Uno used purely as a regulated 5V brick over USB (USB jack -> Uno's 5V/GND pins -> breadboard rails). No code is uploaded to the Uno and no GPIO is used.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Press and hold the button and a red LED starts blinking, about once a second, like a tiny lighthouse on your breadboard. Let go and it goes dark. Tap out short and long presses and you are flashing real Morse code.

**Why it's fun**: Sailors used to flash messages between ships at night with big lamps just like this, and now you have a pocket-sized version on your desk. Learn the dots and dashes for your name, then flash it across the room to your dad and see if he can read it back.

## Parts list

- 1x LM386 audio power amp (the star - rewired as a slow relaxation oscillator that flashes an LED in Morse-code rhythm, NOT as an audio amp this time)
- 1x Tactile push-button 3x6x5mm (the "telegraph key")
- 1x 10uF electrolytic cap (the timing cap - this, together with the 100K feedback resistor, sets the flash rate)
- 1x 100uF electrolytic cap (Vcc bypass - keeps the supply quiet)
- 1x 100K resistor (the feedback resistor - the cap charges through this; with the 10uF it gives a roughly 1-second flash period)
- 2x 10K resistors (a half-supply reference divider on pin 2)
- 1x 470R resistor (current limit for the LED on the output)
- 1x 5mm red LED (the visible "telegraph lamp")
- 1x Breadboard
- M-M jumper wires
- 1x Arduino Uno (used ONLY as a regulated 5V/GND brick through its USB jack - no code uploaded, no GPIO touched)

Note on the "telegraph" angle: the inventory has no speaker or buzzer, so this build is a *visible* code-practice oscillator - a blinking lamp instead of a beep. That's historically real too: in the 1800s the Royal Navy and the army practised Morse on Aldis lamps and heliographs (mirror-reflected sunlight). Same code, same rhythm, light instead of sound.

## Safety first - read this before plugging in

Electrolytic caps have a polarity stripe marked on the side. **Backwards = they can heat up, vent, and occasionally pop.** Both caps in this build are electrolytic. Before you connect 5V:

- 10uF timing cap: **plus (long leg) toward LM386 pin 3, stripe (short leg) toward GND.**
- 100uF supply cap: **plus (long leg) toward LM386 pin 6 (Vcc), stripe (short leg) toward GND.**

Eyeball both stripes BEFORE you plug the USB cable in. If you smell anything warm once power is on, unplug immediately.

## Wiring notes

LM386 pinout (notch up, looking down at the chip):

```
        +---v---+
   1 GAIN | 1   8 | GAIN  8
   2 -IN  | 2   7 | BYPASS 7
   3 +IN  | 3   6 | VCC    6
   4 GND  | 4   5 | OUT    5
        +-------+
```

1. Plant the LM386 across the breadboard's centre channel, notch to the LEFT. Pin 1 is top-left, pin 4 is bottom-left, pin 5 is bottom-right, pin 8 is top-right.
2. **Power rails:** Uno's 5V pin to the breadboard's red rail, Uno's GND to the blue rail. The Uno is just a tidy regulated 5V source - we never upload anything.
3. **The "telegraph key":** the tactile push-button breaks the 5V line BEFORE it reaches LM386 pin 6. One leg of the button to the +5V rail, the other leg to pin 6. Press = chip powered = LED starts blinking. Release = silent and dark.
4. **Vcc bypass:** 100uF cap from LM386 pin 6 (+ long leg) to GND rail (stripe / short leg). Plant it close to the chip.
5. **GND:** LM386 pin 4 to the GND rail.
6. **Half-supply reference on pin 2 (-IN):** two 10K resistors in series from +5V to GND. The middle of that pair sits at +2.5V. Wire that midpoint to pin 2. This gives the chip's inverting input a fixed "decision line" at half-supply.
7. **The timing cap:** 10uF from pin 3 (+ long leg) to GND (stripe). This is the cap whose voltage will slowly swing up and down - the swinging voltage is what eventually drives the LED.
8. **The feedback resistor (the slow part):** 100K from pin 5 (output) back to pin 3 (+IN). This is the wire that charges the 10uF cap from the output. When the output is high, the cap charges up. When the output flips low, the cap discharges back through the same 100K. The roughly 1-second cap voltage charge/discharge against the 2.5V threshold on pin 2 is what makes the output flip flip flip at about 1 Hz - a visible flash rate.
9. **LED output:** pin 5 -> 470R resistor -> LED anode (long leg). LED cathode (short leg) to GND. Pin 5 will swing roughly between 0V and ~4V, so the LED visibly turns on and off.

Why this topology actually oscillates (and the old draft didn't): the LM386 here is acting like a comparator with hysteresis. Pin 2 is held at a fixed 2.5V reference. Pin 3 watches the cap voltage. When the cap charges above 2.5V the output slams low; when it discharges below 2.5V the output slams high. The 100K + 10uF set the time it takes to cross the threshold (RC = 1 second), which sets the visible flash rate. **Without the RC time constant there is no oscillation frequency at all** - a pure resistor-only feedback path just latches to a rail.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - there is no code, no microcontroller, no Arduino IDE. The Uno is only here because its USB jack gives us a clean, regulated 5V to feed the breadboard. The LM386 chip and the handful of resistors and caps do all the work the moment power touches them.

**Power-up procedure (do this slowly, in order):**

1. **Power OFF check first.** Before you go anywhere near the USB cable, eyeball the two electrolytic caps one more time. Long leg of the 10uF on LM386 pin 3, stripe toward GND. Long leg of the 100uF on pin 6, stripe toward GND. If either stripe is on the wrong side, pull the cap and turn it around now.
2. **Plug in the Uno's USB cable** to your laptop or to a USB phone charger. The Uno's own green "ON" LED should light up. That is the only thing that should light up so far - the red LED on your breadboard should still be dark, because the button is not pressed.
3. **(Optional but cool) Put your multimeter on DC volts** and touch the black probe to the blue (GND) rail and the red probe to the red (+5V) rail. You should see something between 4.9V and 5.1V. That is your "power is really there" check.
4. **Press and hold the tactile button.** Within a second or two, the red LED should start blinking, roughly once per second - on, off, on, off, like a slow lighthouse. Let go and it goes dark again.
5. **Tap out your name in Morse.** Short press = dot, long press = dash. The LED blinks the whole time you are holding, so a "dash" is just you holding the button longer.

**What "it worked" looks like:** button held = LED blinks about once a second; button released = LED dark and silent; nothing on the breadboard gets warm to the touch.

If you want to dig deeper, the **bench-test guide** (the bash script in the Code section) walks you through every test point with a multimeter - TP1 through TP6 - so you and your dad can poke around and see the half-supply voltage on pin 2, the slow sawtooth on pin 3, and the square-wave output on pin 5. Treat it as a treasure map for the circuit.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Electrolytic cap backwards.** This is the #1 thing to get wrong on this build. Long leg = plus, short leg / stripe = minus. If the LED never blinks AND a cap is getting warm, unplug right away and check the 10uF and 100uF orientations.
- **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no light. The long leg (anode) goes toward the 470R resistor coming from pin 5; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Pull it out, spin it 180 degrees, push it back in.
- **Button on the wrong pins.** Tactile buttons have 4 legs but only 2 real connections - the other 2 are just mechanical. If pressing the button does nothing, rotate the button 90 degrees in its holes and try again.
## Talking points

- The headline lesson is this: **an oscillator is a comparator looking at its own slow-moving output.** The LM386 here is doing nothing fancy. It looks at pin 3 (the cap), compares it to pin 2 (the 2.5V reference), and yanks the output high or low. The output yank slowly drags pin 3 in the opposite direction through the 100K. By the time pin 3 crosses the threshold, the comparator flips. Then the whole thing happens in reverse. That endless back-and-forth IS the oscillation.
- **Two things are required for oscillation, not just one.** A common beginner story is "feedback makes an amplifier oscillate." That's only half true. You need positive feedback AND a frequency-determining element - a capacitor that takes time to charge, or an LC tank, or a phase-shift network. Without something to set the timing, the loop either sits at one rail (latched) or whirls at the chip's gain-bandwidth limit, which is way above audio. Here the 100K + 10uF do the timing.
- **The LM386 datasheet gain-cap myth.** The classic LM386 use is to drop a 10uF cap between pins 1 and 8 to set audio gain to ~200. We are NOT doing that here - pins 1 and 8 are left empty. The chip's default gain of 20 is plenty for the comparator-style behaviour we want, and a gain cap on 1-8 wouldn't change the flash rate.
- **Why an LED instead of a speaker?** This kit has no speaker or piezo. Historically code-practice oscillators came in two flavours: an audio beeper (most common, the "buzzer" approach) and a flashing lamp (the Aldis-lamp / heliograph tradition). Both teach the same Morse rhythm. We're building the lamp version because that's what the inventory supports.
- **Real telegraph keys clicked.** When you release the button you may notice the LED lingers for a moment before going dark - that's the 100uF supply cap still draining. The original 1800s telegraph keys made an audible click on release too, for related reasons (an inductive armature relaxing). The flicker is your bug-free version of that click.

## Things to change once it works

- **Faster flash rate:** swap the 100K feedback resistor for 47K - period drops from ~1 s to ~0.5 s. Or swap the 10uF timing cap for 4.7uF for the same effect. Period scales roughly with R x C.
- **Slower flash rate (lighthouse mode):** swap the 100K for 220K, or the 10uF for 22uF. Period stretches to a couple of seconds.
- **Two LEDs that take turns:** add a second LED + 470R reversed across the first - cathode to pin 5, anode to GND. When pin 5 is high the first LED lights; when pin 5 is low the second lights. Now you have a heartbeat: one LED on, then the other.
- **Make it audible later:** if you ever pick up a small 8-ohm speaker or piezo disc, the same circuit will drive it - just shrink the timing cap to 22 nF and the resistor to 10K so the oscillation lands in the audible 500 Hz range, and put a coupling cap in series with the speaker. The topology stays the same; only the RC values change.
- **Practice real Morse code:** S = dit dit dit, O = dah dah dah, E = dit, T = dah. Hold the button for short presses (dits) and long presses (dahs). The classic timing rule is "a dah is three dits long."

## Why this is interesting

The thing worth remembering from this build is that **an oscillator is just a feedback loop that includes a delay**. The LM386 isn't special - any chip with an output, an input, and some gain can do this trick if you give it a slow path back to itself. The 100K + 10uF is the delay. Without that delay the chip can't tell where the threshold is from where it just was, so it locks up. With the delay, every crossing of the threshold is "news" the chip has to react to. That endless reaction IS what we call oscillation.

This pattern shows up everywhere once you spot it: the heartbeat of a 555 timer is the same idea (cap charges through R, threshold flips an internal latch, latch discharges cap), a digital clock crystal works on the same principle (a quartz disc that takes a fixed time to flex and unflex), even the cycle of a washing machine's agitator is a mechanical version. Get the delay right and you get the rhythm you want.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Telegraph-style code practice oscillator - bench-test guide.
# No microcontroller. Use a multimeter (DMM) to confirm the circuit
# before you start tapping. The whole thing should draw < 15 mA.
# If you smell anything hot, pull power IMMEDIATELY.
#
# CRITICAL POLARITY CHECK (do this BEFORE plugging in 5V):
#   - 10uF cap:  + (long leg) toward LM386 pin 3,
#                stripe / short leg toward GND.
#   - 100uF cap: + (long leg) toward LM386 pin 6 (Vcc),
#                stripe / short leg toward GND.
#
# Reversed electrolytics can heat up, vent, or pop. Always eyeball
# both stripes before powering up.
#
# Test points are labelled in the wiring_diagram. Probe with the
# black DMM lead on GND and the red lead on each test point.

set -e

cat <<'TESTS'
==============================================
LM386 Telegraph-Style CPO - bench-test guide
==============================================

Step 0: Eyeball check, power OFF
  - LM386 notch faces LEFT (pin 1 top-left, pin 8 top-right).
  - 10uF cap: + leg on pin 3, stripe on GND rail.
  - 100uF cap: + leg on pin 6 (Vcc side of the button), stripe on GND.
  - Two 10K resistors form a divider from +5V to GND; their midpoint
    goes to pin 2.
  - 100K resistor links pin 5 (output) to pin 3.
  - 470R + LED: pin 5 -> 470R -> LED anode (long leg) -> LED cathode
    -> GND.

Step 1: Power ON, button NOT pressed
  Plug the USB cable into the Uno. Do not press the button yet.
  TP1 (+5V rail)             -> expect  +4.9 to +5.1 V DC
  TP6 (LM386 pin 6, Vcc)     -> expect  ~0 V DC (rises briefly if the
                                100uF still holds charge from a
                                previous run - wait ~30 s for it to
                                drain through leakage, then re-probe)
  TP5 (LM386 pin 2, -IN)     -> expect  ~2.5 V DC (half-supply, set by
                                the 10K + 10K divider, present even
                                with the chip unpowered)
  LED                        -> dark

Step 2: Press and HOLD the tactile button
  TP6 (LM386 pin 6, Vcc)     -> expect  +4.8 to +5.0 V DC
  TP5 (LM386 pin 2, -IN)     -> still   ~2.5 V DC
  TP3 (LM386 pin 3, +IN)     -> expect  a slow sawtooth between
                                roughly 1 V and 3 V, swinging once
                                per second. A DMM in DC mode will
                                bounce; AC mode shows ~0.5 V AC.
  TP2 (LM386 pin 5, output)  -> expect  square wave between ~0 V and
                                ~4 V at about 1 Hz. DMM in DC mode
                                will average around 2 V.
  LED                        -> flashes about once per second

Step 3: Tap dits and dahs
  Short press (~0.5 s)  = dit  (LED gives a brief flash)
  Long  press (~1.5 s)  = dah  (LED gives a longer flash)
  SOS = dit dit dit  ...  dah dah dah  ...  dit dit dit

  Note: because the oscillator starts fresh each time you press, the
  very first flash of each press may be slightly off-rhythm. Real
  1800s lamp operators dealt with the same thing.

Step 4: Troubleshooting
  LED never lights:
    - Probe TP2 (pin 5) with DMM in DC mode while holding the button.
      If pin 5 reads a steady value near 0 V or near 4 V (not flipping),
      the feedback loop is broken - re-check the 100K from pin 5 to
      pin 3 and the 10uF from pin 3 to GND.
    - Confirm the LED is the right way round (long leg toward the
      470R / pin 5 side).
  LED on but does not blink:
    - Check the 100K wire. Without it pin 3 floats and the output
      latches.
    - Check the divider: pin 2 must sit at ~2.5 V. If pin 2 is at 0 V
      or 5 V, one of the 10K resistors is open or in the wrong row.
  Flashes way too fast (looks like a dim steady glow):
    - The timing cap or feedback resistor is wrong. Confirm 10uF
      (not 100 nF) and 100K (not 100R).
  LED stays lit dimly even with button released:
    - The button is wired across the wrong rows. It should break the
      +5V line between the rail and pin 6, not bridge pin 5 to GND.

TESTS
