projects.name: TDA2822D Stereo Earbud Amp
projects.power_supply: Single 9V PP3 battery via a snap clip feeds Vcc (pin 5) and GND (pin 4) of the TDA2822D, with a 100uF 16V bulk decoupling cap across the rails close to the chip.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone into one end and your earbuds into the other. Hit play and the music comes out loud and clear in both ears, left and right, powered by a tiny 9V battery.

**Why it's fun**: This is the first thing you build that turns into a real piece of audio gear you can actually use. Pull out a battery-powered headphone amp you made yourself at the kitchen table, plug in, and listen to your own music through it.

## Parts list

Allocations below are the canonical parts list. A few items are NOT in the kit inventory and you'll need to bring your own:

- **Bring-your-own (not in kit inventory):**
  - 9V PP3 battery with snap clip (the power source).
  - 3.5mm stereo input jack or a sacrificial 3.5mm cable (tip = L, ring = R, sleeve = GND).
  - A pair of earbuds (32 ohm typical). Do NOT plug in big 4 ohm bookshelf speakers - the TDA2822D is a small-signal chip.

- **From the kit (see allocations):**
  - 1x TDA2822D dual audio power amp.
  - 1x breadboard.
  - 1x 100uF 16V cap (bulk supply decoupling).
  - 2x 10uF caps (input DC blocking).
  - 2x 100uF 16V caps (AC bypass at IN-).
  - 2x 470uF 16V caps (output DC blocking).
  - 2x 4.7R resistors (output series damping).
  - 1x Arduino Uno + 2x 10K resistors - ONLY for the optional test-tone procedure. Skip them if you go straight to a phone as the audio source.

## Wiring notes

### TDA2822D pinout (DIP-8, looking down at the chip with the notch at the top)

```
        +--U--+
OUT1  1 |     | 8  OUT2
IN1-  2 |     | 7  IN2-
IN1+  3 |     | 6  IN2+
GND   4 |     | 5  VCC (9V)
        +-----+
```

Pin reference for the build:
- Pin 1 OUT1, Pin 8 OUT2 - speaker outputs (left and right).
- Pin 3 IN1+, Pin 6 IN2+ - non-inverting (signal) inputs.
- Pin 2 IN1-, Pin 7 IN2- - inverting inputs. We use these to set AC gain.
- Pin 4 GND, Pin 5 VCC - power.

**Important correction vs older "bootstrap cap" tutorials:** the TDA2822 family does NOT have bootstrap pins. Pins 2 and 7 are the inverting inputs. The 100uF caps you'll see in this design go from each IN- pin to GND - they're AC bypass caps that short the IN- pin to ground for audio frequencies, giving the chip its maximum closed-loop gain (~39 dB) while leaving the internal DC bias path intact. Different role, different physics from the bootstrap caps used on a TDA2003 or TDA2030.

### Power

- 9V battery (+) -> Vcc rail. Battery (-) -> GND rail.
- 100uF 16V bulk cap across the rails, leads as short as possible, sitting between pin 5 and pin 4. Long leg (+) goes to the Vcc rail.

### Per channel (mirror image for left and right)

For the LEFT channel (the RIGHT channel uses pin 6, pin 7, pin 8 in the same shape):

1. Audio source -> 10uF input cap (+ side toward the chip) -> chip pin 3 (IN1+).
2. Chip pin 2 (IN1-) -> 100uF 16V cap (+ side toward the chip pin) -> GND rail. This is the AC-bypass cap that sets gain.
3. Chip pin 1 (OUT1) -> 4.7R resistor -> 470uF 16V output cap (+ side toward the chip) -> LEFT earbud (+).
4. LEFT earbud (-) -> GND rail.

For the RIGHT channel: pin 6 IN2+, pin 7 IN2-, pin 8 OUT2. Otherwise identical.

### Input wiring from a 3.5mm jack

- TIP -> LEFT 10uF input cap -> pin 3.
- RING -> RIGHT 10uF input cap -> pin 6.
- SLEEVE -> GND rail.

### Electrolytic polarity rules of thumb

- Bulk cap (100uF on Vcc): + to Vcc, - to GND.
- Input caps (10uF): + toward the chip pin (the chip side sits at a slight positive bias due to the internal DC path; the source side is near 0V).
- IN- AC-bypass caps (100uF): + toward the chip pin (the chip side sits at the internal bias voltage, the GND side is 0V).
- Output caps (470uF): + toward the chip (chip side at ~4.5V, earbud side at 0V).

Get any of these backwards and the cap will leak, heat up, or eventually pop. Voltage rating: every electrolytic in this build is rated for 16V or higher, which is comfortable headroom on a 9V supply.


## Flash it and run it

This project is a real analog amplifier - the **TDA2822D chip plus a handful of caps and resistors** do all the work the moment power touches them. But there is an **optional** test-tone helper sketch you can run on an Arduino Uno that plays a 440 Hz tone in the left earbud and an 880 Hz tone in the right, swapping every 2 seconds, so you can confirm left and right are not crossed before you plug in a phone. The "Power-up procedure" further down shows how to run the amp on its own without any code at all.

**Option A - Skip the Uno and just play music.** Jump to the **Power-up procedure** below. Wire a 3.5mm jack to the input caps (tip = LEFT, ring = RIGHT, sleeve = battery GND), snap on the 9V battery, plug in your earbuds, hit play on your phone. Done.

**Option B - Run the test-tone helper first.** This needs the Arduino IDE and takes about 5 minutes.

**Software you need:**

- **Arduino IDE 2.x** - free download from [arduino.cc/en/software](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software). Install it, open it once, let it finish setting itself up.

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. **USB driver.** Your Uno is a CH340 clone (the dark rectangular chip next to the USB jack). Plug it in: if a COM port shows up in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, you are already set. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers), then unplug and replug.
2. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno.**
3. No extra libraries needed - `tone()`, `pinMode`, `Serial`, and `delay` are all built in.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno in with the chunky **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the printer-style one). The green ON LED on the Uno lights up.
2. **Tools -> Port -> COM*** (Windows) or **/dev/cu.usbmodem*** (macOS) or **/dev/ttyACM0** (Linux). If you only see one port, that is it.
3. Paste the sketch from the **Code** section into a new IDE window. Nothing to edit - no WiFi passwords, no pin numbers to change.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon up top). The TX and RX LEDs on the Uno will blink for a couple of seconds, then the IDE says **Done uploading**.
5. **Tools -> Serial Monitor** at **115200 baud** (bottom-right dropdown).

**What "it worked" looks like:**

- Serial Monitor prints `TDA2822D test: 440 Hz LEFT, 880 Hz RIGHT.` followed by a `Swapped: ...` line every 2 seconds.
- With the test wiring connected (D9 -> 10K -> LEFT input cap, D10 -> 10K -> RIGHT input cap, Uno GND -> battery GND) **and the 9V battery snapped on the amp**, you hear a **low buzz in the left earbud and a high buzz in the right** for 2 seconds, then they swap, then they swap back. If the tones are reversed, your earbud wiring (tip vs ring) is swapped.
- Once you have confirmed the channels, **unplug the Uno entirely**, pull the test wires off, and continue with the regular audio source.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Earbuds going into the OUTPUT, not the INPUT.** The 470uF caps go on the *output* side (pins 1 and 8 of the TDA2822D) and feed the earbuds. The 10uF caps go on the *input* side (pins 3 and 6) and feed the audio source. Swapping these will make the amp silent and may pop the earbud.
- **9V battery on the wrong terminal.** The snap clip is keyed but it is easy to twist the wires on later. Red lead = battery + = chip pin 5. Black = battery - = chip pin 4 and breadboard GND rail.
- **Electrolytic cap polarity.** Every electrolytic on this board (10uF, 100uF, 470uF) has a stripe pointing to its negative leg. Get any of them backwards and at best the amp is silent, at worst the cap pops. Long leg = +, short leg / stripe = -.
- **Serial Monitor at 9600.** The sketch uses 115200. If the Serial Monitor shows garbage, fix the baud dropdown.

## Talking points

- **This is your first stereo amp.** Up to now you've only built mono amps (LM386). Stereo is just "do it twice in one package."
- **What you actually save with a dual chip.** The TDA2822D is two complete amplifiers sharing one Vcc/GND pair. The savings aren't the transistors inside (those still doubled) - it's that the package, the supply pins, and the ground pin are shared. You go from two chips plus two sets of supply wiring to one chip plus one set.
- **DC blocking caps everywhere.** Audio is AC riding on top of a DC level. The chip biases its outputs to mid-supply (~4.5V) so the signal has room to swing both up and down. But your earbud coil doesn't want 4.5V DC pushing constant current through it - that wastes battery and heats the coil. The 470uF cap on each output blocks the DC and only lets the AC swing through. Same idea on the input: your phone's audio output sits near 0V already, but you cap-block in case the source has any DC offset.
- **Why 470uF on the output specifically?** At low frequencies the output cap and the earbud impedance form a high-pass filter. With a 32 ohm earbud and 470uF, the cutoff is around f = 1 / (2 * pi * R * C) ~ 10 Hz, well below anything you can hear. If you used 10uF here, the cutoff would be ~500 Hz and the project would sound tinny because all the bass would be filtered out.
- **What the IN- bypass caps actually do.** This is the part that beginner tutorials get wrong (and that an earlier draft of this project got wrong too). The TDA2822 has internal resistors that set a closed-loop gain when IN- is left to its internal bias point. When you AC-couple IN- to GND through a big cap, you're saying "for audio frequencies, hold IN- at ground." That makes the chip run at its maximum gain (~39 dB, around 90x). Remove the cap and gain drops a lot. So these caps are gain-set caps, NOT bootstrap caps - bootstrap is a different trick used on different chips (like the TDA2003).
- **The 4.7R series resistor on each output is mostly defensive.** If you short an earbud lead by accident, this tiny resistor limits the current spike enough to give the chip's internal protection time to react.

## Things to change once it works

- **Add a volume pot:** replace the wire between the audio source and each 10uF input cap with a 10K log-taper pot wired as a voltage divider. Ganged stereo pots give you a single volume knob.
- **Add a real Zobel network on each output** (~10R in series with 100nF to GND, right at the OUT pin) to suppress any HF oscillation if you upgrade to longer speaker leads.
- **Try 4 ohm or 8 ohm small speakers** (still low power - this chip is rated to about 650 mW per channel at 4 ohm, 9V). With 32 ohm earbuds it's much quieter, which is what you want for hearing safety.
- **Swap the 9V battery for a USB-C 5V supply:** the chip works down to 3V. You'll get less volume but it'll run for hours off a power bank. The 9V PP3 also sags fast under load - dropping to 5V regulated will actually be more consistent.
- **Bridge mode:** if you only need mono but want more volume into a single 8 ohm speaker, the TDA2822 can be wired in BTL (bridge) mode. That's a different schematic - worth building as a follow-up project.

## Why this is interesting

You now have three audio amps in the kit (LM386 mono low-power, TDA2822D stereo low-power, TDA2030A mono high-power) and they all solve "make audio louder" but with different trade-offs. Building this one teaches you that "stereo" is not a special technology - it's just two independent mono amps that happen to live in the same package and share a power rail. That mental model carries over to almost everything multi-channel in electronics: stereo ADCs are two ADCs in one package, dual op-amps are two op-amps sharing pins 4 and 8, quad comparators are four of the same thing on one die.

It also teaches a very practical lesson about copying tutorials from the internet: a common mistake (one this project's first draft made) is to confuse the TDA2822's IN- pins with the bootstrap pins on a TDA2003. Same DIP-8 outline, different chip family, different pin functions. Always check the datasheet pinout for the exact part number.

projects.name: NE5532 Hi-Fi Headphone Preamp
projects.power_supply: 9V battery (or 9V DC wall-wart, centre-positive) feeding the breadboard rails directly. The op-amp draws under 10 mA, so a single 9V will last many hours of listening. If the rail sags below ~6.5V the NE5532 starts to clip - swap the battery.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone or laptop into one end and your headphones into the other. Music goes in, music comes out, but cleaner and louder, with no static or hiss in the quiet parts.

**Why it's fun**: You built the same kind of audio booster that lives inside real recording studio gear, from a handful of parts on a breadboard. Hand the headphones to your dad, play his favourite song, and watch his face when he realises YOU made the thing the sound is coming through.

## Parts list

- 1x NE5532 Op-Amp (audio dual) - the "U1" in the schematic; both halves used (one per stereo channel)
- 4x Capacitor 1uF 50V (electrolytic) - AC coupling caps (2 input, 2 output)
- 4x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - 2 input bias resistors to virtual ground, 2 feedback path resistors
- 2x Resistor 100R (1/8W 1%) - output build-out resistors to protect against headphone-cable capacitance
- 2x Resistor 22K (1/8W 1%) - virtual-ground bias divider
- 1x Capacitor 100uF 25V (electrolytic) - power-rail bulk decoupling
- 1x Capacitor 100uF 16V (electrolytic) - virtual-ground filter cap (kills supply hum on the mid-rail)
- 1x LED 5mm Red + 1x Resistor 470R (1/8W 1%) - power-on indicator (470R picks the dim end of the inventory's 220R-470R LED range)
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm - build surface
- Jumper wires M-M

You also supply: a 9V battery (or 9V wall-wart with the centre pin positive), a 3.5mm stereo audio input (e.g. a cut-up old aux cable), a 3.5mm stereo headphone jack for the output, and a pair of headphones (32-ohm or higher impedance is happiest - see talking points for why).

## Wiring notes

This is a pure-analog project - no microcontroller, no code on a chip. You will validate it with a multimeter (see the "code" field) before you plug in headphones.

Power: connect the 9V battery + to the top rail and battery - to the bottom rail. The bottom rail IS ground for the whole circuit. Drop the 100uF 25V bulk cap straight across these rails as close to where the battery wires arrive as possible - it stops the rail sagging when the op-amp briefly draws current.

Virtual ground: the NE5532 runs from a single supply, so we fake a second rail by splitting +9V in half with the two 22K resistors. The junction of those resistors is "virtual ground" - it sits at about 4.5V and behaves like a quiet 0V reference for the op-amp. The 100uF 16V cap sits between that node and real ground - it shunts any leftover ripple to ground so the virtual rail is glass-smooth. Mark that breadboard row as **TP2** with a Sharpie or a flag - you'll come back to it during testing.

NE5532 pinout (top view, pin 1 dot at top-left):
- Pin 1 = Output A (Left channel out)
- Pin 2 = Inverting input A
- Pin 3 = Non-inverting input A (Left channel in)
- Pin 4 = V- (ground)
- Pin 5 = Non-inverting input B (Right channel in)
- Pin 6 = Inverting input B
- Pin 7 = Output B (Right channel out)
- Pin 8 = V+ (+9V)

Each channel is a unity-gain non-inverting buffer:
1. Input audio -> 1uF coupling cap -> NE5532 pin 3 (or pin 5 for right) AND a 10K resistor to virtual ground (this gives the input something to bias against without loading the source).
2. Output pin 1 (or pin 7) wired straight to inverting input pin 2 (or pin 6) - this is the unity-gain feedback path. The 10K from inverting input to virtual ground sets the DC reference.
3. Output pin 1 (or pin 7) -> 1uF coupling cap -> 100R build-out resistor -> headphone jack tip (left) or ring (right).
4. Headphone jack sleeve goes to real ground.

The two 1uF coupling caps are polarised: the + leg of the INPUT cap faces the op-amp input, the + leg of the OUTPUT cap faces the op-amp output. Both op-amp pins sit at ~4.5V, source and headphones sit at 0V DC, so + faces the higher-voltage side.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and it starts working the second power touches it. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no USB cable. Just a 9V battery and a multimeter.

**Power-up procedure (do this BEFORE plugging in headphones or an audio source):**

1. Double-check your work one more time. Walk your finger along each wire from the battery + all the way to NE5532 pin 8, then from pin 4 back to battery -. Then check that both 22K resistors are sitting between +9V and ground, with their middle junction going to the 100uF 16V cap (that is your virtual ground row, TP2).
2. Look at the four 1uF coupling caps and the two 100uF caps. Electrolytics have a stripe down one side - that side is the **minus** leg. The 100uF 25V bulk cap stripe goes to the ground rail. The 100uF 16V virtual-ground cap stripe also goes to ground. The two **input** 1uF caps have their stripe (minus) on the side facing the NE5532 (pin 3 and pin 5). The two **output** 1uF caps have their stripe on the side facing the headphone jack.
3. Clip the 9V battery on. The red LED should light up (dim is correct - we picked 470R on purpose so it does not blind you in a dark room or steal current from the audio).
4. **Headphones still unplugged.** Put your nose close to the breadboard for ten seconds. No smell of hot plastic? No part getting warm to the touch? Good. If anything smells or warms up, pop the battery off right away and re-check polarity on the chip and the caps.
5. Grab the multimeter and walk through the steps in the "code" field (TP1 power rail, TP2 virtual ground, TP3 and TP4 output DC offset). Do not skip step 3 - that is the one that protects your headphones from a thump.
6. Once all four test points read what they should, **then** plug headphones into the output jack and a phone or laptop into the input jack. Start with the volume on your phone turned all the way DOWN, press play, and creep the volume up. Music should come through clean, with no buzz, hiss, or crackle in the quiet bits between songs.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Electrolytic caps in backwards.** The stripe is the minus side. If the 100uF 16V virtual-ground cap is flipped, TP2 will drift instead of sitting steady at ~4.5V, and you will hear a "whoomp" that fades over a few seconds when you connect the battery. Pop the battery off, turn the cap around, try again.
- **NE5532 rotated 180 degrees.** The little dot or notch on the chip marks pin 1 - it must point the same way as on the wiring diagram. A backwards chip puts +9V on pin 4 (which expects ground) and the chip will get hot fast. If your finger says "ouch" near the chip, that is the reason.
- **No sound, but all four test points read fine.** Nine times out of ten this is the audio cable, not the circuit. Cheap 3.5mm aux cables sometimes have a broken solder joint inside the moulded plug. Try a different cable, or wiggle the plug while music is playing - if the sound cuts in and out, the cable is the culprit, not your build.
## Talking points

- **Why an op-amp here?** A modern phone's headphone output can already drive headphones, so what is this thing for? It is a *buffer* - it gives the source a low-current, low-impedance load to look at, and presents the headphones with an even lower-impedance source. Long cables and weird passive volume pots can mess with sound; a buffer immunises against that.
- **Why this specific chip?** The NE5532 has been in pro studio mixing desks since the 1970s. Two op-amps in one 8-pin package, very low noise (~5 nV/sqrt(Hz)), high output current (can drive 600-ohm loads cleanly), and it slews fast enough to handle audio without slewing-induced distortion. It is the "default" audio op-amp.
- **Why single supply with a fake ground?** Op-amps normally want a positive AND negative supply so their output can swing both above and below zero. A 9V battery only gives positive. The fix is to *redefine* "ground" - put it halfway up the battery using two equal resistors. Now the op-amp sees +4.5V and -4.5V, but the battery still sees a normal single supply. The trade-off: anything fed into or taken out of the circuit must be AC-coupled with a capacitor so the 4.5V offset doesn't get exported.
- **Mind the supply floor.** The NE5532 needs at least about 6V across pins 8 and 4 to behave linearly (the datasheet minimum is +/-3V dual, i.e. 6V single). A tired 9V alkaline can sag below that under load and the symptoms look like circuit faults - distortion, weird DC offsets, low output. If TP1 in the test procedure reads under 6.5V, swap the battery before troubleshooting anything else.
- **Why AC coupling?** Audio is AC - a wiggle around zero. The op-amp output wiggles around 4.5V. Headphones are voice coils - feeding 4.5V DC into them would push the cone hard to one side, make them run hot, and eventually fry them. The 1uF cap blocks DC but lets the audio wiggles through.
- **Why the 100R build-out resistor (and why headphone impedance matters).** Long headphone cables have capacitance to ground. Op-amp + cap = potential oscillator at high frequency, which manifests as a screech or audible distortion. A small series resistor breaks that feedback loop, and it limits short-circuit current if the headphone plug ever bridges tip to sleeve. The catch: that 100R is in series with the headphone's impedance, so it forms a voltage divider with it. With 32-ohm earbuds, the output you hear is 32 / (32 + 100) = about 24% of the op-amp swing, which not only sounds quieter but - because moving-coil headphones have impedance that rises with frequency in the bass - audibly thins out the low end. With 250-ohm studio cans, the divider becomes 250 / 350 = 71%, much closer to flat. That's why higher-impedance headphones are happiest here.

## Things to change once it works

- **Add a volume pot.** A 10K log/audio-taper stereo pot at the INPUT (before the 1uF cap) gives you a volume knob. Use log taper, not linear - human hearing is logarithmic.
- **Add gain.** Right now this is unity gain (input volts = output volts). If your source is too quiet, replace the feedback wire (pin 1 to pin 2, or pin 7 to pin 6) with a 10K resistor, and add a 10K from pin 2 (or pin 6) to virtual ground via a 47uF cap. Now gain = 1 + 10K/10K = 2x. The cap is important - it makes DC gain = 1 so any offset is not amplified.
- **Try a JRC4558 in the same socket** (an inventory item, pin-compatible). It is the op-amp inside the Tube Screamer guitar pedal - warmer, slightly noisier. A great ear-training A/B test.
- **Upgrade the coupling caps to film** (not in this inventory, but worth knowing). Polypropylene or polyester film caps measure better than electrolytics at audio frequencies. Most "audiophile" preamp builds replace exactly these four caps.
- **Power it from a dual-rail bench supply** instead of inventing a virtual ground. Connect pin 4 to -9V and pin 8 to +9V, then real ground IS ground - no bias resistors, no virtual-ground cap, no input/output coupling caps needed. The circuit gets simpler and quieter.

## Why this is interesting

This is one of those projects where you build the same thing the pros use, on a breadboard, for the price of a sandwich. Every studio mixing console has dozens of NE5532s humming away in the signal path. Building one yourself demystifies what a preamp actually does (mostly: nothing, just very cleanly) and gives you a permanent ear-comparison reference: now when an audio review says "warm" or "clean" or "noisy" you have a baseline. The non-inverting buffer pattern reappears in every analog project from here on - sensor front-ends, microphone preamps, ADC drivers - so the wiring will start to look familiar fast.

AC coupling caps - 2 at each input (block DC from source), 2 at each output (block any op-amp DC offset from headphones)
Power-on indicator (optional but useful to see when the 9V battery is connected)
The star. Both halves used: U1A buffers Left, U1B buffers Right
Build surface - one breadboard fits both channels with the NE5532 straddling the centre gutter
Output build-out resistors - protect the op-amp from capacitive headphone-cable loads and limit short-circuit current
Input bias resistors to virtual ground (2x) and feedback path to set unity gain (2x)
Virtual-ground bias divider - splits the 9V single supply into a stable mid-rail reference for both channels

Current-limiting resistor for the power LED - inside the 220R-470R inventory convention. Picks the dim end of the range (~17 mA at 9V) to save battery and avoid distracting brightness in a listening setup

projects.power_supply: USB-C charger or laptop port (5V) feeds the 2-pin pigtail. The LM317T regulates it down to ~3.3V via a 220R/390R divider on the ADJ pin, with electrolytic bypass caps on Vin, Vout and ADJ.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug in a USB-C cable from any phone charger. A green LED glows on the breadboard and the red (+) rail becomes a clean 3.3V power source you can run your ESP32 boards from.

**Why it's fun**: This is your own pocket-sized power station. Once you build it, every future project on the breadboard just plugs in next to it and works, no batteries, no soldering, no buying a special supply.

## Parts list

- 1x LM317T Adjustable Regulator - the workhorse, set to ~3.3V via two resistors on the ADJ pin
- 1x USB-C Female Chassis Connector (2P pigtail) - 5V input from any USB-C source
- 1x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - R1 in the LM317 divider (Vout to ADJ)
- 1x Resistor 390R (1/8W 1%) - R2 in the LM317 divider (ADJ to GND)
- 1x Capacitor 22uF 50V (electrolytic) - input bulk cap, sits across Vin and GND right at the LM317 legs
- 1x Capacitor 10uF (electrolytic, mixed voltage) - output cap, sits across Vout and GND right at the LM317 legs
- 1x Capacitor 4.7uF 50V (electrolytic) - ADJ-to-GND bypass cap, boosts ripple rejection
- 1x LED 5mm Green - power-good indicator on the 3.3V rail
- 1x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - current-limit resistor for the green LED
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - everything lives here, no soldering
- 1x Pin Header 1x40 Male Breakaway (2.54mm) - break off a 2-pin piece to anchor the USB-C pigtail
- 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - short jumpers to route output to the breadboard's (+) rail

## Wiring notes

The LM317 in TO-220 has three legs viewed from the front (text side facing you, legs pointing down): **pin 1 = ADJ (left), pin 2 = Vout (middle), pin 3 = Vin (right).** This is the OPPOSITE of the L7805 pinout - the regulator family is not pin-compatible. Get this wrong and the input voltage hits the ADJ pin directly and the part dies.

Layout on the breadboard:

1. Plant the LM317 across three adjacent rows in the middle of the board.
2. **Input cap (22uF):** plug it across pin 3 (Vin) and a (-) rail row. **Stripe (the marked leg) is the negative leg - it goes to GND.** Reverse-polarity electrolytics heat up, sometimes loudly. The datasheet's minimum input cap is 0.1uF, but a bigger electro holds the rail up during ESP32 radio bursts.
3. **Output cap (10uF):** across pin 2 (Vout) and a (-) rail row. Stripe to GND. The LM317 datasheet specifically calls for 1uF tantalum *or* 10uF electrolytic on the output for loop stability. The bigger value is the right pick when using electrolytics because their ESR makes the smaller cap less effective.
4. **Resistor divider (the bit that sets Vout):** R1 (220R) goes from pin 2 (Vout) to pin 1 (ADJ). R2 (390R) goes from pin 1 (ADJ) to the (-) rail. The LM317 always works to keep 1.25V across R1, which forces a known current through R2, which sets Vout. Math: Vout = 1.25 * (1 + R2/R1) = 1.25 * (1 + 390/220) = 3.47V theoretical. Real-world resistor tolerance plus the LM317's own Vref tolerance puts the actual reading somewhere in the 3.30 to 3.45V band - all comfortably inside the ESP32-C3's 3.0 to 3.6V supply spec.
5. **ADJ bypass cap (4.7uF):** across pin 1 (ADJ) and (-) rail, stripe to GND. This one isn't strictly required but it lifts the LM317's power-supply ripple rejection by about 15dB - the divider would otherwise pass input ripple straight into the ADJ pin and back out to Vout.
6. **USB-C pigtail:** red goes straight to pin 3 (Vin). Black goes to the (-) rail. Anchor the flimsy pigtail wires by jamming the bare ends into a 2-pin male header pressed into the breadboard.
7. **Power LED:** pin 2 (Vout) -> 220R -> LED anode (long leg) -> LED cathode (short leg, flat side of the dome) -> (-) rail. ((3.3V - 2.0V Vf for green) / 220R = ~5.9mA, comfortably visible.)
8. **Rail jumpers:** short M-M jumper from pin 2 row to the (+) rail; another from the LM317 had-no-pin-2-no-this-is-Vout row... actually, just from pin 2 to (+) rail and from any GND row to the (-) rail. The (+) rail now sits at ~3.3V.

There is intentionally no series fuse-resistor on the input. A 10R in series with VBUS would drop 0.5V at typical ESP32 idle currents and a destructive 2V at 200mA bursts - that defeats the entire point of building a clean rail. Polyfuses are the right answer for inrush/short protection and they aren't in this kit, so this build trusts the USB-C source's own current-limiting (every modern charger has it).


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and it starts working the second power touches it. The "code" for this project is actually a multimeter checklist, not a sketch.

**What you need on the bench:**

- A multimeter (DMM) set to "DC V", 20V range (or auto-range).
- A USB-C cable plugged into any phone charger, laptop port, or USB power bank.
- The breadboard fully wired up per the Wiring notes section above.

**Before you plug in (do this every time, with your dad watching):**

1. Look at every electrolytic cap. The stripe down the side of the cap is the NEGATIVE leg. Every stripe should be pointing at a (-) rail row. If even one is backwards, fix it now - powering up a backwards electrolytic makes it hiss, swell, and sometimes pop.
2. Look at the LM317 from the front (writing facing you, legs pointing down). Left leg = ADJ, middle = Vout, right = Vin. If this looks flipped, the part is the wrong way round - turn it around before plugging in.
3. Put the multimeter on the continuity setting (the one that beeps). Touch one probe to the USB-C VBUS wire, the other to the USB-C GND wire. It should NOT beep. If it beeps, there is a short somewhere on the board - find it before applying power.

**Power-up:**

1. Plug the USB-C cable into the pigtail.
2. The green LED on the breadboard should light up right away. That is your "power good" sign.
3. Put the black DMM probe on the (-) rail. Leave it there for every reading.
4. Touch the red probe to the (+) rail (the 3.3V output). You should read between **3.30V and 3.45V**, and the number should be rock steady - not wandering up and down.
5. If you want to be thorough, walk through TP1 to TP7 in the bash script in the Code section. Each test point tells you a different part of the regulator is doing its job.

**How you know it worked:** the green LED is on, the (+) rail measures inside the 3.30-3.45V band, and the number does not move when you wiggle the USB-C cable. That is a working 3.3V brick. Any ESP32 project you build next on the same breadboard can now grab power from this rail.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Cap polarity backwards.** The stripe on an electrolytic is the negative leg and goes to GND. Plug it in the other way and the cap heats up and can pop. If a cap is warm to the touch after a few seconds, unplug immediately and check the stripe.
- **LM317 pinout flipped.** The LM317 is NOT pin-compatible with the L7805. Left leg is ADJ, right leg is Vin. If you wire it like a 7805, Vin from USB-C lands on the ADJ pin and the regulator dies in a puff. Double-check this with the datasheet picture before powering on.
- **Reading 1.25V instead of 3.3V.** That means the 390R resistor (R2, from ADJ to GND) is missing, in the wrong holes, or has a broken lead. With no R2, the LM317 just outputs its own internal reference of 1.25V. Pull the resistor, check the colour bands (orange-white-brown-brown for 390R), and re-seat it.
- **No green LED but voltage is fine.** The LED is in backwards. It will not be damaged - just flip it around. Long leg (anode) goes toward the (+) rail through the 220R resistor; short leg (cathode) goes to GND.
## Talking points

- **Why dropout actually matters here:** Linear regulators need a minimum voltage between Vin and Vout to function (called the dropout voltage). The LM317's is about 1.5 to 2V. With ~5V in and 3.3V out, we have ~1.7V of headroom - just barely enough. This is why the original L7805 plan failed: 5V in / 5V out is below an L7805's dropout, so the output simply sags. Picking the LM317 at 3.3V is the simplest way to make a clean rail from a USB source.
- **Why three caps of different sizes?** The 22uF on the input is a "water tower" - it stores charge so when the load suddenly demands more current, the LM317's input pin doesn't sag below dropout. The 10uF on the output is a "shock absorber" that keeps the regulator's feedback loop stable - without it, some loads will cause the regulator to oscillate. The 4.7uF on the ADJ pin stops input ripple from being injected back into the output by the resistor divider.
- **Why polarity matters:** Electrolytic capacitors are made by growing a thin oxide insulator using a DC current in one specific direction. Reverse the polarity and the oxide dissolves, the cap conducts, heats up, and eventually vents (sometimes with a satisfying pop). Stripe on the can = negative leg, always to GND in this circuit.
- **Why linear, not switching?** A buck switcher is more efficient (less heat) but kicks high-frequency noise onto its output rail. Linear regulators are pin-quiet by comparison, which is exactly what an analog sensor or a sensitive radio (the ESP32-C3 *is* a radio) wants. The trade is heat: power lost = (Vin - Vout) * Iload. At 5V in, 3.3V out, 100mA load, that's 170mW. The TO-220 tab can dissipate that without a heatsink.

## Things to change once it works

- **Add 0.1uF ceramic caps** in parallel with each electrolytic. The kit doesn't include them but they're cheap and they handle high frequencies that the electrolytics miss due to their internal series resistance. Doing this is what would let the project actually claim "low noise".
- **Take the LM317 to other voltages.** Same circuit, different R2. Vout = 1.25 * (1 + R2/220). R2 = 680R gives 5.1V. R2 = 1K gives 6.9V. R2 = 1.5K gives 9.8V. The LM317 spans 1.25V to 37V from this one circuit.
- **Heatsink the LM317** if you ever feed it from a 9V or 12V supply and pull more than ~100mA. The TO-220 tab can bolt to a small finned heatsink with an M3 screw.
- **Lay it out on a Double-Sided Prototype PCB** once the layout works on breadboard. Soldered joints have lower resistance than breadboard tie-points, which matters at higher currents.
- **About the original "weak USB cable" problem:** this brick does not fix that. If the cable drops voltage upstream, less voltage reaches the brick, and the brick passes the sag along (it can only regulate down, not up). The right answer for cable-drop brownouts is a better cable plugged into a wall charger, not a regulator downstream. What this brick *does* fix is "the USB rail is dirty enough to upset analog sensors" - it gives you a known-clean 3.3V from any 5V source.

## Why this is interesting

This is the bypass-cap-and-resistor-divider muscle memory project. Every regulator the rest of the kit can build (LM317 at any voltage, all the L78xx fixed regulators) shares the same shape: input cap, output cap, set the voltage, indicator LED. Once Andy has built this once and probed all seven test points with a DMM, every future power supply in the kit is a variation on the same theme. It also teaches the single most important lesson in linear regulator design: **dropout is not optional** - you cannot get 5V out of an L7805 fed from 5V in. Picking the LM317 at 3.3V isn't a workaround; it's the *correct* part choice for this input/output combination.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# LM317 3.3V Brick - Multimeter verification procedure
# ----------------------------------------------------
# This is a pure-analog power supply project, so the right test instrument
# is a multimeter (DMM) in DC volts mode, NOT a microcontroller. Reading a
# 3.3V rail with an Arduino Uno's ADC (5V reference) wastes half the ADC
# range and adds error - and worse, hides the regulator's behaviour behind
# a noisy ADC. So: probe the test points below with a DMM and tick them off.
#
# Set the DMM to "DC V", 20 V range (or auto-range).
# Black probe to the breadboard (-) rail (GND) for every reading except where
# noted otherwise.
#
# ---- Bench-up sequence (do this BEFORE plugging in USB-C) ----
#   1. Inspect cap polarities. The stripe on every electrolytic is the negative
#      leg. Stripe goes to GND. Get this wrong and the cap will vent.
#   2. Inspect LM317 leg order (TO-220, text side facing you, legs down):
#        pin 1 = ADJ (left)
#        pin 2 = Vout (middle)
#        pin 3 = Vin  (right)
#      NOTE: this is OPPOSITE to the L7805 pinout. Swap them by accident and
#      Vin meets ADJ and the part will let the smoke out.
#   3. DMM on continuity (beeper). Probe USB-C VBUS to USB-C GND on the
#      pigtail side. Should NOT beep. If it beeps you have a short - find it
#      before applying power.
#
# ---- Test points with USB-C plugged in ----
#   TP1: USB-C VBUS to GND   -> expect 4.75 to 5.25 V (depends on charger)
#   TP2: LM317 pin 3 (Vin) to GND
#                            -> within ~0.05 V of TP1 (no series resistor now)
#   TP3: LM317 pin 2 (Vout) to GND
#                            -> 3.30 to 3.45 V, rock steady
#                               (theoretical: 1.25 * (1 + 390/220) = 3.47 V;
#                                resistor tolerance + LM317 Vref tolerance
#                                spread it across that band)
#   TP4: LM317 pin 1 (ADJ) to GND
#                            -> TP3 minus 1.25 V (the LM317's internal Vref)
#                               i.e. about 2.05 to 2.20 V
#   TP5: Across the 22uF input cap
#                            -> same reading as TP2
#   TP6: Across the 10uF output cap
#                            -> same reading as TP3
#   TP7: Green LED anode to GND
#                            -> same as TP3 (no drop yet)
#         Green LED cathode to GND
#                            -> ~2.0 V (the LED's forward voltage above GND)
#
# ---- Pass criteria ----
#   TP3 reads 3.30 - 3.45 V with no load            -> PASS
#   TP3 sags below 3.20 V with no load              -> FAIL, see troubleshooting
#   TP3 reads ~Vin (~5 V)                            -> ADJ pin is floating or
#                                                       R2 is open. DISCONNECT.
#   LM317 too hot to touch within 30s, no load      -> oscillation or backwards
#                                                       cap. DISCONNECT.
#
# ---- Loaded test (after no-load passes) ----
#   Connect a 100R 1/4W+ resistor between the (+) rail and (-) rail. That draws
#   ~33 mA, similar to an ESP32 idle current.
#   TP3 should drop by no more than ~30 mV. If it sags significantly, the input
#   cap is too small or the USB cable is dropping voltage upstream.
#
# ---- Why no Arduino sketch ----
#   Power supplies are characterised by amplitude (DMM), ripple (scope), and
#   transient response (scope + electronic load). An MCU ADC can't do any of
#   those three well. A 3.50 GBP DMM does the first one perfectly.

echo "LM317 3.3V Brick verification - follow the steps in this script as a checklist."
echo "No actual commands to run; this is a bench procedure."

projects.name: LM317T Constant-Current LED Driver
projects.power_supply: 6.5 V to 12 V DC from a 9 V battery or bench supply, fed to the +V rail of the breadboard (a 9 V battery is the easy choice; the LM317 needs ~3 V of dropout above the LED + Rset stack, so anything under ~6.5 V will fall out of regulation).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hook up a 9V battery and the LED glows at the perfect brightness. Now swap in a fresh battery, or a weaker one, or wiggle the wires around - the LED stays the exact same brightness. It refuses to get any brighter or dimmer.

**Why it's fun**: This is your first taste of a real engineering trick: a circuit that fights back to keep itself steady, no code required. Try to make the LED flicker by tapping the battery on and off - you can't, and that's the magic.

## Parts list

- 1x LM317T Adjustable Regulator (TO-220, the star of the show)
- 1x Resistor 56R (1/8W 1%) - this is "Rset", the only resistor that matters
- 1x LED 5mm Red - the load we are driving (at a safe ~22 mA)
- 1x Capacitor 10uF (electrolytic, rated >=16V) - input bulk decoupling
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm
- A handful of M-M jumper wires
- A 6.5 V to 12 V supply (a 9 V battery is perfect, or a bench supply)

No microcontroller. No code. Just one IC, one resistor, and a multimeter to prove it works.

**LED derating note (important):** a generic 5mm through-hole LED is rated for ~20 to 30 mA continuous. We deliberately target ~22 mA with a 56R Rset to stay inside that envelope. If you ever see a tutorial that calls for 100 mA or more through a plain 5mm LED, ignore it - the LED will dim within hours and die within days. Higher currents belong on 1W "power LEDs" with a proper heatsink, not on indicator LEDs from a bag of 100.

## Wiring notes

The LM317T has three legs. Looking at the front (text side), they are, left to right: **ADJ (pin 1), Vout (pin 2), Vin (pin 3)**.

The trick is that the LM317 always tries to hold exactly **1.25 V between its Vout pin and its ADJ pin**. In the normal "voltage regulator" hookup you use two resistors to bleed that reference into a divider. In this hookup you put a single resistor between Vout and ADJ, and the LED hangs off the ADJ pin.

Result: the LM317 forces 1.25 V across that one resistor, which by Ohm's law forces a fixed current through it. And since the LED is in series with that resistor, the LED gets that same fixed current. The current is `I = 1.25 V / R`. With `R = 56R`, that is **~22 mA**, a safe, indicator-LED-friendly value.

Build order on the breadboard:

1. Drop the LM317T into the board so its three legs land on three separate rows.
2. Wire **Vin (pin 3)** to the +V rail.
3. Wire the 10uF cap (rated **>=16V**, since we are running up to 12V on the rail) from +V rail to GND rail, observing polarity (long leg / no stripe = +). If you have a 0.1uF ceramic handy, dropping it in parallel with the electrolytic right at the Vin pin is conventional LM317 hygiene - not required, but it cleans up high-frequency noise the electrolytic is too slow to handle.
4. Wire the **56R resistor between Vout (pin 2) and ADJ (pin 1)**.
5. From **ADJ (pin 1)**, jumper to the **LED anode** (the long leg).
6. **LED cathode** (short leg, flat side) goes to the GND rail.
7. Connect your power: +V rail to +6.5V to +12V, GND rail to supply ground.

There is no separate current-limiting resistor for the LED in this build - the whole circuit is the current limiter. That is the point.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and the LED lights up the second power touches the rails. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no code. Your "program" is the 56R resistor.

**Power-up procedure (do this with your dad watching):**

1. **Eyeball it before plugging in.** Check three things one more time: the LM317's flat metal tab is facing the way the diagram shows, the long leg of the 10uF cap is on the +V rail (short leg / stripe on GND), and the long leg of the LED is on the ADJ pin side.
2. **Set your multimeter to DC volts** (the V with a straight line, not the squiggly one) and clip it across the +V rail and GND rail with no power yet. It should read 0.
3. **Connect the 9V battery** (or turn on your bench supply, set to anywhere from 6.5V to 12V). Watch the meter jump up to the supply voltage, and watch the **red LED turn on at a nice steady glow**. That's it - the circuit is working.
4. **Try the magic test.** Without unplugging, gently squeeze the battery clip so the voltage sags a bit, or if you have a bench supply, slowly turn the knob from 12V down toward 7V. The LED brightness **should not change**. That refusal to dim is the LM317 doing its job.
5. **Now grab the multimeter to prove it with numbers.** Follow Step 2 in the bash script above: switch the meter to DC volts and touch the probes to **Vout (pin 2)** and **ADJ (pin 1)** of the LM317. You should read **1.20 V to 1.30 V**. That tiny voltage across the 56R resistor is what sets the ~22 mA going through the LED.
6. **(Bonus, optional) Measure the actual current.** Step 3 in the script walks through it: pull the wire from the LED's short leg to the GND rail, set the meter to **DC mA** (200 mA range), and put the meter inline where that wire used to be. Expect around 20 to 24 mA. That's the punchline of the whole project - the LM317 is holding that current rock-steady.

**Common gotchas:**

- **LM317 pinout backwards.** The legs are ADJ-Vout-Vin (1-2-3) reading left to right with the text facing you. Get this wrong and the LED simply will not light - no damage, just no glow. Pull power, rotate the chip, try again.
- **LED in backwards.** Long leg goes to the ADJ pin, short leg (flat side of the plastic) goes to GND. Backwards = no light, no damage. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in.
- **Electrolytic cap polarity backwards.** The long leg is + and goes to the +V rail; the side with the stripe is - and goes to GND. Backwards on a 10uF cap at 9V usually just gets warm, but on a bad day it can pop with a little puff of smoke. Double-check before you connect the battery.
- **Supply voltage too low.** A tired 9V battery that reads 6V under load will drop the LM317 out of regulation, and you'll see the LED go dim or flicker. Swap in a fresh battery or bump the bench supply up to 9V.
## Talking points

- The LM317 has a tiny internal reference, about 1.25 V, that it works very hard to hold across two of its pins (Vout and ADJ). Everything else in the LM317 - the pass transistor, the error amp, the protection - is in service of that one number.
- In the textbook hookup (two resistors making a divider on ADJ) you trick that 1.25 V into becoming a higher output voltage. Here we skip the divider entirely. With only a resistor across the reference, the LM317 has no choice but to push exactly `1.25 V / R` amps through it. That current then flows through whatever you stick in series with it - in our case, an LED.
- Why is this better than a plain resistor in series with an LED? Because LED forward voltage changes. It changes with temperature (around -2 mV/degC), it changes between parts in the same bag, and it changes as the LED ages. With a plain resistor driver, those Vf shifts become current shifts, and current is what determines LED brightness and lifespan. With a current source, the LM317 absorbs the Vf shifts in its own dropout headroom and the LED keeps the same current. That is the whole game.
- Headroom matters: the LM317 needs Vin to be at least about 3 V above its own Vout pin to stay in regulation. With a red LED (Vf ~2 V) and 1.25 V across Rset, the LM317's Vout pin sits at ~3.25 V above ground, so Vin needs to be at least ~6.25 V. A 9 V supply gives comfortable headroom. The difference between Vin and Vout is dissipated as heat in the LM317.
- This is the same trick used inside cheap LED bulbs and LED strip drivers, just scaled up. Real designs swap the LM317 for a switch-mode controller for efficiency, but the topology - "current sense resistor across a fixed reference voltage" - is identical.

## Things to change once it works

- **Change the current (safely).** Swap the 56R for a different value: 120R gives ~10 mA (a gentler glow), 27R gives ~46 mA (right at the edge of what a generic 5mm LED can tolerate - run it briefly only). The math is always `I = 1.25 / R`.
- **DO NOT use 10R (~125 mA) with a generic 5mm LED.** That current is 4-6x the LED's continuous rating - it will degrade in minutes and fail. If you genuinely want 125 mA from this circuit, you need either a 1W power LED on a small heatsink, or a series chain of several LEDs so each one's brightness can be moderated through better thermal mass (and you will need a higher Vin to cover the chain plus dropout). The LM317 itself is happy to source that current; it is the indicator LED that is not.
- **Drive a different LED color.** Blue and white LEDs need ~3.3 V Vf - you may need to bump Vin to 12 V to stay in headroom.
- **Watch it self-regulate.** Run a stiff supply at 9 V and confirm ~22 mA. Drop the supply to 7 V. The current should stay locked until you fall below dropout, at which point the LED goes dark suddenly rather than fading.
- **Mind the heat.** At 22 mA with 9 V in and ~3.25 V out, the LM317 burns about (9 - 3.25) x 0.022 = 0.13 W. The TO-220 will be only slightly warm. For sustained higher currents, bolt it to a small heatsink.
- **Series more LEDs.** As long as Vin is high enough to cover Vf_total + 3 V of dropout + 1.25 V across Rset, you can stack LEDs in series on the ADJ pin and every one gets the same current. This is exactly how multi-LED panels are wired.

## Why this is interesting

Most people meet the LM317 once, as the "adjustable 5 V supply" demo, and never look at it again. But it has a secret second job that is arguably more useful: **it is a near-ideal precision current source with a one-resistor BOM**. That is a remarkable feat for a 1970s-era three-terminal chip. The same circuit topology - "force a known reference across a sense resistor" - shows up everywhere, from real LED drivers to laser diode controllers to bench-supply current limit circuits. Build this once and the rest of analog regulator design starts to look familiar.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ============================================================
# LM317T Constant-Current LED Driver - bench test procedure
# ============================================================
# This is a pure-analog project. There is no MCU and no code.
# Instead, follow this multimeter procedure to prove the circuit
# is doing what the datasheet says: holding a fixed current
# regardless of LED forward voltage drift.
#
# Tools needed:
#   - Digital multimeter (DMM) set to DC volts, then to DC mA
#   - 9V battery OR bench supply set to 9V (anything 6.5V to 12V works)
#
# Test point map (matches the wiring diagram):
#   TP1 = LM317 Vin pin (pin 3, the input)
#   TP2 = LM317 Vout pin (pin 2, the output, top of Rset)
#   TP3 = LM317 ADJ pin (pin 1) = bottom of Rset = LED anode
#   TP4 = LED cathode = where the cathode wire meets the GND rail
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: Power-off sanity check
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# With power disconnected, measure resistance from TP2 to TP3.
# Expected: ~56 ohms (your Rset). If you read kilohms or open,
# the resistor is wrong or not seated. Fix before powering on.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 2: Verify the reference voltage (the LM317 magic number)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Power the circuit. LED should be glowing steadily.
# DMM in DC volts, measure between TP2 (Vout) and TP3 (ADJ).
# Expected: 1.20 V to 1.30 V (datasheet says 1.25V nominal).
# This is the LM317 holding its internal reference across Rset.
# If you see this, the regulator is in regulation. Done.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 3: Verify the current (Ohm's law in action)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Compute I = V(TP2,TP3) / 56 ohms.
# Example: 1.25 V / 56 R = 0.0223 A = ~22 mA.
# Now confirm by measurement: open the LED-cathode-to-GND
# connection (pull the wire that runs from the LED's short leg
# to the GND rail) and insert the meter inline there. Set DMM
# to DC mA (start on the 200 mA or higher range to be safe).
# Expected: within ~5 percent of the computed value above.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 4: Prove it is a CURRENT source, not a voltage source
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# This is the cool part. While running:
#   a) Change Vin. Drop it from 9V to 7V (or swap to a different
#      supply in the 6.5-12V range). Re-measure the LED current.
#      It should barely move. A voltage source would change the
#      current a lot - this does not, because the LM317 fights
#      to keep 1.25V across Rset.
#   b) Touch the LED gently with a finger to warm it. Its forward
#      voltage drifts down ~2 mV/degC. A plain resistor driver
#      would let the current creep up. Here the current stays put.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 5: Headroom check (why Vin must be > Vled + Vrset + ~3V)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# The LM317 needs about 3V of dropout between its own Vin and
# Vout pins to regulate. Measure Vin - Vout (TP1 - TP2). It
# must be at least ~3 V for the chip to stay in regulation.
#
# Now slowly drop Vin from 9V toward 5V and watch the LED.
# At some point (around 5.5-6V for a red LED) it will go DARK,
# not just dim - that is the regulator falling out of compliance,
# the chip can no longer hold 1.25V across Rset because there
# is not enough voltage left in the budget. That sudden cliff
# is the experiment working as intended.
#
# That is the whole circuit. One IC, one resistor, no math
# beyond I = 1.25 / R. Same trick lives inside cheap LED bulbs.
echo "Run the steps above with your multimeter. Nothing to execute."
learning_concepts: Ohm's law sets the current via Vref/Rset
Why LEDs prefer current drive over voltage drive

projects.name: ULN2803 Knight Rider Light Bar
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from laptop USB (5V). The 5V rail also feeds the ULN2803 COM pin (10) and the LED anodes through 220R resistors; the chip sinks each LED cathode to GND when its input pin goes HIGH.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Eight LEDs in a row light up one at a time, with a glowing dot that zooms left, then right, then left again, forever. It looks exactly like the front of KITT, the talking car from Knight Rider.

**Why it's fun**: You built the same effect that 80s TV used on a real car prop, and once it works you can crank the speed dial in the code to make the dot bounce slow and lazy or so fast it almost blurs into a solid line. Show it to your friends with the lights off and watch them lean in.

## Parts list

- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (the brain - sends the "which LED" pattern)
- 1x ULN2803APG Darlington Array - the star of the show: eight transistor pairs in one chip
- 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - everything lives here, no soldering
- 8x 5mm LEDs - 5 Red + 3 Yellow (we only have 5 red in stock, the yellows finish the bar)
- 8x 220R resistors - one per LED to keep them from burning out
- Jumper wires (M-M for the breadboard, F-M from Uno to breadboard)

## Wiring notes

The ULN2803 is the trick that makes this clean. It has 18 pins:

- Pins 1-8 on the left are INPUTS (IN1-IN8). Wire these to Arduino pins D2 through D9.
- Pins 11-18 on the right are OUTPUTS (OUT1-OUT8). Each one connects to the CATHODE (short leg, flat side) of one LED.
- Pin 9 is GND - connect to Arduino GND and the breadboard ground rail.
- Pin 10 is COM - connect to the breadboard +5V rail (this is the "load supply").

For each LED:

- Anode (long leg) -> one end of a 220R resistor
- Other end of the 220R -> the breadboard +5V rail
- Cathode (short leg, flat side) -> ULN2803 output pin (OUT1 for LED1, OUT2 for LED2, etc.)

Arrange the eight LEDs in a row on the breadboard so the chase is visible as a moving dot.

Power rails: Arduino 5V -> breadboard red rail. Arduino GND -> breadboard blue rail. ULN2803 pin 9 to blue rail, pin 10 to red rail.

When the Arduino sets D2 HIGH, the ULN2803 pulls OUT1 to ground - current flows from +5V through the resistor, through the LED, through the chip to ground. LED on. When D2 goes LOW, the chip opens the circuit. LED off. Same for the other seven.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno.
2. Install the Arduino IDE and open it once so it finishes setting itself up.
3. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**.
4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. The `pinMode`, `digitalWrite`, and `delay` functions are all built in.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the big square-ish printer-style plug goes into the Uno). You should see a little green LED on the Uno light up.
2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM*** on Windows, or **/dev/cu.usbmodem*** on a Mac, or **/dev/ttyACM0** on Linux. If you see more than one, unplug the Uno, look again, plug it back in, and grab the one that just reappeared - that is the Uno.
3. Open the sketch in the IDE. Nothing to edit - there are no passwords or placeholders in this one. (If you want to change the chase speed later, find `STEP_MS = 80` near the top and try `30` for blazing fast or `200` for lazy.)
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, second from the left at the top). The bottom of the IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Uploading...". The two tiny LEDs on the Uno labeled **TX** and **RX** will flicker while the code transfers.
5. When the bottom of the IDE says "Done uploading", look at the breadboard. The dot should already be bouncing left -> right -> left across the eight LEDs. There is no Serial Monitor needed for this project - the LEDs themselves are the output.

**You know it worked when** the lit LED slides smoothly from one end of the row to the other, bounces off the end, and slides back. If only one LED ever lights up and never moves, see the gotchas below.

**Common gotchas:**

- **An LED is dark and never lights up.** It is probably in backwards. LEDs only work one way. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees so the long leg (anode) is on the +5V/resistor side and the short leg (flat side, cathode) is on the ULN2803 output side, push it back in. No damage done - LEDs just refuse to light when reversed.
- **The dot jumps over a gap (LED 3 stays dark while the others chase).** That LED's wire is in the wrong row on the breadboard. Trace from Arduino D4 -> ULN2803 IN3 (pin 3) -> ULN2803 OUT3 (pin 16) -> LED 3's short leg. One of those four hops is in the wrong hole.
- **All eight LEDs are off, nothing happens.** Either the ULN2803 is upside down (the little notch or dot must point toward pin 1, which is the IN1 side wired to Arduino D2), or pin 9 (GND) and pin 10 (+5V COM) are swapped. Swapping those two will not blow the chip up immediately, but nothing will light. Double-check: pin 9 to the blue rail, pin 10 to the red rail.
## Talking points

- The whole point of the ULN2803 is replacement of eight separate transistor circuits. If you wanted to drive eight LEDs with discrete BC547s, you would need 8 transistors plus 8 base resistors - sixteen extra parts and a maze of wires. Here it is one chip.
- "Darlington" means two transistors in a row inside the chip, which gives huge current gain - a tiny 5V signal from the Arduino can switch loads up to 500 mA per channel.
- The chip is a SINK driver, not a source driver. It pulls outputs DOWN to ground, it does not push UP to +5V. That is why the LED anodes go to +5V and the cathodes go to the chip. This is "current sinking" or "low-side switching" and it is the most common way driver ICs work.
- Pin 10 (COM) has internal flyback diodes built in. We do not need them for LEDs, but they exist so the same chip can drive relays and motors without exploding from coil kickback. Free feature.
- The "Knight Rider" scan pattern - dot moves left, then right, then left - is one of the first 80s TV special effects done with simple electronics. Same trick was used for the actual car prop, just with more LEDs.

## Things to change once it works

- Change the scan speed. Lower `STEP_MS` from 80 to 30 - lightning fast. Raise to 200 - lazy bouncing ball.
- Add a fade trail. Instead of just on/off, PWM the LEDs so the previously-lit ones glow dimly for a frame or two. (The Uno only has 6 PWM pins, so this needs software PWM - good intermediate challenge.)
- Swap to a different pattern: all-on/all-off blink, alternating odd/even, random sparkle.
- Build the same circuit with eight discrete BC547 transistors instead of the ULN2803 to feel why driver ICs were invented.
- Drive a real load. The ULN2803 can handle ~500 mA per channel - swap LEDs for small 5V relays, small DC motors, or solenoids (one per channel) and you have an 8-output controller.

## Why this is interesting

This is the "one chip swallows eight transistors" moment. You wire it once and suddenly your breadboard is uncluttered, your code is clean, and the same circuit pattern scales to relays, motors, stepper coils, and segment displays. The ULN2803 is one of those parts that has been in continuous production since 1980 because nothing replaced its sweet spot: lots of cheap medium-current low-side switches in one DIP package. Knowing how to use it unlocks a huge category of projects with almost no effort.

projects.name: PC817 Optoisolated Relay Trigger Board
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered from USB; load-side 5V tapped from the ESP32 Vin rail for the first build (shared ground, no real isolation yet - cut later for a separate brick).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Tell the ESP32 to flip a tiny switch, and CLICK - a real relay snaps shut and a green LED lights up. You hear the click, you see the light, and the chip in the middle controls it all without ever touching the LED's wires.

**Why it's fun**: That click sound is the same one in dishwashers, garage doors, and old arcade machines - now you can make it happen on command. Even cooler: the two halves of the circuit never touch each other, they only talk through a flash of invisible light inside a little black chip.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the controller side - 3.3V logic)
- PC817 optocoupler (the isolation barrier - an LED facing a phototransistor in a 4-pin DIP)
- BC337 NPN BJT in TO-92 (the muscle that switches the relay-module input)
- 1-channel Relay Module (active-LOW; we treat it as the "load" stage)
- 1K resistor (limits current into the PC817 input LED)
- 10K resistor (base pull-down so the BC337 stays off when the opto is dark)
- 330R resistor + green 5mm LED (a visible "load" the relay switches so you can see the result)
- Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumper wires

## Wiring notes

The whole point of this board is that there are two electrical "sides" that should not share copper. **In the first build they DO share copper** - we cheat and power both sides off the ESP32's USB rail so you only need one cable. That means this initial build is a wiring exercise, not a real isolation demo. The PC817 is sitting in the signal path ready to do its job; "Things to change once it works" walks you through cutting the one jumper that makes the isolation real.

- **Controller side (left):** ESP32 GPIO 23 -> 1K resistor -> PC817 pin 1 (LED anode). PC817 pin 2 (LED cathode) -> ESP32 GND. That is all the MCU sees.
- **Load side (right):** PC817 pin 4 (collector) ties to the load-side +5V rail. PC817 pin 3 (emitter) drives the BC337 base **directly** (no series resistor), with a 10K from base to load-side GND as a pull-down. BC337 emitter sits on load-side GND. BC337 collector ties to the relay module's IN pin. The relay module's VCC and GND go to the load-side +5V and GND. The relay then switches COM/NO into a 330R + green LED loop.

**Why no series base resistor?** The PC817's phototransistor is already current-limited - it can only deliver as much collector current as its CTR (current transfer ratio) lets through for the input LED current we're using. Stacking a 10K series resistor in front of the BC337 base would form a divider with the 10K pull-down and cut available base drive roughly in half. At 2.1 mA forward current through the PC817 LED (3.3V GPIO minus the LED's ~1.2V Vf, divided by 1K), the phototransistor's output is on the low end of its CTR curve, so we want every milliamp of base drive reaching the BC337. Direct emitter-to-base, with only the 10K pull-down for safety, is the cleaner topology.

The 10K base pull-down is the safety belt: if the phototransistor is dark, the BC337 base must be at a clean GND. Without it, the base floats and ambient light leaking into the PC817 (or even capacitive coupling) can twitch the relay.

The relay module is active-LOW. BC337 saturated pulls IN close to load-side GND, which the module reads as "energize". When the opto is dark, BC337 is off, IN floats high through the module's own onboard pull-up, and the relay sits open.

**Note on the relay module:** most off-the-shelf 1-channel relay modules already contain their own onboard PC817 (or similar) on the IN pin. Adding our own discrete PC817 + BC337 in front of it gives "double isolation" that the project does not strictly need. We are doing it anyway because the whole point is to **build the topology by hand** instead of trusting a hidden chip on someone else's PCB - you cannot probe what you cannot see.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste:
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`
   then click OK.
2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Type "esp32" in the search box and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". It is a big download, so go grab a snack.
3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> "NodeMCU-32S". (If you do not see it, scroll - the list is long.)
4. No extra libraries are needed for this sketch. It only uses the built-in Arduino functions (`pinMode`, `digitalWrite`, `Serial`, `delay`).

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S into your laptop with a **USB micro-B data cable** (the same shape as old phone chargers). Make sure it is a data cable, not a charge-only one - if your laptop does not see the board at all, that is the first thing to swap.
2. Tools -> Port -> pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on Mac it is `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`.
3. No passwords or placeholders in this sketch - nothing to fill in. Just open the `.ino` file.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). You will see "Connecting....." dots scroll in the bottom panel. If the dots keep going for more than about 10 seconds, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until the upload starts, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-reset and you will not need this, but the first flash on a new board sometimes needs the nudge.)
5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." and a green "Done uploading" bar, the code is on the chip.
6. Tools -> Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of that window to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). You should immediately see:

   ```
   PC817 Optoisolated Relay Trigger - boot
   Toggling GPIO 23 every 2 seconds.
   Listen for the relay click. Watch the green LED.
   OPTO ON  -> relay CLOSED (LED should be lit)
   OPTO OFF -> relay OPEN   (LED should be dark)
   OPTO ON  -> relay CLOSED (LED should be lit)
   ...
   ```

   At the same time you should hear a soft **click... click... click...** from the relay module every 2 seconds, and the green LED should flash on and off in time with the clicks. That is the moment it all comes together: the chip is talking, the relay is snapping, the LED is winking. High-five your dad.

**Common gotchas:**

- **No COM port shows up when you plug the board in.** Nine times out of ten this is a charge-only USB cable. Swap it for one you know carries data (try the cable that came with a phone, not the one that came with a battery pack). On Windows you may also need the CP210x or CH340 USB-serial driver - the Arduino IDE will usually warn you if it is missing.
- **"Connecting....._____....._____" forever during Upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down while clicking Upload, and let go once you see the percentage start counting up. The board is just stubborn about entering flash mode on the first try.
- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `?@@?N??$??`.** The baud rate in the Serial Monitor window does not match the code. Click the dropdown in the bottom-right corner and pick **115200**.
- **You hear the click but the green LED never lights (or it stays lit all the time).** The LED is probably in backwards - it only lights one way around. Flip it 180 degrees in the breadboard (long leg = anode = the 330R side, short leg = cathode = GND side). No damage, just no glow until you flip it.
## Talking points

- A PC817 is just an LED pointed at a phototransistor inside a black 4-pin package. There is no wire between them - the only connection is light. That is what "galvanic" means: no shared metal.
- This matters because the load side can be at a totally different voltage, polarity, or ground reference, and nothing bad can flow back into the ESP32.
- The BC337 is here because the PC817 phototransistor, at the low LED current we are driving (2.1 mA), is operating well below its rated test point (typically 5 mA) - so the available collector current is modest, maybe a few mA. The BC337 amplifies that into the tens of mA the relay module's IN pin can pull cleanly. (The PC817 phototransistor's absolute max collector current is 50 mA, so the part is not the limit - the operating point is.)
- Three switching stages in series: MCU pin (small signal) -> PC817 LED + phototransistor (isolated signal) -> BC337 (boosted signal) -> relay coil (mechanical contact). Each stage takes a weaker signal and produces a stronger one with the right characteristics for the next stage.
- The "active-LOW" relay quirk is worth pointing out: counterintuitively, the BC337 turning ON makes the relay's IN pin go LOW, and LOW is what the module wants to energize. Trace it carefully so you do not get inverted logic in software.

## Things to change once it works

1. **Make the isolation real.** Right now the load-side +5V rail comes from the ESP32's Vin (USB 5V) pin, so both grounds are tied together and there is no actual isolation - the PC817 is just relaying a signal. Cut that single jumper between ESP32 Vin and the load-side +5V rail, and feed the load side from a separate USB charger or bench supply. The green LED keeps blinking. The ESP32 still drives it. But now there is no copper path between the two sides - that is the entire reason this circuit exists.
2. **Drive a real load.** Replace the green LED + 330R with a 12V DC fan or LED strip wired through COM/NO. (Keep the load-side supply matched to the load, and remember the relay rating is for DC switching here - no mains AC.)
3. **Tune the LED current.** At 3.3V GPIO and a 1.2V LED drop inside the PC817, 1K gives about 2.1 mA forward current. That is on the low end of the PC817's useful range - if turn-on feels sluggish or unreliable with a particular part, drop the resistor to 470R for ~4.5 mA and you will get crisper transitions. (The PC817 LED can take 50 mA absolute max, so there is plenty of headroom.)
4. **Add a freewheel diode if you wire a coil directly.** The relay module already has one onboard, but if you ever drive a bare relay coil with the BC337 collector, you need a 1N4007 across the coil cathode-to-collector or the BC337 will die from coil kickback.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project in the kit where you can honestly say "the microcontroller and the load do not share any copper" - once you cut the jumper in step 1, anyway. That is the principle behind every safe mains-switching board, every industrial PLC input, and every USB-isolator dongle. The schematic is small, but the idea scales: every time you see a black 4-pin IC near a relay or a SCR or an SSR, that is an optocoupler doing exactly what this circuit does. Building it from discrete parts - rather than just buying a pre-made isolated relay board and trusting the chip you cannot probe - means you can see each stage, measure it, and break it. That is the fastest way to internalize why the topology exists at all.
