projects.name: BC327 High-Side Load Switch for the Laser
projects.power_supply: USB-C into the XIAO ESP32-C3; the board's 5 V rail powers the laser and the 3.3 V GPIO drives the BC547 inverter.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Type a command on your laptop and a real red laser beam clicks on. Type another and it clicks off. Wave your hand through it in a dusty room and you can see the line cutting through the air.

**Why it's fun**: It is your first actual laser, and YOU are the switch. Stick it in a cardboard box with a mirror and you have the start of a spy-movie tripwire for your bedroom door.

## Parts list

- Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (3.3 V GPIO control signal)
- BC327 PNP BJT in TO-92 (high-side pass transistor for the 5 V rail)
- BC547 NPN BJT in TO-92 (small inverter that pulls the BC327 base down)
- KY-008 red laser module (the load being switched)
- 1x 10K resistor (base pull-up keeping BC327 off by default)
- 2x 1K resistor (one for the XIAO -> BC547 base, one for BC547 collector -> BC327 base)
- Breadboard, jumper wires (USB cable powers everything off the XIAO's 5 V rail)

## Wiring notes

**Pin label sanity check first.** On the XIAO ESP32-C3 silkscreen, the pin printed "D2" is GPIO4 internally (the silk numbering starts at D0=GPIO2, D1=GPIO3, D2=GPIO4, and so on). This project uses the pin physically labelled **D2**, which the sketch refers to as `CTRL_PIN = 4`. Wire to the silk-labelled D2 pin and the code is correct.

**KY-008 pin identification.** Flip your KY-008 over and read the silk. You should see three letters: `S`, `+` (or no label / middle), and `-`. KY-008 clones genuinely disagree about whether the middle pin is VCC, NC, or the cathode. Treat your own module's silk as the ground truth and only connect what is explicitly labelled. The safe routing for this project is: BC327 collector to the **S** pin, GND rail to the **-** pin, and the third pin left **disconnected**. Do not tie the middle pin to +5 V unless your specific module's silk clearly says so - on the clones where S already has a built-in current-limit resistor, paralleling another +5 V into a mislabelled middle pin will bypass the limiter and burn the laser diode.

The whole point of the circuit is to switch power on the *high side* of the load (between +5 V and the laser) rather than the low side (between the laser and GND). Low-side switching with an NPN works, but it lifts the laser's ground above true GND while it's off, which makes shared-ground setups misbehave. High-side switching keeps the laser's GND tied solidly to system GND at all times.

A PNP transistor (BC327) turns ON when its base is pulled *below* its emitter. The emitter sits at +5 V. To turn it on, you have to pull the base down to roughly +4.3 V or lower. A 3.3 V ESP32 GPIO going HIGH cannot do that directly: HIGH is already 1.7 V below +5 V, but it can't sink current from a 5 V rail through the base on its own without back-feeding the GPIO protection diodes. So we use a small NPN (BC547) as an inverter:

1. XIAO 5V pin -> breadboard +5V rail. XIAO GND -> GND rail.
2. XIAO D2 (GPIO4) -> 1K -> BC547 base. BC547 emitter -> GND. (Classic NPN low-side switch driving the base of the PNP.)
3. BC547 collector -> 1K -> BC327 base. This 1K limits base current when the NPN saturates and pulls the PNP base near GND.
4. 10K from BC327 base to +5V. This is the default-off pull-up: with the GPIO low and the BC547 off, the 10K holds the BC327 base at +5 V, so V_BE = 0 and the PNP stays off.
5. BC327 emitter -> +5V. BC327 collector -> KY-008 S pin. KY-008 - pin -> GND.

**Boot-safety: who actually keeps the laser off when the board powers up?** The hero here is the **10K base pull-up**. The instant the XIAO is plugged in, GPIO4 is a high-impedance input (it's not driving anything), but the 10K is already holding the BC327 base at +5 V, so the laser is guaranteed off. The `digitalWrite(CTRL_PIN, LOW)` call *before* `pinMode(CTRL_PIN, OUTPUT)` is a complementary trick that makes the GPIO's very first driven state a clean LOW (no momentary HIGH glitch at the instant the pin flips from input to output). The 10K is the safety net; the digitalWrite-before-pinMode is good hygiene on top.

**BC327 V_EB headroom (worth knowing).** When the BC547 saturates it pulls the BC327 base down to roughly +0.2 V, while the emitter sits at +5 V. That's V_EB ~ 4.8 V against the BC327 datasheet's V_EBO(max) = 5 V. It works fine off USB +5 V (which actually sags closer to 4.8 - 5.1 V at the board), but the margin is thin. If you ever swap in a 5.5 V supply or move to a higher rail, raise the BC547 collector via a small additional series resistor or insert a base-voltage clamp so the BC327 base never sits below ~1 V.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):**

1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste this link: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK.
2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so go grab a snack.
3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the list.
4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. Everything it uses (`Serial`, `digitalWrite`, `pinMode`) is built in.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the XIAO into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (the same kind that charges most newer phones). The little orange LED on the XIAO should light up.
2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new one that appeared when you plugged it in. On Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`; on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyACM0`. If you are not sure which is new, unplug the XIAO, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the one that just showed up.
3. There are no passwords or placeholders to change in this sketch. It runs as-is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow pointing right at the top-left). You will see "Compiling" then "Uploading" at the bottom. The XIAO ESP32-C3 has a built-in USB-serial bridge, so you should NOT have to hold any BOOT button. If it gets stuck on "Connecting...", unplug, plug back in, and click Upload again.
5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, make sure the baud rate dropdown is set to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code).
6. You should see:

   ```
   BC327 high-side switch demo
   HIGH on D2/GPIO4 = laser ON, LOW = laser OFF
   ON  (1 s)
   OFF (1 s)
   ```

   And at the same time, the **red laser dot** on the KY-008 should be blinking on and off, once per second. Point it at a piece of white paper on the bench (NOT at anyone's face, and NOT at the cat). If the room is a little dusty you can wave your hand near the module and see the red line cutting through the air for a split second.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Laser stays on forever, no blinking.** You almost certainly wired the BC327 base directly to GPIO4 instead of going through the BC547 inverter. Without the inverter, the base is never pulled down to "off", so the PNP stays on. Double-check that the BC547 collector (not the GPIO) is what feeds the 1K resistor going into the BC327 base.
- **Laser stays off forever, even with serial showing "ON".** Check the BC327 orientation. TO-92 transistors are easy to flip 180 degrees on the breadboard. With the flat side facing you and legs pointing down, the BC327 pinout is **Emitter - Collector - Base** (left to right). The BC547 is the opposite: **Collector - Base - Emitter**. Mixing them up is the #1 cause of "circuit does nothing".
- **Upload fails with "Failed to connect" or "No serial port".** Some USB-C cables are charge-only and have no data wires. Try a different cable (the one that came with your phone is usually fine). Also make sure you picked the right port under Tools -> Port - if no new port appears when you plug the XIAO in, that is the cable's fault, not the board's.
## Talking points

- High-side vs low-side switching: where in the load loop you put the switch matters. Mains-AC light switches are high-side for a reason - the lamp socket and bulb threads stay at neutral when the switch is off, which is the safe state.
- PNP turn-on: V_BE for a PNP is positive when the emitter is more positive than the base. "Pull the base down to turn it on" is the mental model.
- Why two transistors instead of one MOSFET: a logic-level P-channel MOSFET would do the same job in one part, but BJTs are cheap, forgiving of static, and the two-transistor pattern shows up everywhere (motor drivers, totem-pole outputs, level shifters). Worth seeing once.
- Default-off pull-up: the 10 K is doing real work. Without it, the BC327 base would float when the BC547 is off, and the laser would do whatever it felt like at boot and on every reset.

## Things to change once it works

- Replace the BC327 with an AO3401 or IRLML6402 P-channel MOSFET on a SOT-23 breakout. The 10 K stays the same; the 1 K from BC547 collector becomes optional. You'll see the laser turn on more crisply because the MOSFET has no V_BE drop.
- Drive the GPIO with `analogWrite()` / LEDC PWM and dim the laser. The switch is fast enough for kHz PWM.
- Add a 100 nF ceramic cap right at the KY-008 power pins to swallow switching noise (useful when you later switch something inductive like a small motor instead of a laser).
- Move the load to a separate 5 V wall supply, keep grounds tied together, and watch the same circuit work unchanged - that's the high-side switch's superpower.

## Why this is interesting

Every beginner trips over one of two things: "my LED is on when it should be off" (because they wired an NPN low-side switch and forgot the load floats high when off) or "my PNP won't turn on" (because they tied the base to a 3.3 V GPIO and expected it to behave like an NPN). This project makes both problems visible in one cheap circuit, and the two-BJT inverter pattern is the same shape you'll find inside half-bridge drivers, level shifters, and totem-pole logic outputs.

projects.name: ULN2003 Servo Sweep Sentinel
projects.power_supply: Two separate USB 5V supplies sharing only GND: USB-to-Uno feeds the logic, LEDs, ULN2003 and PIR; a second USB-C into a TP4056 board feeds the SG90 servo so its current spikes cannot brown out the Uno.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Walk past it and a little flag on a stick swings back and forth while a row of five red lights pulses like a warning sign. Stand still and everything goes quiet again, waiting for the next person to wander by.

**Why it's fun**: Hide it around a corner and prank your sister when she walks past. It is your very own motion-triggered alarm, like the ones in spy movies, except you built it.

## Parts list

- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone, XL) - the 5V brain
- 1x ULN2003AN Darlington Array (7-ch) - the muscle that sinks current for the LED row
- 1x HC-SR501 PIR Motion Sensor - the trigger
- 1x SG90 Servo (9g micro) - waves the warning flag, on its OWN 5V supply
- 5x LED 5mm Red - the "warning bank"
- 5x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - one current limiter per LED (see math in Talking points)
- 1x 470uF and 1x 100uF electrolytic - bulk reservoir on the servo rail, local decoupling on the ULN2003
- 1x TP4056 USB-C charger/protection board - second, independent 5V source for the servo
- 1x Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumpers

## Wiring notes

**Two power rails, one ground.** This is the single most important idea in the build.

- *Rail A (Uno rail):* USB feeds the Uno, the Uno's `5V` pin feeds the breadboard's left `+5V` rail. That rail powers the LEDs, the ULN2003 (`COM` pin 9), and the HC-SR501.
- *Rail B (Servo rail):* A second USB-C cable goes into the TP4056 board; its `OUT+` becomes the breadboard's right `+5V` rail. The SG90's red wire is the ONLY thing on that rail.
- *Grounds:* The Uno's `GND`, the TP4056's `OUT-`, the PIR's GND, the LED cathodes' return path through the ULN2003 `GND` pin (8), and the SG90's brown wire ALL meet at the breadboard's shared `GND` rail. Without this common ground the servo signal makes no sense to the Uno.

Why bother? The SG90 yanks 600-700 mA when it stalls or changes direction, and the Uno's onboard 5V LDO can only deliver ~500-800 mA total. Sharing the rail will brown out the Uno - the 470 uF cap from the original draft just delays the moment of failure. Splitting the rails fixes it for real, and the optocouplers... wait, no, the ULN2003 has no opto stage; the *split rails* are what isolates the noise here.

**ULN2003 pinout (16-pin DIP):**
- Pins 1..7 = inputs IN1..IN7
- Pin 8 = GND
- Pin 9 = COM (tie to the Uno's +5V rail - this is the return path for the internal flyback diodes)
- Pins 10..16 = outputs OUT7..OUT1 (mirror image of the inputs)

**Connections:**
- Uno `D7` -> ULN2003 IN1, IN2, IN3, IN4, IN5 all tied together (one GPIO drives five channels in parallel - the whole point of the project)
- LED anodes -> Uno's `+5V` rail through a 220R each
- LED cathodes -> ULN2003 OUT1..OUT5 (pins 16, 15, 14, 13, 12)
- ULN2003 pin 8 (GND) -> shared GND rail
- ULN2003 pin 9 (COM) -> Uno's `+5V` rail
- 100 uF cap across the Uno's `+5V`/GND right next to the ULN2003
- HC-SR501: VCC -> Uno's `+5V`, GND -> shared GND, OUT -> Uno `D2`
- SG90: red -> TP4056's `+5V`, brown -> shared GND, orange -> Uno `D9` (PWM-capable)
- 470 uF cap across the TP4056's `+5V`/GND right next to the servo header

**Electrolytic polarity - DO NOT SKIP.** Both caps are polarised. The *longer* lead (and the side without the white stripe) is `+` and goes to the +5V rail. The *shorter* lead (white stripe) is `-` and goes to GND. Backwards-installed electrolytics get hot, leak, and occasionally pop loudly. If you're not sure which lead is which, look for the printed stripe down one side of the can.

**HC-SR501 jumper.** Set its onboard jumper to **repeat-trigger (H)** mode. In this mode `DOUT` stays HIGH for the whole time motion is being seen, so the sketch's `lastMotionAt` keeps refreshing naturally. The code also works in single-trigger (L) mode, just feels slightly twitchier - the `ALARM_HOLD_MS` window bridges the gaps between pulses. The two pots: time delay fully anticlockwise (shortest), sensitivity around mid-travel.


## Flash it and run it

You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)).

**One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):**

1. Open the Arduino IDE. Go to Tools -> Board -> "Arduino AVR Boards" -> **Arduino Uno**.
2. The Servo library is already built into the IDE, so there is nothing extra to install. Nice.
3. The board is a CH340 clone, so if your laptop says "unknown device" when you plug it in, you need the CH340 driver once. Search "CH340 driver" + your operating system, install it, and reboot. After that the Uno shows up as a normal COM port forever.

**Every time you flash:**

1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a USB-A-to-USB-B cable (the big square-ish plug, the same kind old printers used). Do NOT plug in the TP4056 servo supply yet - we want the servo quiet while we upload.
2. In the IDE, go to Tools -> Port and pick the one that just appeared (Windows: something like `COM4`, Mac: `cu.usbmodem...`, Linux: `/dev/ttyACM0` or `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If you are not sure which one it is, unplug the Uno, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the new one.
3. Open the sketch file. There is nothing to fill in - no WiFi password, no secret keys. Just leave it as is.
4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). The little TX and RX lights on the Uno will flicker for a few seconds. When the bottom of the IDE says "Done uploading.", you are good.
5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (this has to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code, or you just see garbage).
6. You should see: `ULN2003 Servo Sweep Sentinel ready.` then `Warming up PIR for 30 seconds...`. Wait. After 30 seconds you get `Armed.` - now plug in the TP4056 USB-C cable so the servo wakes up. Wave your hand in front of the white dome of the PIR. The five red LEDs should snap on and the servo should start sweeping the flag back and forth. Stand still for 5 seconds and everything goes quiet again.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `@?xJ??`** - your baud rate is wrong. Set it to 115200 in the bottom-right corner of the Serial Monitor.
- **PIR fires non-stop the moment it powers up** - that is normal for the first 30-60 seconds while the sensor warms up. The code already waits 30 seconds before arming; just don't wave at it during the warm-up.
- **LEDs stay dark even though the Serial Monitor says "Armed."** - check the LED direction. The long leg (anode) goes to +5V through the 220R resistor; the short leg (cathode) goes to the ULN2003 output pin. Backwards LEDs don't break, they just don't light. Also double-check that pin 9 of the ULN2003 (COM) is wired to +5V - without it the internal flyback diodes have no return path and the chip won't sink current properly.
## Talking points

- **Why a Darlington array at all?** A single Uno pin is only spec'd for 20 mA continuous (40 mA absolute max). Five LEDs at ~9 mA each is ~45 mA - over budget for one pin. The ULN2003 lets the Uno *say* "on" with a tiny logic-level signal while seven internal Darlington pairs do the actual current-sinking work. Each output can sink up to 500 mA, but the package's total dissipation limits the sum to roughly 230 mA sustained at room temp - which is still plenty for a 45 mA LED bank.
- **It is a sink driver, not an "inverter".** When `D7` goes HIGH, an NPN Darlington inside the chip turns on and *pulls its output pin down toward GND*. Current then flows from +5V -> 220R -> LED -> output pin -> GND. There's no logic inversion happening - the input directly enables the sink transistor. That's why every LED's *anode* faces +5V: the chip can only pull down, never push up.
- **Why 220R and not 330R?** Do the loop math. Red LED forward drop ~2.0 V, ULN2003 Vce(sat) at this current ~1.0 V, supply 5.0 V. That leaves (5 - 2 - 1) = 2.0 V across the resistor. At 220R that's ~9 mA per LED, nice and bright. At 330R it would be ~6 mA - dim. People copy 330R off Uno-direct-drive tutorials without accounting for the chip's Vce(sat); now you won't.
- **Why two separate 5V supplies?** Because the SG90's stall current (600-700 mA) is larger than the Uno's onboard LDO can deliver (~500 mA from USB). Without splitting, every direction change browns out the Uno: the PIR false-triggers, the serial output cuts, the LED bank flickers. The 470 uF cap is a buffer, not a fix.
- **Rollover-safe timing.** Notice the sketch stores `lastMotionAt = millis()` and compares with `(now - lastMotionAt) >= ALARM_HOLD_MS`. The naive `alarmUntil = millis() + HOLD; if (millis() < alarmUntil)` pattern breaks once every 49.7 days when `millis()` wraps. Unsigned subtraction wraps too, but it gives the correct elapsed time anyway. Learn it once, use it forever.
- **The PIR's 30 second warmup is real.** The pyroelectric element is genuinely settling. The sketch sits in `delay(30000)` exactly once at boot - the one place a blocking delay is actually fine.

## Things to change once it works

- Use the spare ULN2003 channels (IN6, IN7) for a buzzer or small DC motor "siren".
- Split the LED bank into two groups on `D7` and `D8` and alternate them for a "police light" effect.
- Replace the PIR with the HC-SR04 ultrasonic and trigger only when something is within, say, 50 cm.
- Add an LCD 1602 to show "INTRUDER" and a counter of how many times today.
- Try collapsing back to a single supply *with* a proper bench PSU (not USB) to see at what current rating the brownout finally stops. Useful intuition for future designs.

## Why this is interesting

Most beginner ULN2003 demos do the *Knight Rider* sequential chase - one channel at a time, 7 channels, one LED at a time. This one inverts that lesson: one logic input fans out to five channels in parallel, deliberately showing that the chip's job is *current capacity*, not channel count. Bolting a PIR and a sweeping servo onto the same array turns a static demo into a complete sense-decide-act loop, and the two-supplies-one-ground architecture is the same trick you'll use on every real project that mixes a logic board with a noisy actuator (motors, solenoids, big LED strips, mains relays). Get this pattern into muscle memory now and you'll save yourself hours of "why does my Uno keep resetting?" debugging later.

projects.name: NE555 Two-Tone Police Siren
projects.power_supply: 9V battery (or 9V bench supply) into the breadboard + rail; one shared rail powers both NE555s and the LM386, with a 100uF bulk cap right next to the chips to keep the amplifier from upsetting the timers.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Flip the switch and a tiny speaker on your breadboard wails "wee-ooo, wee-ooo" exactly like a police car driving by. A red LED blinks in time with the sound, so you can see the siren as well as hear it.

**Why it's fun**: You built a real siren out of a handful of parts and zero code. Hide it in a shoebox, sneak up behind your sister, flip the switch, and watch her jump.

## Required external parts (you supply)

- **8 ohm speaker, 0.5-1 W**. Any salvaged small speaker works. Not in the kit - this is a hard prerequisite. Without it the project does not finish.
- **9V power source.** Either a fresh 9V battery + barrel/snap clip wired to the breadboard rails, or a 9V bench supply.

## Parts list (from inventory)

- 2x NE555 Timer IC (U1 = slow sweep oscillator, U2 = fast audio oscillator)
- 1x LM386 Audio Power Amp (U3 = drives the speaker)
- 4x 10K resistors (R1/R2 timing pair for U1, R5 modulation series, R6 LM386 input series)
- 3x 470R resistors (R3/R4 timing pair for U2, R_LED current-limit for the sweep-indicator LED)
- 1x 22uF electrolytic (C1, slow timing cap)
- 2x 10uF electrolytic (C2 modulation coupling, C3 LM386 input coupling)
- 3x 100uF electrolytic (C4 rail decoupling, C5 LM386 output coupling, C6 LM386 pin-7 bypass)
- 1x 1uF 50V electrolytic (C7 fast 555 timing cap)
- 1x 5mm red LED (visual sweep indicator - so you can SEE the woop-woop)
- 1x 400-point breadboard
- M-M jumper wires

## The math (so you can trust the parts choice)

NE555 astable frequency: **f = 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)**.

- **U1 slow stage** with R1=R2=10K, C1=22uF: f = 1.44 / (30K * 22uF) approx **2.2 Hz**. That's the "wee-ooo" rate.
- **U2 fast stage** with R3=R4=470R, C7=1uF: f = 1.44 / (1.41K * 1uF) approx **1020 Hz** centre. When U1's square wave is AC-coupled into U2's pin 5 (CV), the comparator thresholds get pushed up and down, sweeping the audio frequency roughly across **500-1500 Hz** - the classic siren range.

The original draft used R3=R4=10K with C7=1uF, which gives only 48 Hz (below the audio band, you'd hear a buzz not a tone). The 470R choice is the fix.

## Wiring notes

The whole circuit lives on one breadboard and runs from a single +9V rail. There is no microcontroller - the two NE555s and the LM386 do everything in pure analog hardware. This is the same trick used in real toy sirens.

**U1 - the slow modulator (~2.2 Hz):**
- pin 1 to GND, pin 8 to +9V
- pin 4 (reset) to +9V
- pin 7 to pin 8 through R1 = 10K
- pin 7 to pin 6 through R2 = 10K
- pin 6 tied to pin 2 (standard astable jumper)
- pin 6/2 to GND through C1 = 22uF (long leg toward pin 6/2, short leg to GND)
- pin 5 (CV) left floating (the kit has no ceramic cap to bypass it; the slow stage doesn't need one)
- pin 3 (output) drives two things in parallel: the red LED via R_LED = 470R to GND (so you can SEE the sweep), AND through C2 = 10uF + R5 = 10K into U2's pin 5

**U2 - the fast audio oscillator (~500-1500 Hz, swept):**
- pin 1 to GND, pin 8 to +9V, pin 4 to +9V
- pin 7 to +9V through R3 = 470R
- pin 7 to pin 6 through R4 = 470R
- pin 6 tied to pin 2
- pin 6/2 to GND through C7 = 1uF (this is what sets audio frequency)
- pin 5 (CV) receives the modulation signal from U1 via C2 + R5. R5 is there as a series limiter so the modulation doesn't slam pin 5 all the way to the rails - it sets the sweep DEPTH (smaller R5 = wider sweep)
- pin 3 (output) is the raw siren waveform - feed it through C3 = 10uF straight into the LM386 input

**C2 polarity** matters here. U1 pin 3 (the cap's "in" side) swings between 0 V and ~8 V, average ~4 V. The CV side of R5 sits at ~6 V (2/3 of 9 V). So the U1 side is, on average, the LOWER-DC side. Put the **negative** (short) leg of C2 toward U1 pin 3 and the **positive** (long) leg toward R5. If you find yourself second-guessing this, a non-polar workaround is two 22uF electrolytics back-to-back negative-to-negative - but a single 10uF oriented as above is fine.

**U3 - the LM386 amplifier:**
- pin 2 (-IN) to GND
- pin 3 (+IN) receives the audio through C3 = 10uF and R6 = 10K series (R6 sets input impedance and slightly attenuates - the LM386 already has internal 50K bias to GND on each input, so no external pull-down is needed)
- pin 4 to GND
- pin 6 to +9V (this is the supply pin - getting 4 and 6 swapped instantly destroys the chip, double-check)
- pin 7 to GND through C6 = 100uF (bypass, kills hiss and "farting")
- pin 5 (output) through C5 = 100uF **directly to the speaker + terminal** (no series resistor - the speaker is the load)
- speaker - terminal to GND

Note: no Zobel network in this build. A real Zobel is R + ceramic cap in series across the speaker, and the kit has no small ceramic caps. The LM386 is happy driving an 8 ohm speaker through just the coupling cap in 99% of hobby builds.

**Power-rail housekeeping:**
- C4 = 100uF across +9V and GND, placed physically close to the 555s. Without this, the LM386 yanking current spikes upsets the timing chips and the siren sounds warbly.


## Flash it and run it

Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives. The siren starts the second power touches it.

**Power-up procedure (do this in order):**

1. **Double-check before you connect the battery.** Look at every electrolytic capacitor (the little black cylinders) and make sure the long leg / "+" stripe goes where the wiring notes said it goes. Backwards electrolytics can pop. Take 30 seconds, it is worth it.
2. **Make sure the speaker is wired in.** One wire to TP7 (after C5), the other to GND. Polarity does not matter on the speaker.
3. **Snap the 9V battery into the clip** (or turn on the bench supply set to 9V). The red LED next to U1 pin 3 should immediately start blinking about twice a second - that is the "wee" rate.
4. **Listen.** You should hear "wee-ooo, wee-ooo" from the speaker right away. The LED blink and the pitch sweep should be in lockstep: LED on = pitch up, LED off = pitch down (or the other way round, depending on which side of C2 you wired).
5. **If it is silent or sounds wrong**, do not start yanking wires. Grab the multimeter and walk through STEP 1 -> STEP 5 in the code/test-procedure section above. Each test point (TP1 through TP7) tells you exactly which stage is broken.

**Common gotchas:**

- **Electrolytic capacitor backwards.** C1 (22uF), C2 (10uF), and C7 (1uF) are the easy ones to flip. Long leg = "+". If the siren is dead silent and TP3 (the slow 555 output) is not blinking, suspect C1 first.
- **Used 10K instead of 470R for R3/R4.** The fast 555 needs the 470R pair to land in the audio band (~1 kHz). With 10K + 1uF you get ~48 Hz, which is below what your ear hears as a tone - it will sound like a faint click-click-click instead of "wee-ooo". Pull R3 and R4 and check the colour bands: 470R is yellow-violet-black-black-brown, 10K is brown-black-black-red-brown.
- **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no blink. Flip it. Long leg goes toward U1 pin 3 (through R_LED = 470R), short leg to GND.
## Talking points

- A 555 in astable mode is just a capacitor charging through resistors, with a comparator that flips the output whenever the cap crosses 1/3 or 2/3 of the supply. Change R or C, change the frequency. **f = 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)** - that's literally the entire 555 design equation.
- The magic is **pin 5, the Control Voltage pin**. Normally it just sits at 2/3 of supply doing nothing. But if you wiggle the voltage on pin 5, you wiggle those comparator thresholds, which wiggles how long the cap takes to charge, which wiggles the output frequency. That is frequency modulation, in one pin.
- U1 cranks out a slow 2.2 Hz square wave. We feed that into U2's CV pin via a coupling cap and series resistor. U2 is oscillating at ~1 kHz, and now its frequency is being pushed up and down twice a second. Your ear hears "wee-ooo wee-ooo".
- R5 is a sweep-depth knob in disguise. The 555's pin 5 has an internal 5K resistor stack to the rails. R5 in series forms a divider with that stack, which attenuates the modulation depth. 10K gives a moderate sweep; drop R5 to 4.7K for a deeper sweep, or up to 22K for a subtle warble.
- The LM386 is one of those classic "first amplifier" chips. Internally it's a fixed-gain amp at 20x by default (you can crank it to 200x by adding a 10uF between pins 1 and 8, see "things to change").
- Why electrolytic caps and not ceramic? At 1uF and above, ceramics get expensive and weird. Electrolytics are cheap and ideal for audio coupling and bulk timing. They DO have polarity though - long leg = positive. Backwards electrolytics can fail dramatically; pay attention on C2 and C5 especially.

## Things to change once it works

- **Make it louder:** drop a 10uF between LM386 pins 1 and 8. That changes the gain from 20x to 200x. Be warned, this also amplifies hiss.
- **Deeper sweep:** lower R5 from 10K toward 4.7K or 3.3K. Pin 5 swings harder, pitch sweeps wider.
- **Sweep faster (panic siren):** swap C1 from 22uF down to 4.7uF or 1uF for quicker "woopwoopwoop".
- **Sweep slower (ambulance):** swap C1 up to 47uF or 100uF for a lazy ooooo-eeeeee-ooooo.
- **Change the pitch:** swap C7. 0.47uF (use 4.7uF if that's all you have - inverse direction, gives a lower note) or smaller resistors push it higher; 2.2uF pushes it lower.
- **Press-to-siren toy:** drop a tactile button between U2 pin 4 and +9V, with a 10K from pin 4 to GND. Siren only sounds while the button is held.

## Why this is interesting

This is the project where a beginner suddenly understands what "modulation" means, because you can hear it AND see it (the red LED blinks in time with the pitch sweep). The same idea - one oscillator pushing another oscillator's frequency around - is exactly how every FM synth, every classic sci-fi sound effect, and every radio transmitter works under the hood. You just built one out of two 75-cent timer chips. The LM386 stage also teaches the "tiny signal goes in, big speaker swing comes out" reflex that every audio project needs.

projects.code:
# NE555 Two-Tone Police Siren - Multimeter Test Procedure
#
# This is a pure analog circuit (no microcontroller). Power it from a
# regulated 9V bench supply (or a fresh 9V battery via a snap clip wired
# to the breadboard + rail). Use a multimeter on DC volts for the slow
# stage, then switch to AC volts (or just listen) for the audio stage.
#
# IMPORTANT - PREREQUISITES:
#   - You must supply an 8 ohm speaker (0.5 W - 1 W). Not in the kit.
#   - You must supply a 9V battery + clip, or a 9V bench PSU.
#
# TEST POINTS (label these on the breadboard with tape):
#
#   TP1 = +9V rail
#   TP2 = GND rail
#   TP3 = U1 pin 3 (slow 555 output, ~2.2 Hz square wave)
#   TP4 = U2 pin 5 (control voltage input on fast 555)
#   TP5 = U2 pin 3 (fast 555 audio output, ~1 kHz centre, swept)
#   TP6 = LM386 pin 5 (amplified audio out, BEFORE the 100uF speaker cap;
#         has a ~4.5 V DC offset on single-supply 9V - use TP7 for clean AC)
#   TP7 = speaker + terminal (after C5, no DC offset)
#
# STEP 1 - Power-on sanity:
#   - Set meter to DC volts, 20V range.
#   - Black probe on TP2, red probe on TP1. Expect 8.8 - 9.2 V.
#   - If you see less than 7V the LM386 is probably oscillating into a
#     brownout. Add another 100uF across the rails right at the chip.
#
# STEP 2 - Slow stage alive:
#   - Watch the red LED on TP3. It should blink visibly, about
#     2 flashes per second. That IS the sweep.
#   - Meter on DC volts at TP3 will bounce between ~0V and ~6-7V as the
#     output toggles. The average will sit around 3-4V.
#   - No blink? Check C1 polarity (long leg = +, into pin 6/2 of U1).
#
# STEP 3 - Modulation reaching the fast 555:
#   - Meter on DC volts at TP4 (U2 pin 5, "CV").
#   - You should see the voltage SWING up and down in time with the LED.
#     Roughly 5V to 7V. That swinging CV pin is what bends the audio
#     pitch up and down - that's the "woop-woop".
#   - If TP4 sits dead still at ~6V, C2 is either missing, wrong
#     polarity, or shorted. Reminder: C2 negative leg toward U1 pin 3,
#     positive leg toward R5.
#
# STEP 4 - Audio coming out of the fast 555:
#   - Switch meter to AC volts, 20V range. Probe TP5.
#   - Expect roughly 2 - 3 V AC. (The meter is averaging a square wave,
#     don't worry about the exact number - any reading above ~1V AC
#     means the oscillator is running.)
#   - You should also already faintly HEAR a buzz from the speaker.
#
# STEP 5 - Amplifier doing its job:
#   - For the cleanest AC reading, probe TP7 (after C5). The coupling
#     cap strips the ~4.5 V DC offset that LM386 pin 5 carries on a
#     single 9V supply, so what your meter sees is the actual audio
#     swing into the speaker. Expect 2 - 4 V AC.
#   - If you probe TP6 directly (pin 5), some cheap DMMs read funny
#     because of the DC offset; TP7 is the honest measurement.
#   - If TP5 has signal but TP7 is silent, check that LM386 pin 6 has
#     +9V and pin 4 has GND - swapping those kills the chip instantly.
#
# STEP 6 - The fun test:
#   - Just listen. You should hear a classic two-tone "wee-ooo wee-ooo"
#     police siren around 500-1500 Hz, sweeping twice a second. If it
#     sounds like a steady whistle with no sweep, go back to STEP 3 -
#     the modulation isn't reaching the CV pin.
#
# TROUBLESHOOTING CHEAT SHEET:
#
#   No sound at all          -> check 9V rail (STEP 1), check LM386 pins 4/6
#   Steady tone, no sweep    -> C2 dead, backwards, or open (STEP 3)
#   Sweep too fast           -> increase C1 (try 47uF)
#   Sweep too slow           -> decrease C1 (try 10uF or 4.7uF)
#   Pitch too low / growly   -> decrease C7 OR lower R3/R4 (try 220R)
#   Pitch too shrill         -> increase C7 (try 2.2uF) OR raise R3/R4
#   Distorted / farty audio  -> add/check the 100uF bypass on pin 7 (C6)
#   Sweep too shallow        -> lower R5 (try 4.7K or 3.3K)
#   LM386 gets HOT           -> power off NOW, pins 4 and 6 are swapped
